| **An edge listed in `tables.<name>.nested_mutations.relationships` is not nestable** | Error *(resolution-level — see phase 3 below)* | A listed edge that fails any eligibility rule ([9.9](#99-nested-mutations)) is a hard error naming the edge and the rule it failed — the user asked for it by name. An **auto-included** edge that fails a rule is silently omitted instead, so one ineligible edge cannot break a build that never asked for it. The same rule rejects a listed name that matches no relationship on the table. |
| **Invalid `api.operations` preset** | Error | If `api.operations`, `tables.<table>.api.operations` or `views.<view>.api.operations` is a string, or carries a `preset`, that doesn't match a known preset (`all`, `read_only`, `append_only`, `no_delete`, `no_hard_delete`), it is a validation error. |
| **An `operations` key under `generation` or `tables.<table>`** | Error | The client has no per-operation switch; it generates every method the schema allows ([4.6](#46-generationconfig)). The key is rejected with a message that names its path and points at `api.operations`, the only per-operation control: `generation.operations: the Go client generates every method the schema allows; use api.operations to control what the API exposes`. A plain unknown-field error would not say where the control went. |
| **A client-only key named in an `api.operations` mask** | Error | `get_many`, `update_many`, `exists`, `count`, `increment`, `stream` and `upsert_many` name client methods no API surface calls ([26.5.1](#2651-exposed-resolver-surface)), so naming one in any `api.operations` block is rejected rather than silently ignored. Every mask key names the client method its surface calls. |
| **An `api.operations` key the schema does not allow** | Warning *(resolution-level — see phase 3 below)* | A per-table mask that sets an operation explicitly `true` when the table's client does not generate the method behind it — `soft_delete` or `restore` on a table without a soft-delete column, `upsert` or `upsert_with_related` without any conflict target, or a `…_with_related` key whose family `nested_mutations` does not enable for the table or for which the table has no eligible edge — warns, naming the key and the missing schema fact. It is read off the table's resolved operations, which are exactly the schema-allowed set, so it needs the eligibility rules to have run. The mask is subtractive, so the key is ignored; the warning is what keeps that from being silent. A global mask that over-reaches is silent, since one mask written for a whole schema will legitimately exceed some tables. |
| **`manifest.formats: []` with `enabled: true`** | Error | At least one format must be enabled when the manifest is on. Closed set: `json`, `markdown`. See [30.2](#302-configuration). |
| **Unknown `manifest.formats` value** | Error | Values outside the closed set `{json, markdown}` are rejected in v1. |
| **`manifest.json_layout` not in `single`/`per_entity`** | Error | Closed set in v1. |
| **`manifest.markdown_dir` placement conflict** | Error | Must be a subdirectory of `output.dir`: cannot be `.`, cannot be absolute or escape via `..`, cannot equal an existing PRD §8.3 artifact subdir (e.g. `graph/`), cannot start with `_` (reserved for `_index.md` / `_conventions.md`). |
| **`manifest.json_per_entity_dir` placement conflict** | Error | Must be a subdirectory of `markdown_dir`: cannot equal `markdown_dir` or `.`, cannot be absolute or escape via `..`, cannot start with `_`. |
| **`manifest.json_filename` is not a bare filename** | Error | Names a file inside `markdown_dir`; cannot contain a path separator. |
| **`tables.<name>.manifest.enabled: true` with global `manifest.enabled: false`** | Error | Per-table flag is opt-*out* only. Cannot opt a single entity in without the package-level opt-in. |
| **`manifest.breadcrumbs.*: true` with `manifest.enabled: false`** | Error | Breadcrumbs only make sense when there is a manifest to point at. |
| **`manifest.embed_in_client: true` with `manifest.enabled: false`** | Error | The runtime methods only make sense when a manifest is being emitted to embed. |
| **`manifest.mcp.emit_project_config: true` with `manifest.enabled: false`** | Error | The MCP registration entry points at the emitted manifest; without one there is nothing to serve. See [31.2](#312-configuration). |
| **`manifest.mcp.project_configs` entry absolute or escaping the module root** | Error | Every target must be a module-root-relative path; absolute paths, empty entries, and any `..` segment are rejected. Enforced regardless of the enabled state (the opt-out removal path walks the same targets). See [31.2](#312-configuration). |
| **`column_map.<col>.name` is not a valid exported Go identifier** | Error | The override becomes a generated struct field, so it must be a legal Go identifier starting with an upper-case letter. A PascalCase keyword (`Type`, `Map`) is accepted. See [8.5](#85-naming-rules). |
| **`column_map.<col>.name` on a non-existent or excluded column** | Error | The override must name a real column that survives `exclude_columns` — otherwise there is no field to rename and the entry is a silent no-op. See [8.5](#85-naming-rules). |
| **`column_map.<col>.name` collides with another resolved field name** | Error *(resolution-level — see phase 3 below)* | Two columns, or a column and a relationship, cannot claim the same Go field on the entity struct. Only collisions an override introduces are reported. See [8.5](#85-naming-rules). |
| **A resolved field name is one the generated code already declares** | Error *(resolution-level — see phase 3 below)* | `Columns`, `ColumnMap`, `HasSelectedColumns`, `And`, `Or`, `ToConditions`, `PKs`, `Input` and `Column` are claimed by generated declarations on the structs a column field lands on, each in the shapes listed in [8.5](#85-naming-rules) "Field Name Resolution". Unlike the collision rule above this one is **not** override-gated — the name is rejected wherever it comes from, including a plain SQL column name and a derived relationship field, because no such name can produce compiling code. View columns are covered too. |
| **`column_map.<col>.type` is not a Go type expression** | Error | The override is written verbatim into the generated struct, so it must parse as a type — an identifier, a qualified identifier, or a composition of those (`*T`, `[]T`, `map[K]V`). Whether the named type exists is the compiler's verdict; sqlgen never loads consumer packages. See [7.1](#71-type-resolution-chain). |
| **`column_map.<col>.type` on a non-existent or excluded column** | Error | The override must name a real column that survives `exclude_columns` — otherwise there is no field to retype and the entry is a silent no-op. See [7.1](#71-type-resolution-chain). |
| **`column_map.<col>.import` without `type`** | Error | An import path with nothing to import for. See [7.1](#71-type-resolution-chain). |
| **Package-qualified `column_map.<col>.type` with no `import`** | Error *(resolution-level — see phase 3 below)* | Nothing else would place the package in the generated file's import block. Literals sqlgen already knows (`time.Time`, `json.RawMessage`, …) are exempt — they resolve their own import. See [7.1](#71-type-resolution-chain). |
| **Package-qualified `type_map` value** | Error *(resolution-level — see phase 3 below)* | `type_map` has no `import` field, so the generated file would reference a package nothing imports. Use `column_map.<col>.type` + `.import` for external types. Literals sqlgen already knows are exempt. See [7.1](#71-type-resolution-chain). |
| **Two UUID libraries resolved in one generated package** | Error *(resolution-level — see phase 3 below)* | Every UUID import path resolved across the generated package — global `overrides.types.uuid`, table-scoped `overrides.types`, and `column_map.<col>.import` alike — must be the same one. View columns participate too, through the global binding they resolve under ([4.9](#49-viewconfig-per-view)). All three supported integrations bind the file-local package name `uuid` and export a type named `UUID`, so a package resolving two of them emits source that does not compile, and the resolved Go type string `uuid.UUID` cannot say which package is meant ([7.4](#74-built-in-type-integrations)). The error names both import paths, at least one table that selected each, and the remedy: split them across separate `output.dir` packages. Per generated package, not per module — two packages in one module, each with its own library, are legal. |
| **Invalid `column_map.<col>.access` value** | Error | `access` must be one of `public`, `read_only`, `write_only`, `hidden`, `internal`. Any other value is rejected. See [Section 32](#32-column-access-control). |
| **`access` on a non-existent or excluded column** | Error | `column_map.<col>.access` must name a real column that survives `exclude_columns`. Classifying an excluded column has no surface to act on and is a config error. |
| **`access` on a primary-key column outside `{public, read_only}`** | Error | PK columns must stay API-readable (the GraphQL `id` argument, cursor encoding, and relationship targeting all require it). `write_only`, `hidden`, and `internal` on any PK member is rejected. See [32.4](#324-validation). |
| **`access` removes a required-on-create column from API input** | Error | A NOT NULL column with no default that is neither auto-generated nor PK-generated cannot be given a role that drops it from the API create input (`read_only` / `hidden` / `internal`) **while** the create / createMany API op is enabled — the API could never satisfy the INSERT. (`write_only` is allowed; server-side Go `Create` is unaffected either way.) See [32.4](#324-validation). |
| **`access` removes the filter surface from the soft-delete column** | Warning | Giving the soft-delete column a role that drops its filter (`write_only` / `hidden` / `internal`) removes the §26.5.3 "pass `deletedAt: {}` to include soft-deleted rows" path from the API. Emitted as a warning — it may be intentional. |

Validation runs in three phases:
1. **Config-level** (before parsing) — driver/dialect mismatch, missing connection, invalid `api.operations` presets, a leftover client `operations` key, client-only keys in an `api.operations` mask, duplicate struct names
2. **Schema-level** (after parsing) — cursor_keys existence, soft_delete type mismatch, struct name collisions from auto-detection, exclude_columns exhaustion
3. **Resolution-level** (during generation) — the few rules that need the naming or type engine to have run, and so cannot be answered from the config text alone: the `api.operations` over-reach warning (which reads each table's resolved operations), the resolved-field-name rules (collision and reserved name), whether a declared relationship's target generates at all (which needs `exclude_tables` and the primary-key rule applied, and the target's `struct_name` resolved), the two rules that ask whether a Go type literal needs an explicit import, and the one-UUID-library-per-package rule, which has to collect the import path every column actually resolved to across the whole package before it can count them. They live in the generator rather than in config validation, and the table above marks them — but `sqlgen validate` still reports them: it builds the table, view and API contexts in memory and discards them, so every phase-3 rule is answered at validate time without loading a template or writing a file.

**Cursor key resolution — fallback semantics.** `cursor_keys` resolution is lenient for inherited values and strict for explicit values. The rationale: explicit configuration is a user assertion that must be honored or flagged; an inherited default should degrade gracefully because the global default cannot know every table's schema shape. Partial matches (some columns present, others missing) always trigger a full fallback — never a subset — because a partial cursor would silently change sort semantics. Resolution rules:

1. **Table, inherited, any column missing, PK present** → use table PK (single or composite). No warning.
2. **Table, inherited, any column missing, no PK** → omit `Connection`. Warning.
3. **Table, explicit, any column missing** → error.
4. **View, inherited, any column missing** → omit `Connection`. Warning. (Views have no PK fallback.)
5. **View, explicit, any column missing** → error.

### 4.14 Config JSON Schema (editor support)

A canonical JSON Schema (draft 2020-12) for `sqlgen.yml` ships at
`cmd/sqlgen/config/schema/v1.json` and is embedded into the CLI binary via
`//go:embed`, exposed as `config.SchemaV1()`. It mirrors the manifest schema
precedent ([§30.4](#304-json-schema)): hand-written, embedded, and versioned by
filename.

**Scope.** The schema is an **editor aid, not a second validator**. It covers
structure, key names, value types, and closed value sets (`dialect`, `driver`,
`layout`, `uuid_version`, soft-delete `type`, operations presets, column
`access` roles, GraphQL `field_casing`, scalar `marshaling`, cache
`serializer`, manifest `json_layout`, relationship `type` / `side`). It does not
express sqlgen's cross-field rules — driver/dialect pairing, `connection`
required by `source`, soft-delete column type compatibility, cursor-key
existence, `marshaler_package` required when `marshaling: external`. Those stay
in [§4.13](#413-config-validation-rules) and remain the job of `sqlgen validate`.

**Strictness.** Every object sets `"additionalProperties": false`. This is the
opposite choice from the manifest schema, which tolerates unknown properties for
forward compatibility, and it is deliberate: the manifest is a produced artifact
read by many consumers, while `sqlgen.yml` is authored by hand, so catching a
misspelled key is the schema's primary value.

**Union types.** Two fields accept either a scalar or a mapping and are modeled
with `oneOf`:

| Field | Scalar form | Object form |
|-------|-------------|-------------|
| `operations` under `api`, `tables.<t>.api` and `views.<v>.api` | preset name | explicit toggle map with optional `preset` |
| `overrides.types.<sql>.nullable` | type name sharing the parent's import | full `NullableVariant` |

Both have a custom `UnmarshalYAML` in `config.go`, so a reflection-derived
schema would model only the object arm and reject the documented
`api: {operations: read_only}` spelling. This is the reason the schema is hand-written.

**Delivery.** `sqlgen init` prepends a `yaml-language-server` modeline to the
config it writes:

```yaml
# yaml-language-server: $schema=https://raw.githubusercontent.com/teandresmith/sqlgen/main/cmd/sqlgen/config/schema/v1.json
```

This is resolved by the VS Code YAML extension, JetBrains IDEs, and Neovim
without any per-user setup or schema-registry entry. The URL is
`config.SchemaV1URL`; the full comment line is `config.SchemaModeline`.

**Versioning.** The schema is versioned by filename (`v1.json`), matching
[§30.5](#305-versioning-policy). A breaking change to the config format adds
`v2.json` and preserves `v1.json` at its published URL.

**Drift.** Nothing in the build ties the hand-written schema to the config
structs, so two tests hold the two directions apart.

`TestSchemaV1_noDriftFromConfigStructs` catches a config field with no schema
entry. It walks every `yaml`-tagged field reachable from `RootConfig` alongside
the schema node that should declare it — resolving `$ref`, merging `oneOf` arms,
descending map values through `additionalProperties` and slices through `items`
— and reports the exact path of anything missing. The walk is path-aware rather
than name-based: a property declared elsewhere in the schema does not satisfy an
unrelated field, so a new `enabled` or `type` under a new block is caught. It
checks presence, not shape; pinning the schema to what reflection can represent
would forfeit the union types and closed value sets above.

The opposite error — a schema strict enough to reject a valid file — is the more
damaging one, because it paints a correct `sqlgen.yml` red in the editor.
`TestSchemaV1_acceptsExampleConfigs` validates every shipped example config, and
`TestSchemaV1_acceptsUnexercisedSurface` covers the blocks no example uses
(roughly half the schema's property names): explicit `connection` and
`introspect`, `manifest.mcp`, `rest` / `grpc`, per-table
`primary_key` and `relationships`, external scalar marshaling, and the
`tenancy.type` shapes. Both over-strict `required` keywords found in review lived
in exactly that untested half.

## 5. SQL Parsing

### 5.1 Schema Model

Parsing produces a schema model containing:

| Element | Description | PostgreSQL | MySQL | SQLite |
|---------|-------------|:----------:|:-----:|:------:|
| **Tables** | Table name, schema, columns, constraints | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| **Columns** | Name, type, nullability, PK, unique, default, FK, auto-increment, generated expression, comment | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| **Constraints** | PRIMARY KEY, UNIQUE, FOREIGN KEY, CHECK, INDEX | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| **Enums** | Named enum types with values | Yes | Inline only | No |
| **Sets** | MySQL SET types with allowed values | No | Inline only | No |
| **Composite Types** | Named struct-like types with attributes | Yes | No | No |
| **Domain Types** | Named alias types with constraints | Yes | No | No |
| **Comments** | Table and column documentation, used as Go doc comments (see [Doc Comment Resolution](#doc-comment-resolution)) | COMMENT ON | Inline COMMENT | No |
| **Multi-Schema** | Schema-qualified names | Yes | No | No |

### 5.2 Dialect Parsers

Each dialect parser lives in the **parser module** (`github.com/teandresmith/sqlgen/parser`), which is separate from the runtime module. This ensures parser dependencies — particularly `pg_query_go/v6` which requires CGO — never appear in the consumer's `go.mod`.

**PostgreSQL** (`pg_query_go/v6`):
- Statements apply one at a time, in file order, as PostgreSQL applies them (see [5.6](#56-multi-file-parsing-order)). A statement sees only what the statements before it left: `COMMENT ON`, or `ALTER TABLE` without `IF EXISTS`, before the table's `CREATE TABLE` is an error, a table moved or renamed mid-file no longer answers to its old name, and that name is free for a later `CREATE`
- ALTER TABLE: ADD/DROP COLUMN, ADD/DROP CONSTRAINT, RENAME COLUMN, RENAME TABLE, SET SCHEMA
- ALTER COLUMN: SET/DROP NOT NULL, SET/DROP DEFAULT, ALTER TYPE
- IF EXISTS / IF NOT EXISTS: ALTER TABLE IF EXISTS, ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS, DROP COLUMN IF EXISTS, DROP CONSTRAINT IF EXISTS
- Parses composite type attributes, domain type constraints, enum values
- Detects auto-increment columns: `serial`/`bigserial`/`smallserial` and `GENERATED { ALWAYS | BY DEFAULT } AS IDENTITY` (SQL-standard identity columns, PostgreSQL 10+)
- `pg_query_go` links against `libpg_query` via CGO. Building the CLI from source therefore requires a C compiler; the pre-built release binaries do not.

**MySQL** (`vitess/sqlparser`):
- Parses CREATE TABLE with columns, constraints, indexes, inline comments
- Inline ENUM values from column type definitions (table-scoped naming: `<table>_<column>_enum`, auto-resolved via `RegisterEnum`)
- Inline SET values from column type definitions (table-scoped naming: `<table>_<column>_set`, auto-resolved via `RegisterSet`)
- ALTER TABLE: ADD/DROP/MODIFY COLUMN, ADD/DROP INDEX, ADD/DROP CONSTRAINT, RENAME COLUMN, RENAME TABLE, CHANGE COLUMN
- Standalone `RENAME TABLE a TO b [, c TO d ...]`, applied pair by pair, left to right
- No native enum type, composite type, or domain type support
- Uses databases instead of schemas

**SQLite** (`rqlite/sql`):
- Parses CREATE TABLE with columns and constraints
- ALTER TABLE: ADD COLUMN, DROP COLUMN (3.35+), RENAME COLUMN, RENAME TABLE
- Generated columns: `GENERATED ALWAYS AS (expr) VIRTUAL|STORED` and shorthand `AS (expr)` (3.31+)
- STRICT tables: recognizes `CREATE TABLE ... STRICT` modifier (3.37+)
- WITHOUT ROWID tables: recognizes `CREATE TABLE ... WITHOUT ROWID` modifier (3.8.2+)
- No MODIFY COLUMN, enum, composite, or domain support
- Type affinity handling (defaults to BLOB)

### 5.3 Relationship Detection

Automatic relationship detection runs after all tables are parsed:

**Many-to-Many (M2M):**
- Table has exactly 2 foreign key columns
- Both FK columns are part of a composite PRIMARY KEY or UNIQUE constraint
- Creates bidirectional relationships (TableA ↔ TableB through JunctionTable)

**One-to-One (O2O):**
- Column has FOREIGN KEY constraint
- Column is marked UNIQUE or part of a UNIQUE constraint

**One-to-Many (O2M):**
- Column has FOREIGN KEY constraint
- Column is NOT unique (default fallback for FKs not matching O2O or M2M)

Relationships can also be manually configured via `tables.<table>.relationships` (see [4.8](#48-tableconfig-per-table)).

### 5.4 Soft Delete Column Detection

For each table, columns are checked against the `soft_delete_columns` list in priority order. The first match determines the soft delete strategy:

- **Timestamp type:** Sets column to `CURRENT_TIMESTAMP` on soft delete
- **Bool type:** Sets column to `true` on soft delete

If no configured column matches any table column, that table has no soft delete support. Hard delete operations are always generated.

### 5.5 Schema Qualification & Table Naming

SQL tables may or may not include a schema prefix depending on the dialect and how the SQL is written. The parser normalizes table names using these rules:

**When parsing SQL files:**

| SQL Declaration | Dialect | `input.schema` | Internal Name |
|----------------|---------|----------------|---------------|
| `CREATE TABLE products (...)` | PostgreSQL | `"*"` (default) or `"public"` | `public.products` |
| `CREATE TABLE public.products (...)` | PostgreSQL | any | `public.products` |
| `CREATE TABLE myschema.products (...)` | PostgreSQL | any | `myschema.products` |
| `CREATE TABLE products (...)` | MySQL | N/A | `products` |
| `CREATE TABLE products (...)` | SQLite | N/A | `products` |

- **PostgreSQL:** If the SQL omits the schema, the table is assigned the `input.schema` value. The default, `"*"`, assigns `"public"`.
- **PostgreSQL foreign keys:** An unqualified `REFERENCES` target resolves the same way, to the `input.schema` value, and not to the schema of the table that declares the key. `CREATE TABLE audit.labels (document_id uuid REFERENCES documents(id))` references `public.documents`, as PostgreSQL's default `search_path` resolves it. A foreign key whose target no parsed table defines is a schema error, because PostgreSQL rejects that DDL too. MySQL (under `FOREIGN_KEY_CHECKS=0`) and SQLite accept such a key, so for them it is not an error and produces no relationship.
- **PostgreSQL views:** An unqualified `CREATE VIEW` or `CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW` name in an `input.views` annotation file ([16.1](#161-annotation-files-file-sourced-views)) resolves the same way, to the `input.schema` value. A view always has a schema, as a table does, so its `hook.TableName` value and its generated SQL are schema-qualified.
- **MySQL/SQLite:** Tables have no schema. The name is always bare.

**Config key matching:**

The schema prefix is **optional** in config keys (`tables`, `views`, relationship `table` references). A bare table name matches regardless of schema:

```yaml
# All valid:
tables:
  products:              # matches "products" in any schema
  public.products:       # matches specifically "public.products"
```

| Config Key | Matches |
|-----------|---------|
| `products` | `products`, `public.products`, `myschema.products` |
| `public.products` | `public.products` only |

**Ambiguity rule:** If multiple schemas contain a table with the same name and a bare (unqualified) config key is used, it is a **validation error**. The user must qualify the key to resolve the ambiguity.

**Relationship references** follow the same rules — `table` and `junction` fields can be bare or schema-qualified:

```yaml
relationships:
  - name: Tags
    type: m2m
    table: tags                  # matches "tags" in any schema
    junction: product_tags       # matches "product_tags" in any schema
```

**How a relationship's `table` resolves.** A schema-qualified `table` (`audit.orders`) names that entity exactly. A bare `table` resolves when exactly one schema has an entity by that name. When two or more do, it is a generation error ([4.13](#413-config-validation-rules)) that names each qualified spelling as the remedy (`qualify it as one of "audit.orders", "public.orders"`), not a silent choice of one. The count takes in every parsed table and view, including one that `exclude_tables` or a missing primary key keeps from generating. Every part of the edge then uses the table it resolved to: the field's type, the O2O join, the loaders, the relationship filter and the nested-mutation surface. The [13.7.3](#1373-validation-rules) duplicate check compares resolved targets too, so `documents` and `public.documents` on one parent are the same target.

**A relationship's `junction` resolves the same way.** A schema-qualified `junction` names that table exactly, and a bare one resolves when exactly one schema has a table or view by that name, counted over the same parsed entities as `table`. When two or more do, it is the same generation error, naming each qualified spelling. Every reader and writer of the junction then uses the table it resolved to: the M2M loader, the relationship filter, the junction's FK metadata and the nested link step. The duplicate check compares the resolved junction too. Unlike `table`, a `junction` that names no parsed table is not an error; it is carried as written.

**MySQL/SQLite users** never need a schema prefix — bare names are the only option and there is never ambiguity.

#### Schema in Generated Code

The schema is stored as part of every table's internal representation and flows through to all generated SQL. This ensures queries always target the correct schema.

**`sql.Table` type:**

```go
type Table struct {
    Schema string // "public", "billing", "" (MySQL/SQLite)
    Name   string // "users"
}
```

All SQL builder functions accept `sql.Table` instead of a raw string. The `Dialect` formats it correctly:

| Dialect | `sql.Table{Schema: "public", Name: "users"}` | `sql.Table{Name: "users"}` |
|---------|----------------------------------------------|---------------------------|
| PostgreSQL | `"public"."users"` | `"users"` |
| MySQL | `` `users` `` | `` `users` `` |
| SQLite | `"users"` | `"users"` |

PostgreSQL always includes the schema in generated SQL — even when only one schema is used. This prevents breakage if a new schema is added later.

**`hook.TableName` values** follow the same rule. The value of a table's or view's constant ([8.3](#83-generated-artifacts--other), [21.2](#212-hook-types)) is `schema.name` whenever the entity has a schema — every PostgreSQL table and view, e.g. `TableProducts = "public.products"` — and the bare SQL name otherwise (MySQL, SQLite). The runtime identifies a table by this value alone: the hook helpers compare it and the cache facade switches on it. Qualifying it always, not only when two schemas share a name, keeps two same-named tables apart (`TablePublicUsers = "public.users"`, `TableBillingUsers = "billing.users"`), makes the value computable from `(schema, name)` alone — which is how `cache.FromEventSubscriber` and an external invalidation source name a table ([27.9](#279-invalidation-strategies)) — and means adding a schema later never changes an existing value.

**Go naming in multi-schema contexts:**

When two schema objects in **different** schemas resolve to the same Go name, both are prefixed with their schema to disambiguate:

| Context | `public.users` | `billing.users` |
|---------|----------------|-----------------|
| Single schema | `User` | N/A |
| Multiple schemas | `PublicUser` | `BillingUser` |

This affects struct names, client accessors (`client.PublicUsers()`, `client.BillingUsers()`), filter types, field options, input types, file names (`public_user_gen.go`, `billing_user_gen.go` — the stem is the singular struct name, [8.5](#85-naming-rules)), and the unified client.

**The trigger is the resolved name, not the SQL name.** Resolution is many-to-one — `public.people` and `audit.person` are two SQL names that both land on `Person` — so grouping by the SQL string leaves a real collision unprefixed. Objects are grouped by the Go name they would take with no prefix, and every SQL name in a group that spans more than one schema is prefixed. Only objects that participate are prefixed: a schema with two schemas but no shared resolved name keeps its plain names. The struct name and its file stem consult one set, so they always move together.

A collision *within* one schema has no prefix to reach for and is a validation error ([4.13](#413-config-validation-rules)). The `struct_name` config override always takes precedence over the derived name, and is subject to the same collision rule.

### 5.6 Multi-File Parsing Order

When `input.paths` lists multiple files or directories, they are parsed in the order specified:

```yaml
input:
  paths:
    - "./migrations/0001_initial.sql"
    - "./migrations/0002_add_products.sql"
    - "./migrations/0003_add_reviews.sql"
```

Within a directory, files are sorted **lexicographically** (alphabetical). The convention of prefixing files with `0001_`, `0002_`, etc. ensures correct ordering.

**Migration file conventions:**

Files matching common "down" migration patterns are automatically skipped:

| Pattern | Skipped? | Example |
|---------|:--------:|---------|
| `*.up.sql` | No | `0001_initial.up.sql` |
| `*_up.sql` | No | `0001_up.sql` |
| `*.down.sql` | Yes | `0001_initial.down.sql` |
| `*_down.sql` | Yes | `0001_down.sql` |
| `*.sql` (no suffix) | No | `0001_initial.sql` |

**Sequential migration application:**

Files are parsed sequentially, and each statement is applied to the accumulating schema model — exactly as SQL migrations would be applied to a real database:

```
File 1: CREATE TABLE products (id UUID, name TEXT, legacy TEXT)
File 2: ALTER TABLE products DROP COLUMN legacy
File 3: ALTER TABLE products ADD COLUMN description TEXT
→ Final schema: products (id UUID, name TEXT, description TEXT)
```

All DDL operations work naturally across files:
- `ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN` extends the table
- `ALTER TABLE DROP COLUMN` removes the column
- `ALTER TABLE RENAME COLUMN` / `RENAME TABLE` renames in place. Foreign keys that reference a renamed table follow it to the new name, as they do in the database. A renamed column is renamed in every constraint and foreign key that names it, on any table
- `ALTER TABLE … SET SCHEMA` (PostgreSQL) moves the table to the named schema, and foreign keys that reference it follow it there
- `ALTER COLUMN SET/DROP NOT NULL`, `SET/DROP DEFAULT`, `ALTER TYPE` modify column properties
- `DROP TABLE` removes the table from the schema
- `DROP TYPE` removes the type (enum, composite, domain)
- `IF EXISTS` / `IF NOT EXISTS` variants are respected for idempotent migrations

**Duplicate definitions are errors:**

If a `CREATE TABLE`, `CREATE TYPE`, `CREATE DOMAIN`, or other `CREATE` statement targets an element that already exists, it is a validation error. Each schema element must be defined exactly once across all files. This catches accidental redefinitions that would also fail against a real database.

**Drop validation:**

`DROP TABLE` and `DROP TYPE` validate that no other schema element references the object being dropped. Dropping a table that is referenced by a foreign key, or dropping a type that is used by a column, is a validation error — matching real database behavior.

### 5.7 Deterministic Output

All schema elements (tables, columns, enums, types) are sorted before generation to ensure deterministic, reproducible output across runs.

## 6. Database Introspection

### 6.1 Source Modes

| Mode | Behavior |
|------|----------|
| `files` | Parse SQL files from `paths` config. Default. |
| `database` | Connect to live database via `connection` config and introspect schema. |
| `both` | Introspect database first (source of truth), then merge file-based changes on top. See below. |

#### `both` Mode — Merge Strategy

The database is the **source of truth**. File-based changes are applied as an overlay using merge semantics:

1. **Introspect** the live database to build the base schema model (tables, columns, constraints, types, enums)
2. **Parse** SQL files from `paths` in order (same rules as `files` mode — see [5.6](#56-multi-file-parsing-order))
3. **Merge** file-based changes into the introspected schema:

| File Statement | DB Has Table? | Behavior |
|----------------|:------------:|----------|
| `CREATE TABLE foo (...)` | No | Add table to schema |
| `CREATE TABLE foo (...)` | Yes | Validation error — table already exists from introspection. Use `ALTER TABLE` to modify. |
| `ALTER TABLE foo ADD COLUMN bar ...` | Yes | Add column to introspected table |
| `ALTER TABLE foo DROP COLUMN bar` | Yes | Remove column from introspected table |
| `ALTER TABLE foo ADD CONSTRAINT ...` | Yes | Add constraint to introspected table |
| `CREATE TYPE ...` / `CREATE DOMAIN ...` | — | Add to schema (merged with introspected types) |
| `DROP TABLE foo` | Yes | Remove table from schema |

**Use case:** The database contains the production schema, and the SQL files contain pending migrations that haven't been applied yet. `both` mode lets the generator produce code that reflects the *future* schema (after migrations run), while the database provides the *current* baseline.

**Conflict rule:** If a file-based column definition conflicts with an introspected column (same name, different type), it is a **validation error**. The file cannot silently redefine what the database already has — use explicit `ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN` to express the change.

### 6.2 Introspector Interface

```go
type Introspector interface {
    Name() string
    Introspect(ctx context.Context, connString string, schema *Schema, opts IntrospectionOptions) error
    Close() error
}
```

### 6.3 Dialect Introspection Capabilities

| Capability | PostgreSQL | MySQL | SQLite |
|------------|:----------:|:-----:|:------:|
| Tables & columns | `information_schema` + `pg_catalog` | `information_schema` | `PRAGMA table_list/table_info` |
| Primary keys | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Foreign keys | Yes | Yes | `PRAGMA foreign_key_list` |
| Unique constraints | Yes | Yes | Limited |
| Check constraints | Yes | Yes | Limited |
| Enum types | `pg_catalog.pg_enum` | No (inline only) | No |
| Composite types | `pg_type` + `pg_attribute` | No | No |
| Domain types | `information_schema.domains` | No | No |
| Comments | `pg_description` | `information_schema` | No |
| Multi-schema | Yes | No (single database) | No |

### 6.4 Filtering

When using `database` or `both` source:
- `input.introspect.schemas` / `input.introspect.exclude_schemas` control which schemas are introspected
- `input.introspect.tables` is an include-list controlling which tables within those schemas are introspected

To filter tables **out** of generation, use the **top-level** `exclude_tables` field at the root of `sqlgen.yml`. It applies regardless of input source (file or introspection). Glob syntax: `*` matches any sequence, `?` matches any single character; patterns are case-sensitive. A table matched by any pattern is dropped from generation. It skips junction tables that should not surface as entities, tables owned by other tooling, and tables that lack a usable primary key — see [4.13](#413-config-validation-rules) and [No-PK tables are skipped](#94b-no-pk-tables-are-skipped). An FK-inferred relationship into an excluded table is omitted from the tables that reference it; a relationship declared into one is an error ([4.13](#413-config-validation-rules)). An excluded junction is not a target, so the M2M edges that read through it are kept:

```yaml
# Top-level (applies to file + introspection inputs)
exclude_tables:
  - temp_*
  - _internal_*
  - report_acl
```

---

## 7. Type System

### 7.1 Type Resolution Chain

For each column, the Go type is resolved in this order:

1. **Column override** (`tables.<table>.column_map.<column>.type`) — literal Go type string, with an explicit `.import`
2. **Table-level type_map** (`tables.<table>.type_map.<column>`) — literal Go type string, no import
3. **Table-level type override** (`tables.<table>.overrides.types.<sql_type>`) — full override config
4. **Global type override** (`overrides.types.<sql_type>`) — full override config
5. **Built-in optional type** (UUID/decimal integrations, when enabled) — see [7.4](#74-built-in-type-integrations)
6. **Built-in dialect mapping** (`gotype` package) — default SQL→Go mapping

A per-column override changes the Go type only — it does not restate what the column *is* to the database. Downstream surfaces that key on the resolved Go type follow the override, which for increment eligibility would enroll a non-arithmetic column in arithmetic the database rejects. That one consequence is guarded: when a column resolves to an arithmetic Go type but its SQL type is a classifiable, non-arithmetic one, the column is left out of the increment surface and generation warns, naming the config key that produced it. Nothing else about the override changes, and the config still generates (see [8.2](#82-generated-artifacts-per-table), "A type override cannot manufacture eligibility"). Domain types are followed to their base before classifying, so a `text` domain is a `text` column here.

Steps 1 and 2 are by **column**; steps 3–6 are by **SQL type**. The two per-column forms differ only in whether they can carry an import: `type_map` cannot, so it is limited to builtins, types in the generated package, and the literals sqlgen resolves imports for on its own; `column_map.<col>.type` pairs with `.import` and is the escape hatch for anything external. Naming an unknown package-qualified type in `type_map`, or in `column_map` without an `import`, is a config error rather than a generated file that references a package nothing imports. See ["Column Overrides"](#column-overrides) and ["Type Map"](#type-map).

Only steps 3–6 carry a `nullable:` wrapper variant. A nullable column resolved by step 1 or 2 gets `*T` (or bare `T` when the type is natively nilable). Steps 1 and 2 also resolve a literal as an opaque type: a slice literal (`[]T`) is *not* treated as an array column, so it filters through the scalar comparator rather than `comparator.Slice[T]`. Use `overrides.types` when array semantics matter.

### 7.2 Built-In Type Mappings

<details>
<summary>PostgreSQL Type Mappings</summary>

| SQL Type | Go Type | Nullable Go Type |
|----------|---------|------------------|
| `text`, `varchar`, `char`, `name` | `string` | `sql.NullString` / `*string` |
| `int2`, `smallint` | `int16` | `sql.NullInt16` / `*int16` |
| `int4`, `integer`, `serial`, `integer GENERATED AS IDENTITY` | `int32` | `sql.NullInt32` / `*int32` |
| `int8`, `bigint`, `bigserial`, `bigint GENERATED AS IDENTITY` | `int64` | `sql.NullInt64` / `*int64` |
| `float4`, `real` | `float32` | `sql.NullFloat64` / `*float32` |
| `float8`, `double precision` | `float64` | `sql.NullFloat64` / `*float64` |
| `numeric`, `decimal` | `float64` | `sql.NullFloat64` / `*float64` |
| `bool`, `boolean` | `bool` | `sql.NullBool` / `*bool` |
| `bytea` | `[]byte` | `[]byte` |
| `timestamp`, `timestamptz` | `time.Time` | `sql.NullTime` / `*time.Time` |
| `date` | `time.Time` | `sql.NullTime` / `*time.Time` |
| `interval` | `time.Duration` | `*time.Duration` |
| `uuid` | `uuid.UUID` | `*uuid.UUID` |
| `json`, `jsonb` | `types.JSON` | `types.JSON` (nil = NULL) |
| `inet` | `net.IP` | `net.IP` |
| `cidr` | `net.IPNet` | `*net.IPNet` |
| `macaddr` | `net.HardwareAddr` | `net.HardwareAddr` |
| `text[]`, `varchar[]` | `[]string` | `[]string` |
| `int2[]`, `smallint[]` | `[]int16` | `[]int16` |
| `int4[]`, `integer[]` | `[]int32` | `[]int32` |
| `int8[]`, `bigint[]` | `[]int64` | `[]int64` |
| `float4[]`, `real[]` | `[]float32` | `[]float32` |
| `float8[]`, `double precision[]` | `[]float64` | `[]float64` |
| `bool[]`, `boolean[]` | `[]bool` | `[]bool` |
| `uuid[]` | `[]uuid.UUID` | `[]uuid.UUID` |
| `numeric[]`, `decimal[]` | `[]float64` | `[]float64` |
| `timestamp[]`, `timestamptz[]` | `[]time.Time` | `[]time.Time` |

**Array type rule:** Any PostgreSQL array type (`T[]`) maps to a Go slice of the base type's **resolved** Go mapping (`[]GoT`) — the base type's built-in mapping, or whatever an `overrides.types.<base>` entry resolves it to. The base type is always resolved in its non-null form, so the element type never carries a `sql.Null*` or pointer shape; nullable array columns use the same slice type (slices are already reference types with a `nil` zero value). `uuid[]` is therefore `[]uuid.UUID` on the default binding and on every UUID integration alike ([7.4](#74-built-in-type-integrations)), all of which spell the Go type `uuid.UUID`; a `numeric` override to `github.com/shopspring/decimal` makes `numeric[]` resolve to `[]decimal.Decimal`.

</details>

### 7.3 Nullable Handling

Controlled by `overrides.use_pointers`:
- **`true` (default):** Nullable columns use `*T` (e.g., `*string`, `*int32`)
- **`false`:** Nullable columns use `sql.Null*` types (e.g., `sql.NullString`, `sql.NullInt32`)

Custom nullable types can be specified per SQL type via `overrides.types.<type>.nullable`.

**`use_pointers` applies only where a `sql.Null*` equivalent exists.** Some Go types have no `database/sql` wrapper to fall back to, so their nullable form is always `*T` regardless of the flag. `uuid.UUID` ([7.4](#74-built-in-type-integrations)) is one of them — the standard library ships no `NullUUID` — alongside `time.Duration` (`interval`) and `net.IPNet` (`cidr`). Setting `overrides.use_pointers: false` does not turn a nullable `uuid` column into a wrapper struct; it stays `*uuid.UUID`, and `IS NULL` is `v != nil`. A consumer who wants the wrapper shape selects a UUID library that ships one, via `overrides.types.uuid` ([7.4](#74-built-in-type-integrations)) — the flag is not the lever for it. This is distinct from reference types (`[]byte`, `net.IP`, `types.JSON`), whose nullable form is the bare type because `nil` is already their zero value.

**A generated file imports `database/sql` under an alias.** sqlgen's own runtime package is `github.com/teandresmith/sqlgen/sql`, so both bind the file-local package name `sql`. A generated file needing both — the row struct carries `sql.NullString` while the table client carries `sql.Dialect` — must alias one of them, and the alias falls on `database/sql` because the runtime qualifier is the one the templates spell. This is a property of generated files only: the Go type sqlgen *names* stays `sql.NullString` everywhere it is written down — in `overrides.types.<type>.nullable`, in the built-in scalar registry ([§26.4.1](#2641-scalar-marshaling)), and in the manifest's published `go_type` ([§30](#30-manifest)) — because that is what a consumer importing `database/sql` themselves would write.

**A Null wrapper is classified by the type it wraps.** Comparator selection ([§11.2](#112-comparator-types)) reads through the wrapper: a nullable `double precision` column takes `comparator.NullableNumber[float64]`, not `comparator.NullableNumber[sql.NullFloat64]` — which does not satisfy `comparator.Numeric` — and a nullable `boolean` or `timestamptz` column takes `NullableBool` / `NullableTime` rather than falling through to a string comparator. The storage shape changes with `use_pointers`; the comparison does not.

### 7.4 Built-In Type Integrations

SQLGen provides first-class support for the standard library's `uuid` package and for popular third-party UUID and decimal libraries. The standard library binding is the default and needs no configuration; the rest are selected via `overrides.types` in `sqlgen.yml` — no build tags required. The code generator knows the type mappings at generation time and emits the correct imports in the generated code. When a third-party library is selected, the consumer's `go.mod` includes it naturally because the generated code imports it directly.

#### UUID Libraries

The standard library's `uuid` package is the **default** binding: a `uuid` column resolves to `uuid.UUID` with no configuration and no entry in the consumer's `go.mod`. Two third-party libraries are supported as **alternative integrations**, selected through `overrides.types.uuid`.

| Integration | `import` value | Go type | Zero value | Nullable Go type |
|-------------|----------------|---------|------------|------------------|
| **Standard library** (default) | `uuid` | `uuid.UUID` | `uuid.UUID{}` | `*uuid.UUID` — **no null wrapper** |
| `github.com/google/uuid` | `github.com/google/uuid` | `uuid.UUID` | `uuid.UUID{}` | `*uuid.UUID` (pointers) or `uuid.NullUUID` |
| `github.com/gofrs/uuid/v5` | `github.com/gofrs/uuid/v5` | `uuid.UUID` | `uuid.Nil` | `*uuid.UUID` (pointers) or `uuid.NullUUID` |

All three match the single SQL type `uuid`, and PostgreSQL is the only dialect that declares one — MySQL and SQLite have no `uuid` SQL type, so no mapping of theirs is affected by the choice.

**Standard library — the default binding.** `uuid` columns resolve to `uuid.UUID` and nullable ones to `*uuid.UUID` with an empty `overrides.types`. Three properties follow from the package's shape and are normative:

- **No null wrapper.** The package ships no `NullUUID`, so `uuid.UUID` is classified `nullPtrOnly` ([7.3](#73-nullable-handling)): a nullable `uuid` column is `*uuid.UUID` and `overrides.use_pointers: false` does not change it. Null is `v != nil`, the value is `*v`. There is nothing for `overrides.types.uuid.nullable` to name, and the integration sets no nullable variant.
- **No `driver.Valuer` / `sql.Scanner`, and none needed — for a `uuid` column.** `database/sql` special-cases `uuid.UUID` in both directions — `driver/types.go` on write, `convert.go` on read, for both `string` and `[]byte` driver values — and pgx routes the type through the same path `github.com/google/uuid` has always taken, unwrapping the named type to its underlying `[16]byte` and wrapping that in `pgtype.byte16Wrapper`, which satisfies `UUIDValuer` and dispatches to `UUIDCodec`. Neither `overrides.types.uuid.convert` nor a custom codec is required on either `output.driver` value. Generated code scans into the resolved type directly and never into `pgtype.UUID`, which would cost a conversion step and lose the nil-pointer NULL representation.

- **A column whose SQL type is *not* `uuid` cannot be retyped to the standard library's `uuid.UUID` under pgx.** The claim above is scoped to the column's SQL type, because that is what pgx's codec lookup keys on: `UUIDCodec` is registered for the `uuid` OID, so a `text` column retyped to `uuid.UUID` through `tables.<t>.column_map.<col>` or `type_map` fails at scan time with `cannot scan text (OID 25) in text format into *uuid.UUID`. The standard library's `uuid.UUID` carries `MarshalText` / `UnmarshalText` but neither `sql.Scanner` nor `driver.Valuer`, so there is nothing for the text path to dispatch to. Both wrapper-backed integrations *do* ship `Scan` / `Value` on the bare `uuid.UUID`, so the same retype works under either of them, and under `output.driver: stdlib` on any integration (`database/sql`'s `convert.go` special-case applies to the destination type, not the column). A project that stores UUIDs in a `text` column and wants them typed selects `github.com/google/uuid` or `github.com/gofrs/uuid/v5` for that generated package.
- **Comparable.** `uuid.UUID` is an array type, so it satisfies `comparable` and `uuid[]` columns filter through `comparator.Slice[uuid.UUID]` ([11.2](#112-comparator-types)).

On the GraphQL surface ([26.4.1](#2641-scalar-marshaling)) a stdlib-bound package declares the `UUID` scalar only: a nullable `uuid` column is a nullable field of scalar `UUID`, no `NullUUID` scalar is declared, and no `MarshalNullUUID` / `UnmarshalNullUUID` pair is emitted. Filter inputs are unaffected — a nullable UUID column takes `NullableIDComparator` under every integration, because comparator selection reads through the wrapper ([7.3](#73-nullable-handling)).

**Alternative integrations.** `github.com/google/uuid` and `github.com/gofrs/uuid/v5` are selected by pointing `overrides.types.uuid.import` at the library. Both ship a `uuid.NullUUID` wrapper, so both offer the wrapper shape for nullable columns — `*uuid.UUID` under `use_pointers: true`, `uuid.NullUUID` under `use_pointers: false`, or `uuid.NullUUID` named explicitly via `nullable:` at either setting. Choosing one is the supported way to keep the wrapper shape, the `NullUUID` GraphQL scalar, and the `.Valid` / `.UUID` field access a consumer may already depend on.

**Three spellings of the zero UUID.** The three integrations agree on the Go type string `uuid.UUID` and disagree on how the zero value is written: google spells it as the composite literal `uuid.UUID{}`, gofrs as the package **variable** `uuid.Nil`, and the standard library as neither — its `Nil` is a **function**, so the literal `uuid.UUID{}` is what the generator must emit. This is why `ZeroValue` is a per-integration field rather than something derived from the type name.

**Generating UUID values.** sqlgen emits UUID-generating calls in two places — the app-strategy primary key ([8.6](#86-primary-key-strategy)) and the generated event ID ([28.8](#288-configuration)) — and the call it emits is the **selected integration's**, resolved at generation time. The three libraries do not agree on the spelling, so this cannot be one fixed string: the standard library and google both export `New()` while gofrs does not, only google exports `NewString()`, `Must` exists in google and gofrs but **not** in the standard library, and the standard library's constructors return a bare `UUID` where the other two return `(UUID, error)`.

| Integration | v4, value | v7, value | v4, string | v7, string |
|-------------|-----------|-----------|------------|------------|
| Standard library | `uuid.NewV4()` | `uuid.NewV7()` | `uuid.NewV4().String()` | `uuid.NewV7().String()` |
| `github.com/google/uuid` | `uuid.New()` | `uuid.Must(uuid.NewV7())` | `uuid.NewString()` | `uuid.Must(uuid.NewV7()).String()` |
| `github.com/gofrs/uuid/v5` | `uuid.Must(uuid.NewV4())` | `uuid.Must(uuid.NewV7())` | `uuid.Must(uuid.NewV4()).String()` | `uuid.Must(uuid.NewV7()).String()` |

The **value** columns are used where the target is a `uuid.UUID`; the **string** columns where it is a Go `string` — a PK overridden to `string`, and every event ID, which is `string` by definition ([28.3](#283-event-structure)). The standard library's v4 cell is `NewV4()` rather than `New()` on purpose: `New` is documented as "an algorithm suitable for most purposes" and is not contractually v4, so an explicit `uuid_version: v4` is honored with the call that names the version. **Which integration a package generates with** is resolved in three steps:

1. **What the package's columns resolved to.** This wins, because it is what the generated files already spell — a generating call in any other library would put a second package named `uuid` beside them, the failure [4.13](#413-config-validation-rules) forbids.
2. **What the global `overrides.types` names**, when step 1 found nothing. Detection is by import path, not by key, on the same scope-independent terms as the rest of this section. This step matters because "no column resolved `uuid`-qualified" and "this package uses no UUID library" are different statements: a `uuid` primary key overridden to a Go `string` leaves an explicit `overrides.types` binding with no resolved type to carry it, and the generated PK must still come from the library the consumer named.
3. **The standard library**, when neither named anything — so a consumer who mentions no UUID library anywhere acquires no module dependency by enabling event IDs.

**Parsing a UUID from a string.** The GraphQL `UUID` and `NullUUID` scalar unmarshalers ([26.4.1](#2641-scalar-marshaling)) turn a wire string into a `uuid.UUID`, and that call is the **selected integration's** on the same terms as the generating calls above. The three libraries disagree here too, and not on the same axis: the standard library and google both export `Parse`, while gofrs exports **no `Parse` at all** — its string constructor is `FromString`.

| Integration | Parse from string |
|-------------|-------------------|
| Standard library | `uuid.Parse(s)` |
| `github.com/google/uuid` | `uuid.Parse(s)` |
| `github.com/gofrs/uuid/v5` | `uuid.FromString(s)` |

All three return `(uuid.UUID, error)`, so only the function name varies and the call site's shape is identical under every integration. The `OrNil` variants gofrs also exports are deliberately not used: an unparseable scalar input is a client error the unmarshaler must report, not silently collapse to the zero UUID.

**All three integrations provide:**
- Correct zero values, per the table above
- v4 and v7 generation, and string parsing, each spelled per the integration — see "Generating UUID values" and "Parsing a UUID from a string" below
- FK string conversion derived automatically from the `.String()` method on the bare type; for the two wrapper-backed integrations, the `UUID` underlying-field unwrap on `uuid.NullUUID` for nullable FK columns, and for the pointer form the `v != nil` guard with a `(*v)` unwrap ([7.5](#75-custom-type-overrides))
- Comparator compatibility — FK values are converted to strings for `comparator.ID`
- Scanner/Valuer compliance for database drivers: through the types' own interface implementations for the two third-party libraries, and through the standard library and pgx integrations described above for `uuid.UUID`

**One UUID library per generated package.** Two UUID libraries cannot coexist in a single generated package, under either `output.layout` value: all three bind the file-local package name `uuid` and all three export a type named `UUID`, so the resolved Go type string `uuid.UUID` carries no information about which package is meant. Imports are resolved **per package**, not per file, so `file_per_table` fails exactly as `single_file` does: the union of the package's imports is resolved once over the concatenated bodies and seeds every emitted file, and the per-file prune that follows is usage-based — it cannot separate two packages that are both spelled `uuid.`. The failure is not only a name collision (`uuid redeclared in this block`); the surviving `uuid` binds to whichever import wins, so a `uuid.NullUUID` needed by one table can silently resolve against a package that has no such identifier. sqlgen rejects this at resolution time rather than emitting a package that does not compile — see the validation row in [4.13](#413-config-validation-rules). The existing `database/sql` → `stdsql` aliasing ([7.3](#73-nullable-handling)) does not generalize to this case, because that collision is against a fixed, enumerable set of identifiers sqlgen itself spells.

A project that genuinely needs two UUID libraries splits them across **separate generated packages** — one `sqlgen.yml` and one `output.dir` each, in the same module. That arrangement is supported, and composes with the multi-package monorepo pattern the manifest and `.mcp.json` emission already handle ([31.2](#312-configuration)).

**Configuration.** The default needs none. To select an alternative integration:

```yaml
overrides:
  types:
    uuid:
      type: uuid.UUID
      import: github.com/google/uuid
      nullable: uuid.NullUUID
```

To name the standard library explicitly — equivalent to omitting the block entirely:

```yaml
overrides:
  types:
    uuid:
      type: uuid.UUID
      import: uuid
```

#### Decimal Library

| Library | SQL Types Matched |
|---------|-------------------|
| `github.com/shopspring/decimal` | `numeric`, `decimal` |

**shopspring/decimal mappings:**

| SQL Type | Go Type | Nullable Go Type | Zero Value |
|----------|---------|------------------|------------|
| `numeric`, `decimal` | `decimal.Decimal` | `*decimal.Decimal` (pointers) or `decimal.NullDecimal` | `decimal.Decimal{}` |

This integration provides:
- Arbitrary-precision decimal arithmetic instead of lossy `float64`
- Correct `NullDecimal` handling when `use_pointers: false`, including the `Decimal` underlying-field unwrap so nullable decimal FK columns stringify correctly in O2M relationship loaders
- Scanner/Valuer interface compliance for database drivers

**If no decimal override is configured**, `numeric`/`decimal` SQL columns map to `float64` / `sql.NullFloat64` (the default).

**Configuration:**

```yaml
overrides:
  types:
    numeric:
      type: decimal.Decimal
      import: github.com/shopspring/decimal
      nullable: decimal.NullDecimal
```

#### Configuration Shorthand

The code generator includes built-in knowledge of these popular libraries (via the `gotype/` packages in the CLI module). When a consumer configures one of these types, the generator automatically resolves the full mapping — zero value, nullable variant, scanner/valuer support, FK conversion, and the wrapper's `underlying_field` (the embedded scalar field used by O2M relationship loaders to unwrap a nullable FK before stringifying) — without the consumer needing to specify every field. Consumers can override any field explicitly via `overrides.types` if they need different behavior. Explicit overrides always take precedence over built-in knowledge, **except** for the FK extraction path — built-in wrappers (`uuid.NullUUID`, `decimal.NullDecimal`, `types.NullDateTime`) always use their canonical underlying field and `Valid` guard, so a user who points `nullable.type` at one of those names cannot accidentally redirect the unwrap to the wrong field.

**Integration detection is scope-independent.** An `overrides.types.<sql_type>` entry naming a known library's import path activates that integration and receives the same enrichment wherever it is declared — globally, or under `tables.<table>.overrides.types`. Identical override text selects the same integration and resolves to the same Go type, zero value and nullable variant at both scopes; nesting depth is not part of integration resolution. The claim is about the built-in integrations, which is what this section governs — a wrapper the consumer declares themselves is [7.5](#75-custom-type-overrides)'s mechanism, not this one. A consumer who drops `nullable:` from a table-scoped `github.com/google/uuid` override gets `uuid.NullUUID` back from enrichment exactly as the same edit at global scope does, and a table-scoped override gains the same FK-extraction metadata (`underlying_field`, `valid_field`) as a global one. "Activates" covers the integration's other SQL types as well: a table-scoped `numeric` override naming `github.com/shopspring/decimal` binds that table's `decimal` columns to `decimal.Decimal` too, exactly as the same entry does globally. A table-scoped activation is still an *integration*, so it enters the chain at step 5 of [7.1](#71-type-resolution-chain) — ahead of a global integration, behind any explicit override at either scope. An explicit value the consumer did write is never overwritten at any scope, per the precedence rule above.

These are the only two scopes. A view carries no `overrides` block ([4.9](#49-viewconfig-per-view)), so a view column resolves its type under the global scope alone; per-view type control is a column's `@type` annotation in the view SQL.

### 7.5 Custom Type Overrides

For types beyond the built-in integrations (UUID, decimal), users define mappings via `OverrideTypeConfig` in the `overrides.types` config section (see [4.7](#47-overrideconfig)). This supports any arbitrary Go type with custom imports, zero values, nullable variants, and conversion logic.

#### Custom Null-Wrapper Types

When a custom type's nullable variant is a wrapper struct (rather than a pointer or `sql.Null*`), the wrapper's underlying-field name and validity-check shape are declared on `nullable.{underlying_field, valid_field, valid_method, valid_invert}` — see [4.7](#47-overrideconfig) for the full field reference. These are required only when the column is reachable through an O2M relationship loader (which needs to skip null FKs and unwrap the underlying scalar before stringifying). For wrappers that follow the `database/sql.NullX` shape, `valid_field: "Valid"` is the default and can be omitted. Three real-world wrapper styles:

```yaml
overrides:
  types:
    # (a) Field-based wrapper with non-default field name.
    text:
      type: pkg.Optional[string]
      import: myapp/pkg/optional
      nullable:
        type: pkg.Optional[string]
        underlying_field: Value
        valid_field: Set         # default would be "Valid"

    # (b) Method-based wrapper — wrapper exposes IsValid()/IsPresent()/Exists().
    numeric:
      type: ids.Money
      import: myapp/pkg/ids
      nullable:
        type: ids.NullMoney
        underlying_field: Money
        valid_method: IsPresent

    # (c) Inverted method — wrapper signals invalidity (time.Time-style).
    #     IsZero() returns true when the value IS zero, so we negate.
    timestamptz:
      type: myapp.Stamp
      import: myapp/pkg/stamp
      nullable:
        type: myapp.NullableStamp
        underlying_field: Stamp
        valid_method: IsZero
        valid_invert: true
```

Cases users do **not** need to declare:
- **Built-in integrations** (`uuid.NullUUID`, `decimal.NullDecimal`, `types.NullDateTime`) — recognized automatically; the existing one-line `nullable: uuid.NullUUID` shorthand keeps working and gets the unwrap-+-guard for free.
- **`database/sql.NullX` types** — recognized by name; no YAML declaration needed.
- **Pointer types** (`*uuid.UUID`, `*string`) — handled by the resolver's pointer fallthrough; no YAML declaration needed.

Example use cases:
- Custom money types (`github.com/Rhymond/go-money`)
- Custom ID types (KSUID, ULID, etc.)
- Domain-specific wrappers around primitive types

---

### 7.6 JSON / JSONB Column Type

The default Go type for `json` and `jsonb` columns (PostgreSQL/MySQL) is `types.JSON`, a shape-polymorphic value backed by `encoding/json.RawMessage`. Because a single `jsonb` column can legally hold any JSON value (object, array, scalar, `null`), the default cannot be `map[string]any` — that would silently break on every column whose stored value is not an object, including columns whose `DEFAULT` clause produces an array.

**Type definition:**

```go
package types

// JSON holds a raw JSON document of any shape — object, array, scalar,
// or null. It is the default Go type for `json` and `jsonb` columns
// when no typed Go struct is configured. Decode opportunistically with
// AsMap/AsSlice/Decode, or override the column's go_type to a concrete
// struct via overrides.types or per-column override for typed access at
// the field level.
type JSON json.RawMessage
```

**Method surface:**

| Method | Returns | Semantics |
|--------|---------|-----------|
| `(*JSON).Scan(src any)` | `error` | `sql.Scanner`. Accepts `[]byte` or `string`. Stores a defensive copy of the raw bytes (drivers may reuse buffers across rows). SQL `NULL` produces a `nil JSON`. No shape validation. |
| `JSON.Value()` | `(driver.Value, error)` | `driver.Valuer`. Returns the raw bytes verbatim. `nil` or empty `JSON` returns SQL `NULL`. |
| `JSON.MarshalJSON()` | `([]byte, error)` | Delegates to `json.RawMessage.MarshalJSON`. `nil` emits `"null"`. |
| `(*JSON).UnmarshalJSON(data []byte)` | `error` | Delegates to `json.RawMessage.UnmarshalJSON` (validates well-formedness). |
| `JSON.MarshalGQL(w io.Writer)` | — | gqlgen `Marshaler`. Writes the raw bytes verbatim; nil/empty writes `"null"`. |
| `(*JSON).UnmarshalGQL(v any)` | `error` | gqlgen `Unmarshaler`. Accepts any shape gqlgen produces (`map[string]any`, `[]any`, primitives, `nil`) and re-encodes to bytes. Unlike the prior `JSONMap.UnmarshalGQL`, this does **not** reject non-object inputs — shape validation is a resolver-layer concern (see §26.4.1). |
| `JSON.Decode(v any)` | `error` | Typed-decode escape hatch. Delegates to `json.Unmarshal(j, v)`. Empty `JSON` returns the stdlib's `"unexpected end of JSON input"` error wrapped with context; `"null"` literal nils out the target via standard `encoding/json` behavior. |
| `JSON.AsMap()` | `(map[string]any, error)` | Strict object decode. Returns an error when the value is not a JSON object (probe with `IsObject` to branch without decoding). |
| `JSON.AsSlice()` | `([]any, error)` | Strict array decode. Returns an error when the value is not a JSON array (probe with `IsArray` to branch without decoding). |
| `JSON.IsNull()` | `bool` | True when the value is empty (SQL NULL) **or** holds the JSON `null` literal. The two are indistinguishable to most application code; `len(j) == 0` distinguishes them where it matters. |
| `JSON.IsObject()` | `bool` | First non-whitespace byte is `{`. Cheap structural probe; does not validate the entire payload. |
| `JSON.IsArray()` | `bool` | First non-whitespace byte is `[`. Cheap structural probe; does not validate the entire payload. |
| `JSON.String()` | `string` | Returns `string(j)` so `%v` / `%s` formatting emit the raw JSON document. No truncation. |

**Typed access — the recommended pattern.** When a column's JSON shape is known and stable, override the column's Go type to a typed struct rather than living on `types.JSON`. This produces a model that scans directly into the typed fields and surfaces shape errors at the database boundary instead of at every read site:

```yaml
# sqlgen.yml
tables:
  asset:
    columns:
      property_tax_rate:
        go_type: "[]assettypes.YearValue"
        import: "example.com/assettypes"
```

```go
// assettypes/year_value.go
package assettypes

type YearValue struct {
    Year  int     `json:"year"`
    Value float64 `json:"value"`
}
```

The column scans as `PropertyTaxRate []YearValue` directly, no per-read decode. `types.JSON` remains for the cases where a column's shape genuinely is dynamic (event payloads, audit-log details, third-party integration responses) or where typing has not been done yet.

**Why not split into `JSONObject` / `JSONArray`?** A jsonb column can hold any JSON value at any time — there is no SQL-level guarantee that the shape is uniform across rows. Splitting at the type level forces every consumer to pick a shape upfront, which is exactly the bug the polymorphic default avoids. Callers that genuinely need shape constraints define a Go struct (or `[]Struct`) and override; that's a stronger guarantee than two narrowly-typed default types.

**`jsonb[]` arrays.** PostgreSQL's `jsonb[]` (a SQL array of jsonb values, distinct from a single jsonb holding a JSON array) resolves to `[]types.JSON`. Each element is independently shape-agnostic and supports the same method surface, so per-element decoding composes cleanly:

```go
for _, t := range asset.Tags {
    if t.IsObject() {
        m, _ := t.AsMap()
        ...
    }
}
```

`jsonb[]` columns are excluded from the generated filter context: `[]types.JSON` is `[][]byte`, which does not satisfy the comparator package's `comparable` constraint. Schemas needing list-of-JSON semantics use a single `jsonb` column holding a JSON array (`'[{...}, {...}]'::jsonb`) rather than `jsonb[]` — `jsonb[]` is queried with PostgreSQL array operators, while a JSON array inside `jsonb` is queried with JSON operators (`->`, `@>`).

**Nullability.** `types.JSON` is a reference type (`json.RawMessage` is `[]byte` underneath), so nullability is conveyed by `nil`. There is no `NullJSON` wrapper — a SQL NULL column scans as `nil JSON`, and `Value()` of a nil/empty `JSON` returns SQL NULL. The gotype resolver classifies it as `nullRef`.

---

## 8. Code Generation

### 8.1 Template Engine

Code generation uses Go's `text/template` with `goimports` post-processing. Templates must be structured carefully to remain maintainable at scale.

#### 8.1.1 Architecture

```
gen/
├── gen.go                  # Orchestrator: calls each generator in sequence
├── context.go              # Shared context-building logic
├── funcmap.go              # Custom template function registry
├── format.go               # goimports formatting + file writing
├── templates/
│   ├── shared/             # Reusable fragments (imported by other templates)
│   │   ├── _field.tmpl         # Field rendering (tags, types, comments)
│   │   ├── _filter.tmpl        # Filter struct + comparator field selection
│   │   ├── _field_options.tmpl # FieldOptions struct generation
│   │   ├── _input.tmpl         # Create/Update input struct generation
│   │   ├── _imports.tmpl       # Import block helper
│   │   └── _doc.tmpl           # Doc comment helper
│   ├── table/              # Table-specific templates
│   │   ├── model.tmpl          # Struct definition
│   │   ├── client.tmpl         # Client struct + constructor
│   │   ├── get.tmpl            # Get, GetMany
│   │   ├── create.tmpl         # Create, CreateMany
│   │   ├── update.tmpl         # Update, UpdateMany, UpdateWhere
│   │   ├── delete.tmpl         # SoftDelete*, HardDelete*
│   │   ├── upsert.tmpl         # Upsert
│   │   ├── exists.tmpl         # Exists, ExistsWhere
│   │   ├── count.tmpl          # Count
│   │   ├── increment.tmpl      # Increment
│   │   ├── pagination.tmpl     # Paginate, Connection
│   │   └── relationships.tmpl  # Relationship loading in GetMany
│   ├── view/               # View-specific templates (read-only subset of table/)
│   │   ├── model.tmpl
│   │   ├── client.tmpl
│   │   ├── get.tmpl
│   │   ├── count.tmpl
│   │   └── pagination.tmpl
│   ├── enum.tmpl           # Enum type generation
│   ├── types.tmpl          # Composite, domain, extra types
│   ├── sorter.tmpl         # Per-table sorter structs with typed sort methods
│   ├── pagination.tmpl     # Shared pagination models
│   ├── connection.tmpl     # Shared cursor pagination models
│   ├── error.tmpl          # Shared error types
│   └── client.tmpl         # Unified client aggregator
```

#### 8.1.2 Design Principles

**One template per concern.** Each CRUD operation gets its own template file. A template should generate one logical unit (e.g., the `Create` and `CreateMany` methods), not an entire file mixing unrelated operations.

**Shared fragments via `{{ template }}`.** Common patterns (field rendering, filter structs, input structs, doc comments) live in `shared/` and are invoked by name. This prevents copy-paste between table and view templates.

**Logic in Go, layout in templates.** Templates should contain minimal conditionals. Complex decisions (which comparator type to use, whether a field is omittable, how to convert a UUID FK) are implemented as custom functions in `funcmap.go` and called from templates. The template itself should read close to the output shape.

**Structured context data.** Each generator builds a typed Go struct (e.g., `TableContext`, `ViewContext`, `EnumContext`) with all data pre-computed. Templates iterate over these structs — they never query the schema or config directly.

#### 8.1.3 Custom Function Map

The `funcmap.go` file registers all custom template functions. Functions are grouped by domain:

| Category | Functions | Purpose |
|----------|-----------|---------|
| **Naming** | `toPascalCase`, `toCamelCase`, `structNamePlural`, `toSingular`, `safeGoIdent` | Name transformations. `structNamePlural` never returns its input ([§8.5](#85-naming-rules)); `toPlural` and `toSnakeCase` are not registered |
| **Types** | `goType`, `isNullableType`, `comparatorType`, `zeroValue` | Type resolution and classification |
| **Soft Delete** | `softDeleteSwitch`, `softDeleteValue` | Soft delete SQL generation |
| **Relationships** | `fkStringExpr`, `fkNullGuard`, `isM2M` | FK conversion and relationship logic |
| **Inputs** | `createInputFieldType`, `updateInputFieldType` | Input struct field classification. `pkAutoGenType` is not registered — the app-strategy primary key's generating call depends on the UUID integration the whole package resolved ([§7.4](#74-built-in-type-integrations) "Generating UUID values"), which no single table context can see, so the expression is pre-computed onto the context |
| **Dialect** | `placeholder`, `quoteIdentifier`, `supportsReturning` | Dialect-aware SQL fragments |

Functions must be **pure** (no side effects) and **deterministic** (same input → same output). They receive only the data passed to them — no global state.

#### 8.1.4 Formatting Pipeline

After template execution, every generated file passes through:

1. **Header injection** — the generated file header is prepended (see below)
2. **`goimports`** (`golang.org/x/tools/imports`) — adds missing imports, removes unused imports, formats code
3. **Write** — output to disk with `0o600` permissions. Output directories are auto-created with `os.MkdirAll` if they do not exist.

If `goimports` fails, the raw template output is included in the error message for debugging. This catches template bugs early.

#### 8.1.5 Generated File Header

Every generated file includes a standard header comment:

```go
// Code generated by sqlgen v1.2.0. DO NOT EDIT.
```

- The `// Code generated ... DO NOT EDIT.` pattern is recognized by Go tooling — `go generate`, `golangci-lint`, and IDEs use it to skip generated files from analysis and formatting.
- The version is the sqlgen CLI binary version (e.g., `v1.2.0`), not the config `version` field. This helps consumers track which sqlgen version produced their generated code.
- The header is always the first line of the file, before the `package` declaration.
- **The header is load-bearing for stale-file cleanup** ([§23.8](#238-stale-file-cleanup)): the sweep deletes an orphaned `*_gen.go` only when it carries this header, which is what keeps another generator's `_gen.go` output — and any file a consumer has adopted by removing the header — out of the sweep. It names `sqlgen` specifically rather than matching Go's generic `// Code generated ... DO NOT EDIT.` form, and that distinction is the whole safeguard.

#### 8.1.6 `go:generate` Integration

Consumers can integrate sqlgen into their `go generate` workflow by adding a directive to any Go file in the project:

```go
//go:generate sqlgen generate
```

Running `go generate ./...` then triggers code generation alongside other generators. This works with the standard Go toolchain and requires no additional build system integration.

#### 8.1.7 Testing Strategy

Every package requires both **unit tests** (fast, isolated, no external dependencies) and **integration tests** (against real databases via `testcontainers-go` for PostgreSQL/MySQL and in-memory for SQLite). Unit tests validate logic in isolation; integration tests verify behavior against real database engines. Both are required — neither alone is sufficient.

**Database test infrastructure:**

Integration tests use `testcontainers-go` to spin up ephemeral PostgreSQL and MySQL containers. SQLite uses in-memory databases (no container needed). A shared test helper provides:

```go
// testutil.NewPostgres(t) → *pgxpool.Pool (testcontainer)
// testutil.NewMySQL(t) → *sql.DB (testcontainer)
// testutil.NewSQLite(t) → *sql.DB (in-memory)
```

Containers are created once per test package (via `TestMain`) and cleaned up automatically. Each test gets its own schema (PostgreSQL) or database (MySQL) for isolation.

Integration tests run by default with `go test ./...`. Use `go test -short ./...` to skip integration tests and run only unit tests for a fast feedback loop. Integration tests must check `testing.Short()` and skip themselves. CI runs the full suite without `-short`.

---

##### Template Tests

**Unit tests (per template):**
Each template should have a corresponding test that:
- Builds a minimal context with representative schema data
- Executes the template
- Verifies the output compiles (via `goimports` + `go/parser`)
- Spot-checks key output patterns (struct names, method signatures)

This catches template regressions without running the full generation pipeline.

##### Parser Tests (`parser/`)

**Unit tests:** Each dialect parser has tests covering:
- DDL parsing: `CREATE TABLE`, `ALTER TABLE` (ADD/DROP/MODIFY COLUMN, ADD/DROP CONSTRAINT), `DROP TABLE`
- Type parsing: all SQL types map to the correct internal schema type
- Constraint extraction: PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, UNIQUE, CHECK, INDEX
- Enum/composite/domain type parsing (PostgreSQL)
- Relationship detection: O2O, O2M, M2M (junction table detection with composite PK)
- Self-referential and circular FK handling
- Multi-file parsing: strict mode (duplicate = error), merge mode (sequential apply, destructive DDL)
- Migration file filtering: `*.down.sql`/`*_down.sql` skipped, `*.up.sql`/`*_up.sql` included
- Edge cases: reserved word column names, quoted identifiers, empty tables, tables with no PK

**Integration tests:** Each dialect parser is tested against a real database:
- Parse a schema file → introspect the same schema from a live database → verify both produce an identical schema model
- ALTER TABLE sequences applied in file order produce the expected final schema

##### Config Validation Tests (`config/`)

**Unit tests:** Each validation rule in Section 4.13 has positive (valid) and negative (error/warning) test cases:
- Driver/dialect mismatch (pgx + MySQL = error)
- Table-level `cursor_keys` referencing non-existent columns (error)
- View-level `cursor_keys` referencing non-existent columns (error)
- Inherited `cursor_keys` missing on table with PK → PK fallback, no warning
- Inherited `cursor_keys` missing on table without PK → `Connection` omitted, warning
- Inherited `cursor_keys` missing on view → `Connection` omitted, warning
- Partial match on inherited `cursor_keys` triggers full fallback (not subset)
- Resolved `cursor_keys` naming a `write_only` / `hidden` / `internal` column → error (§32.4); exempt when `Connection` is off or the keys do not resolve
- Table with no PK and no `primary_key.columns` override → skipped from generation, warning
- `primary_key.columns` lists a non-existent column → error
- `primary_key.columns` lists a nullable column → error
- `primary_key.columns` columns lack a UNIQUE constraint → warning (not error — uniqueness may be app-enforced)
- `primary_key.columns` set alongside an auto-detected PK → override wins silently (no warning)
- `soft_delete_columns` type mismatch (e.g., `varchar` column)
- Struct name collisions (auto-detected and explicit `struct_name`)
- `exclude_columns` removing all columns (warning, table skipped)
- `input.schema` on MySQL/SQLite (warning, ignored)
- Missing `connection` for `database`/`both` source
- Invalid `api.operations` preset names; a leftover `operations` key under `generation` or `tables.<t>` (error naming `api.operations`); a client-only key in an `api.operations` mask
- A per-table `api.operations` key set `true` that the table's client does not generate (warning, resolution-level)
- Two-phase validation: config-level errors detected before parsing, schema-level errors detected after

##### SQL Builder Tests (`sql/`)

**Unit tests:** Each builder function (Appendix A) is tested per dialect:
- `BuildSelect`: column selection, WHERE clause from filters, ORDER BY, LIMIT/OFFSET, schema-qualified table names
- `BuildInsert`: single and multi-row, RETURNING clause (PostgreSQL/SQLite), omitted columns for DB defaults
- `BuildUpdate`: `omittable.Value[T]` handling (only set fields in SET clause), empty update (no-op), RETURNING
