| `CreateMany` | `(ctx, []*CreateInput, ...func(*CallOptions[FO])) → ([]*Entity, error)` | Batch insert. Returns `ErrNilInput` when any element is nil ([9.4c](#94c-nil-input-handling)). Splits into batches of `generation.batch_size`. Returns all created entities. Sub-batches are not auto-rolled back — wrap in transaction for atomicity. |
| `Update` | `(ctx, pk, *UpdateInput, ...func(*CallOptions[FO])) → (*Entity, error)` | Partial update. Only fields where `IsSet()` is true are in the SET clause. If no fields are set, no UPDATE is executed and the current entity is returned unchanged. Returns `ErrNilInput` when input is nil ([9.4c](#94c-nil-input-handling)) — distinct from an empty-but-non-nil input, which is the documented no-op. Returns `ErrNotFound` if PK does not exist (configurable, see [9.5](#95-edge-case-behaviors)). Honours the empty-`FieldOptions` skip like every sibling write method — a non-nil `FieldOptions` that selects nothing suppresses the trailing re-fetch and the method returns `nil, nil` ([9.6](#96-per-call-options)), on the empty-update path as well as the normal one. |
| `UpdateMany` | `(ctx, []UpdateItem, ...func(*CallOptions[FO])) → ([]*Entity, error)` | Batch update. Each item is (pk, input). Returns `ErrNilInput` when any item's `Input` is nil ([9.4c](#94c-nil-input-handling)). Returns all updated entities. |
| `UpdateWhere` | `(ctx, *Filter, *UpdateInput, ...func(*CallOptions[FO])) → ([]*Entity, error)` | Bulk update all rows matching filter. Returns all affected entities. Returns `ErrNilInput` when input is nil, checked before the filter ([9.4c](#94c-nil-input-handling)). Returns `ErrEmptyFilter` if filter produces zero conditions. Idempotent — returns empty slice when no rows match. |
| `Upsert` | `(ctx, *CreateInput, {Table}ConflictTarget, ...func(*CallOptions[FO])) → (*Entity, error)` | Insert or update on conflict. Returns `ErrNilInput` when input is nil ([9.4c](#94c-nil-input-handling)). Conflict target is a generated type-safe enum restricting to valid unique constraints (see [9.5 Upsert Conflict Keys](#upsert-conflict-keys)). Dialect-aware: PostgreSQL uses `ON CONFLICT ... DO UPDATE SET`, MySQL uses `ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE`. |
| `UpsertMany` | `(ctx, []*CreateInput, {Table}ConflictTarget, ...func(*CallOptions[FO])) → ([]*Entity, error)` | Batch insert-or-update on conflict. Mirrors `Upsert`'s signature — one conflict target for the whole batch, drawn from the same generated enum. Returns `ErrNilInput` when any element is nil ([9.4c](#94c-nil-input-handling)). Splits into batches of `generation.batch_size`, one statement per sub-batch ([25.1](#251-query-count-guarantee)). **Inputs resolving to the same conflict target are deduped before the statement is built, last occurrence wins** — PostgreSQL rejects an `ON CONFLICT ... DO UPDATE` that would affect one row twice, while MySQL and SQLite accept it and keep the last row, so the dedupe is what makes one spelling behave identically on all three. Returns one entity per deduped input on every dialect, the `DO NOTHING` branch included: entities come from a re-fetch by key, never from `RETURNING` ([9.5 Batch upsert](#batch-upsert--dedupe-return-shape-and-key-resolution)). A sub-batch whose written keys the input cannot name — a database-generated key, or any conflict target that does not cover the primary key — adds a key-resolution read ([9.7](#97-pk-resolution-and-entity-return-path)). Generated whenever `Upsert` is, that is, when the table emits a conflict target ([4.6 Operations](#operations)). |
| `CreateWithRelated` | `(ctx, *Create{Table}WithRelatedInput, ...func(*CallOptions[FO])) → (*Entity, error)` | Creates the row together with rows on its eligible relationships, in one transaction. See [9.9](#99-nested-mutations). |
| `UpdateWithRelated` | `(ctx, pk, *Update{Table}WithRelatedInput, ...func(*CallOptions[FO])) → (*Entity, error)` | Updates the row and applies a verb block per eligible relationship, in one transaction. See [9.9](#99-nested-mutations). |
| `UpsertWithRelated` | `(ctx, *Upsert{Table}WithRelatedInput, {Table}ConflictTarget, ...func(*CallOptions[FO])) → (*Entity, error)` | Inserts or updates the row and applies the same verb blocks `UpdateWithRelated` accepts, in one transaction. See [9.9](#99-nested-mutations). |
| `Increment` | `(ctx, pk, IncrementInput[{Table}IncrementColumn], ...func(*CallOptions[FO])) → error` | Atomic column increment/decrement. Column is restricted to numeric non-identifying columns — neither PK, FK, nor the tenant column — via the generated `{Table}IncrementColumn` enum. Negative amount performs decrement. Returns `ErrNotFound` if PK does not exist (configurable). |

**The three `…WithRelated` methods are separate methods, not extra arguments on the three they compose.** `Create` and `Upsert` share one `Create<T>Input` — on the GraphQL surface `create<Table>` and `upsert<Table>` are projected from the same input type ([26.5.1](#2651-exposed-resolver-surface)) — so a nested member added to it would be advertised on both and honoured by neither reliably: the schema would accept a field the executor drops. Each nested method therefore takes its own wrapper input type that *contains* the flat one rather than restating its fields. Nested methods are emitted only when the base operation they compose is also enabled ([4.13](#413-config-validation-rules)) and the table has at least one eligible relationship ([9.9](#99-nested-mutations)).

### 9.3 Delete Operations

| Method | Signature | Description |
|--------|-----------|-------------|
| `SoftDelete` | `(ctx, pk, ...func(*CallOptions[FO])) → (*Entity, error)` | Sets soft delete column and returns the updated entity. Only generated if table has a matching soft delete column. Idempotent — returns `nil, nil` if PK does not exist. |
| `SoftDeleteMany` | `(ctx, []pk, ...func(*CallOptions[FO])) → ([]*Entity, error)` | Batch soft delete. Returns all affected entities. |
| `SoftDeleteWhere` | `(ctx, *Filter, ...func(*CallOptions[FO])) → ([]*Entity, error)` | Conditional soft delete. Returns all affected entities. Returns `ErrEmptyFilter` if filter produces zero conditions. Idempotent — returns empty slice when no rows match. |
| `Restore` | `(ctx, pk, ...func(*CallOptions[FO])) → (*Entity, error)` | Clears soft delete column, restoring a soft-deleted row, and returns the restored entity. Only generated if table has a matching soft delete column. Idempotent — returns `nil, nil` if PK does not exist. |
| `RestoreMany` | `(ctx, []pk, ...func(*CallOptions[FO])) → ([]*Entity, error)` | Batch restore. Returns all restored entities. |
| `RestoreWhere` | `(ctx, *Filter, ...func(*CallOptions[FO])) → ([]*Entity, error)` | Conditional restore. Returns all restored entities. Returns `ErrEmptyFilter` if filter produces zero conditions. Idempotent — returns empty slice when no rows match. |
| `HardDelete` | `(ctx, pk, ...func(*CallOptions[FO])) → error` | Physical DELETE. Always generated. Idempotent — returns `nil` if PK does not exist. |
| `HardDeleteMany` | `(ctx, []pk, ...func(*CallOptions[FO])) → error` | Batch hard delete. |
| `HardDeleteWhere` | `(ctx, *Filter, ...func(*CallOptions[FO])) → error` | Conditional hard delete. Returns `ErrEmptyFilter` if filter produces zero conditions. Idempotent — returns `nil` when no rows match. |

### 9.4 Pagination Operations

| Method | Signature | Description |
|--------|-----------|-------------|
| `Paginate` | `(ctx, PaginateInput[Filter], ...func(*CallOptions[FO])) → (*PaginateResult[Entity], error)` | Offset-based pagination with total count. Delegates to `Count` and `GetMany` internally. |
| `Connection` | `(ctx, ConnectionInput[Filter], ...func(*CallOptions[FO])) → (*Connection[Entity], error)` | Relay cursor pagination. Sort order determined by `cursor_keys` — no custom sorts. Use `Paginate` for custom sort orders. |

**Shared generic input/output types** — generated once per package, not per table:

```go
type PaginateInput[F any] struct {
    Filter *F
    Limit  int
    Offset int
}

type ConnectionInput[F any] struct {
    Filter *F
    First  *int
    Last   *int
    After  *string
    Before *string
}

type IncrementInput[C ~string] struct {
    Column C
    Amount int
}

type PaginateResult[T any] struct {
    Items           []*T
    TotalCount      int64
    TotalPages      int
    PageSize        int
    CurrentPage     int
    HasNextPage     bool
    HasPreviousPage bool
}
```

### 9.4a Streaming Operations

`Stream` is an iterator-style read for memory-bounded bulk processing — ETL exports, background re-indexing, large analytics aggregations. It uses Go 1.23+ `iter.Seq2[*Entity, error]` to yield rows one at a time as the driver returns them, without materializing the full result set into memory.

Stream is generated for every table, alongside `Get`, `GetMany`, `Connection`, etc. It has no GraphQL projection, so no `api.operations` key names it. The relationship-topology constraint is enforced at the type level — `StreamFieldOptions` simply does not contain relationship fields — so consumers cannot misuse it.

#### Signature

```go
Stream(
    ctx context.Context,
    input *Stream{Table}Input,
    opts ...func(*CallOptions[Stream{Table}FieldOptions]),
) iter.Seq2[*{Table}, error]
```

#### Generated input type

A dedicated input struct strips out fields that don't apply to streaming:

```go
type StreamProductsInput struct {
    Filter *ProductFilter `json:"filter"`
    Sorts  []sql.Sort     `json:"sorts"`
    // No Limit, no Offset — streams have no bounds by design.
}
```

The contract is enforced by the type, not by runtime validation. There is no way to set `Limit` or `Offset` on a Stream input — the fields don't exist.

#### Generated FieldOptions type

A dedicated FieldOptions struct contains only scalar column bools — no relationship fields:

```go
type StreamProductFieldOptions struct {
    ID        bool
    Name      bool
    Price     bool
    CreatedAt bool
    // No relationships. Stream cannot load O2O, O2M, or M2M relationships.
}
```

This is intentional and enforced by the type system. Stream does not emit JOINs in the SELECT and does not perform the parent-ID-batching pass that O2M/M2M loading requires. If a consumer needs relationship data alongside streamed rows, they should:

1. Use `Connection` in a loop instead (each page calls `GetMany` internally and supports all relationship types), or
2. Stream the parents, then issue a separate batched query for related data per processing batch.

#### Yielded type

Stream yields `*{Table}` — the same entity struct used by `Get`/`GetMany`. Relationship fields on the yielded value (`p.Reviews`, `p.Company`, `p.Tags`) are at their zero value (nil slice / nil pointer). This matches the existing pattern for `GetMany` calls without those FieldOptions selected, so consumers won't be surprised.

#### Constraints

- **`input.Limit` / `input.Offset` not representable.** The type doesn't have these fields.
- **No relationships.** `Stream{Table}FieldOptions` has only scalar columns.
- **Cache always bypassed.** `CallOptions.SkipCache` is forced to `true` regardless of caller setting. Streaming a million rows through a cache layer makes no sense — the cache is for hot-path entity reads.
- **DB connection held for the duration of iteration.** Long-running streams reduce pool capacity for concurrent requests. Document and accept the tradeoff.
- **Refused inside a transaction unless the caller opts in.** See *Stream inside a transaction* below.
- **Not resumable across processes.** The cursor is in-process. `Connection` is the method for pausing and resuming, since its cursor is durable across processes.
- **Not exposed via the GraphQL/REST API layers.** Stream is a backend primitive for Go consumers, not a surface for external clients.

#### Stream inside a transaction

`Stream` is the only generated method that runs **consumer code inside an open result set** — the `yield` body executes between `Next()` calls, with the connection still streaming. Inside a transaction that is the transaction's only connection, and it is held by the transaction's reservation for the whole iteration ([18.5](#185-concurrent-safety)). The two contracts are incompatible: `Stream`'s is *the connection stays open across caller code*, a transaction's is *one connection, one statement at a time*. A consumer who writes inside the stream loop on the same `txCtx` — an ordinary ETL spelling — is issuing a statement mid-iteration, and waits on a reservation it holds itself.

**`Stream` therefore refuses a transaction by default.** The guard runs before any SQL is issued, mirroring the [9.6a](#96a-lock-modes) `LockMode` precondition and surfaced through `yield` because `Stream` returns an iterator:

```go
if database.InTransaction(ctx) && !options.AllowInTransaction {
    yield(nil, fmt.Errorf("stream %s: unsupported inside a transaction — use Connection in a loop, "+
        "or set AllowInTransaction for a snapshot-consistent stream that issues nothing else on this txCtx", table))
    return
}
```

**The opt-in is `CallOptions.AllowInTransaction`.** It exists for the one workload the refusal would otherwise strand: a snapshot-consistent scan under `RepeatableRead` / `ReadOnly` that issues no other statement on that `txCtx`. `Connection`-in-a-loop gives the same snapshot but pays a `COUNT` plus keyset conditions per page, which is the overhead this method exists to avoid.

The rule the opt-in commits the caller to is the same one [18.5](#185-concurrent-safety) states for
every other door into a transaction: **drain or close a result set before issuing the next statement
on that `txCtx`.** An opted-in `Stream` holds its result set open for the whole iteration, so
"issues nothing else on this `txCtx`" is that rule applied to a loop whose body is caller code.

Three things the opt-in does and does not do:

- **An opted-in `Stream` still holds the reservation** for the whole iteration. It is the ordinary read described in [18.5](#185-concurrent-safety), not a bypass. A concurrent reader on the same `txCtx` therefore queues behind it safely; opting the stream *out* of the reservation would restore the data race the reservation exists to remove, and is not offered.
- **The obligation is documentary and cannot be verified.** Nothing can detect "will you issue another statement". A caller who opts in and then writes inside the loop meets the self-hold case — a wait bounded only by `ctx` or `TxOptions.Timeout`, which also stalls pool teardown while it lasts.
- **It does not propagate through `nestedChildOptions`.** Like `LockMode` and `FieldOptions`, it is meaningful to the call that sets it and is not inherited by the inner calls a nested mutation makes ([9.9](#99-nested-mutations)).

**`AllowInTransaction` is emitted unconditionally**, on every generated `CallOptions[FO]`, exactly as `LockMode` and `SkipEvents` are. `CallOptions` already carries fields meaningful on only a subset of methods — `SkipEvents` on mutations, `LockMode` on reads — and `Stream` is generated on every table ([4.6 Operations](#operations)), so the only thing a gate could key on is whether the package has a table at all — a schema accident, not a mode the consumer chose. The tenancy fields are gated because tenancy is a project-wide mode a package either has or does not. The manifest's `conventions.call_options.fields` list carries it for the same reason it carries `LockMode` — an agent reading the manifest needs to know a field exists that decides whether a method works at all ([30.4.1](#3041-conventions-block)).

**The alternative, and when to prefer it.** `Connection` in a loop delegates to `GetMany` with a `LIMIT`, so each page is one complete, fully-drained query and caller code runs *between* pages rather than inside a result set. It needs no opt-in and no guard, and it is the right answer for reading inside a transaction in general — see the decision table below.

#### Hook integration

Stream fires the query-hook chain once per call, with `Op: hook.OpStream` — **except when the in-transaction guard refuses the call**, which returns through `yield` before the chain is built, so a refused `Stream` issues no SQL and fires no hooks at all, global authorization included. That matches [9.6a](#96a-lock-modes)'s `LockMode` precondition, which likewise rejects before the chain. Tenancy, soft-delete, and other condition-injecting hooks add WHERE conditions to the input the same way they do for `OpGetMany`. The cache hook does not need an op-specific dispatch — Stream forces `options.SkipCache = true` in the method body (see Constraints above), and the existing `cacheSkipper` short-circuit (Section 27) routes the call straight to `next` without any read-through or write-through.

Read-side events do not fire on `OpStream` (consistent with `OpGetMany` — only mutations emit events).

#### Implementation pattern

```go
func (c *productClient) Stream(ctx context.Context, input *StreamProductsInput, opts ...func(*CallOptions[StreamProductFieldOptions])) iter.Seq2[*Product, error] {
    return func(yield func(*Product, error) bool) {
        options := resolveCallOptions(opts)
        options.SkipCache = true

        // Refused before any SQL and before the hook chain is built.
        if database.InTransaction(ctx) && !options.AllowInTransaction {
            yield(nil, fmt.Errorf("stream products: unsupported inside a transaction — use Connection in a loop, "+
                "or set AllowInTransaction for a snapshot-consistent stream that issues nothing else on this txCtx"))
            return
        }

        // stopped is true while the loop body runs, and stays true once it
        // breaks or panics out of yield; yield must not be called after either.
        var stopped bool
        emit := func(p *Product, err error) bool {
            stopped = true
            if !yield(p, err) { return false }
            stopped = false
            return true
        }

        _, err := c.executeQuery(ctx, options.SkipHooks, &hook.QueryContext{
            Op: hook.OpStream, Table: TableProducts, Schema: "public",
            Input: input, CallOptions: options,
        }, func(ctx context.Context, q *hook.QueryContext) (any, error) {
            conn := database.Conn(ctx, c.querier)

            columns := productScalarColumns
            if options.FieldOptions != nil {
                if selected := options.FieldOptions.Columns(); len(selected) > 0 {
                    columns = selected
                }
            }

            var conds []sql.Condition
            if input.Filter != nil {
                conds = input.Filter.ToConditions(c.dialect)
            }

            query, args := sql.BuildSelect(c.dialect, c.table, sql.SelectOptions{
                Columns:    columns,
                Conditions: conds,
                OrderBy:    input.Sorts,
                // No Limit, no Offset, no Joins.
            })

            rows, err := conn.Query(ctx, query, args...)
            if err != nil {
                emit(nil, fmt.Errorf("stream products: %w", err))
                return nil, nil
            }
            defer rows.Close()

            for rows.Next() {
                p, err := scanProductRow(rows, columns)
                if err != nil {
                    if !emit(nil, err) { return nil, nil }
                    continue
                }
                if !emit(p, nil) { return nil, nil }
            }
            if err := rows.Err(); err != nil {
                emit(nil, err)
            }
            return nil, nil
        })
        // A recovered panic (21.6) or a hook's abort error (21.5) is the chain's
        // return value; Stream has no error return, so it is yielded last.
        if err != nil && !stopped {
            yield(nil, err)
        }
    }
}
```

#### Consumer usage

```go
// ETL: process every product over $100, sorted by ID.
for p, err := range client.Products.Stream(ctx, &StreamProductsInput{
    Filter: &ProductFilter{
        Price: &comparator.Number[float64]{Gt: new(100.0)},
    },
    Sorts: []sql.Sort{{Column: "id", Desc: false}},
}) {
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("stream: %w", err)
    }
    if err := processProduct(p); err != nil {
        return err
    }
}

// Early termination via break — defer rows.Close handles cleanup.
for p, err := range client.Products.Stream(ctx, input) {
    if err != nil { return err }
    if shouldStop(p) { break }
    process(p)
}
```

#### When to choose Stream vs. Connection-in-a-loop

Both approaches handle "iterate over many rows" workloads. Pick based on what the workload needs:

| Need | Use |
|------|-----|
| Relationships (O2O, O2M, M2M) loaded with each row | `Connection` in a loop |
| Resumability across processes (save the cursor, resume tomorrow) | `Connection` in a loop |
| Pool-friendliness on long reads (release the connection between pages) | `Connection` in a loop |
| Reading inside a transaction | `Connection` in a loop |
| Minimal per-page round-trip cost on millions of rows | `Stream` |
| Scalar-only column projection over a large filtered set | `Stream` |
| Single-process backend job (ETL, re-indexing, exports) | `Stream` |

The *reading inside a transaction* row is the one that is enforced rather than advised: `Stream` refuses a transaction unless `CallOptions.AllowInTransaction` is set, and the opt-in is for a scan that issues nothing else on that `txCtx`.

`Connection`-in-a-loop pattern (when relationships or resumability are required):

```go
cursor := ""
for {
    page, err := client.Products.Connection(ctx, ConnectionInput[ProductFilter]{
        First:  new(1000),
        After:  &cursor,
        Filter: filter,
    }, func(o *CallOptions[ProductFieldOptions]) {
        o.FieldOptions = &ProductFieldOptions{Reviews: ...}  // works fine
    })
    if err != nil { return err }
    for _, edge := range page.Edges {
        process(edge.Node)
    }
    if !page.PageInfo.HasNextPage { break }
    cursor = *page.PageInfo.EndCursor
}
```

The two methods are complementary. The relationship-topology constraint on `Stream` (enforced by `StreamFieldOptions`) makes the choice unambiguous — a read that needs related data will not type-check against `Stream`, which leaves `Connection`.

---

### 9.4b No-PK tables are skipped

When a table has no primary key — neither a `PRIMARY KEY` clause in the schema nor a `tables.<name>.primary_key.columns` override (see [8.6](#86-primary-key-strategy)) — sqlgen **skips the table from generation entirely**. No client interface, model struct, filter type, cache entry, event hook, or `hook.TableName` constant is emitted for it. Other tables are unaffected; the rest of the schema generates normally. That includes the tables its foreign keys reference: the FK-inferred relationship into the skipped table is omitted from them, since there is no type to name. A relationship *declared* into it is an error ([4.13](#413-config-validation-rules)).

A warning is emitted at generation time naming each skipped table (see [4.13](#413-config-validation-rules)) so the omission is never silent. The warning text directs users toward either:

1. **Declare the PK explicitly** via `tables.<name>.primary_key.columns: [...]` (see [§8.6](#86-primary-key-strategy)) — the override promotes the named columns to the PK position and the table generates with the full PK-keyed client surface as if it had a native `PRIMARY KEY` clause.
2. **Fix the schema** (`ALTER TABLE ... ADD PRIMARY KEY (...)`) — preferred; makes the contract explicit at the DB level.
3. **Silence the warning** via top-level `exclude_tables` (see [6.4](#64-filtering)) when the table is genuinely not part of the consumer's surface.

The override path is the recommended workaround for real-world schemas where uniqueness is added post-`CREATE TABLE` via `ALTER TABLE ... ADD CONSTRAINT ... UNIQUE` (counter / junction / ACL tables) — the override tells sqlgen which UNIQUE-covered column set acts as the row identity without requiring a DDL change. See the postgres example (`cmd/sqlgen/testdata/examples/postgres/`) — the `counters` and `rate_limits` tables both exercise this path with single-column and composite overrides respectively.

**Rationale.** Every generated entity method is keyed on the primary key in some way — `Get` / `Update` / `HardDelete` take a PK argument directly; `CreateMany` re-fetches inserted rows via a PK-filter `IN` clause; cache keys and event payloads identify rows by PK. A "filter-only" reduced surface omitting the PK-keyed methods would require special-case branches throughout the templates, cache builder, and event builder; sqlgen holds the simpler "tables must have a PK" contract instead. Tables that are intentionally PK-less retain a one-line escape hatch via `primary_key.columns`.

---

### 9.4c Nil input handling

Every generated method that takes a pointer input must behave predictably when a caller passes `nil`. A nil pointer is an ordinary thing to write — an unfiltered read is spelled `GetMany(ctx, nil)` far more naturally than `GetMany(ctx, &GetUsersInput{})` — so **no generated method may panic on a nil input**, and none may silently do the wrong thing.

The rule splits on direction, because "no values supplied" means something coherent on a read and nothing coherent on a write.

**Reads — `GetMany`, `Stream` — normalize `nil` to the zero-value input.** The normalization happens at the top of the method, before the hook context is built, so a hook never observes a nil `QueryContext.Input` either. This invents no behavior: the zero-value input is already a legal, meaningful argument (no filter, no sorts, no limit), and every sibling read already treats "no criteria" the same way — `Count(nil)` counts all rows, `ExistsWhere(nil)` tests for any row, and `PaginateInput` / `ConnectionInput` are value types whose zero value pages everything. `GetMany(ctx, nil)` and `GetMany(ctx, &Get<T>Input{})` are therefore the same call.

**Writes — `Create`, `Update`, `Upsert` — return [`ErrNilInput`](#22-error-handling).** These must *not* normalize to the zero value. A zero `Create<T>Input` is a legal argument that writes a row: it sends each required field's zero value, and with no required field the row takes every column's default — a nullable column with no `DEFAULT` takes NULL. That last case supplies no column at all, and the INSERT takes the dialect's all-defaults form ([Appendix A](#appendix-a-sql-builder-functions)). Treating a nil input as the zero value would therefore turn a caller's mistake into a silently written row — worse than the panic it replaces. The guard runs before the mutation executor, so a nil input fires no hook, publishes no event, and invalidates no cache entry.

`UpdateWhere` takes both a filter and an input, and checks the **input first**: argument validity is a property of the call, while `ErrEmptyFilter` is a safety guard on what the filter compiles to, so `UpdateWhere(ctx, nil, nil)` reports `ErrNilInput`. A non-nil input with an empty filter still returns `ErrEmptyFilter`.

`ErrNilInput` is distinct from `ErrEmptyFilter` (a `*Where` op whose filter compiles to zero conditions) and from the documented no-op of an **empty but non-nil** `Update<T>Input`, which still returns the current entity unchanged. Bulk write variants distinguish the two nils. A nil **slice** is simply no rows: `CreateMany(ctx, nil)` and `UpdateMany(ctx, nil)` do nothing, since nil and empty already mean the same thing there. A nil **element** is the same caller error a nil single-row input is, and returns `ErrNilInput` — skipping it silently would drop a row the caller asked to write. `Update<T>Item.Input` is a pointer, so a zero-valued item carries a nil one and is rejected on the same rule; `[]Update<T>Item{{ID: id}}` is a shape that compiles naturally.

**Why this is stated here rather than left to each operation.** The failure mode is not uniform, and the quietest case is the easiest to miss. Panic recovery ([§21.6](#216-panic-recovery)) turns an unguarded nil dereference into an error rather than a crash, so a read the caller meant as "no criteria" returns `sqlgen: panic in …` instead of rows — and on `Stream` that error arrives only as the iterator's final yield, after zero rows. A rule that only covered the loud panics would leave that one standing.

---

### 9.5 Edge Case Behaviors

#### Batch Failure Semantics

`CreateMany`, `UpdateMany`, `HardDeleteMany`, and `SoftDeleteMany` split their input into sub-batches of `generation.batch_size`. If any sub-batch fails, the operation returns an error immediately. **Previously executed sub-batches within the same call are not automatically rolled back.**

Consumers are expected to wrap batch mutations in a transaction when atomicity is required:

```go
err := database.WithTransaction(ctx, db, "bulk_insert", func(txCtx context.Context) error {
    // Same client — txCtx carries the transaction, resolved internally via database.Conn()
    _, err := client.Products().CreateMany(txCtx, inputs)
    return err // on error: entire transaction rolls back, including earlier sub-batches
})
```

Without a transaction, partial writes from successful sub-batches persist. This is the consumer's responsibility — the generated code does not implicitly wrap batch operations in transactions.

#### Empty Update Handling

When `Update` is called with an `UpdateInput` where no fields are set (all `omittable.Value` fields are unset), no `UPDATE` statement is executed. The method fetches and returns the current entity unchanged. This avoids a no-op database round-trip for the write while still returning the expected entity. **One exception, per [9.2](#92-write-operations):** a non-nil `FieldOptions` that selects nothing suppresses that fetch too, and the method returns `nil, nil` — so an empty input under an empty `FieldOptions` issues no statement at all.

#### Idempotent Where Operations

`UpdateWhere`, `SoftDeleteWhere`, `RestoreWhere`, and `HardDeleteWhere` are idempotent — when no rows match the filter, they return `nil` (no error). This simplifies consumer code by not requiring callers to distinguish "nothing matched" from success.

#### Non-Existent PK Behavior

When an operation targets a PK that does not exist in the database:

| Operation | Default Behavior | Rationale |
|-----------|-----------------|-----------|
| `Update` | Returns `ErrNotFound` | The caller expects to modify an existing entity. A missing PK is likely a bug. |
| `Increment` | Returns `ErrNotFound` | Same as Update — expects an existing entity. |
| `HardDelete` | Returns `nil` (idempotent) | Deletion is the desired outcome. The row not existing achieves the goal. |
| `SoftDelete` | Returns `nil` (idempotent) | Same rationale as HardDelete. |
| `Restore` | Returns `nil` (idempotent) | Same rationale — restoring a non-existent row is a no-op. |

**Configuration:** The Update/Increment behavior is configurable globally and per-table via `generation.strict_updates`:

| Value | Behavior |
|-------|----------|
| `true` (default) | `Update`/`Increment` returns `ErrNotFound` when PK does not exist |
| `false` | `Update`/`Increment` returns `nil` (idempotent, no error) |

```yaml
# Global: strict by default
generation:
  strict_updates: true

# Per-table override: make audit_logs updates idempotent
tables:
  audit_logs:
    strict_updates: false
```

Delete operations are always idempotent regardless of this setting — there is no `strict_deletes` option.

#### Upsert Conflict Keys

The `conflictKeys` parameter tells the database which unique constraint to use for conflict detection. The parser extracts all PRIMARY KEY and UNIQUE constraints from the schema (section 5.1), and the generator produces a **type-safe enum** restricting `conflictKeys` to valid options. Invalid conflict targets are caught at compile time, not runtime.

**Generated conflict target type:**

The generator produces a named type with one constant per unique constraint. Each constant maps to a set of columns via a generated lookup, so composite unique constraints are fully supported.

```go
// Generated per table
type ProductConflictTarget int

const (
    ProductConflictPK          ProductConflictTarget = iota // PRIMARY KEY (id)
    ProductConflictSKU                                      // UNIQUE (sku)
    ProductConflictRegionSlug                               // UNIQUE (region, slug)
)

// Generated — maps each constant to its column set. Used internally by the SQL builder.
var productConflictColumns = map[ProductConflictTarget][]string{
    ProductConflictPK:         {"id"},
    ProductConflictSKU:        {"sku"},
    ProductConflictRegionSlug: {"region", "slug"},
}
```

**Naming:** Constants are named `{Table}Conflict{Name}` where `Name` is derived from:
- **Single column:** PascalCase of the column name (e.g., `sku` → `SKU`)
- **Composite columns:** PascalCase concatenation of column names (e.g., `(region, slug)` → `RegionSlug`)
- **Explicit constraint name override:** If the derived name is ambiguous, the SQL constraint name is used (stripped of table prefix and `_key`/`_unique` suffixes)

**Usage:**

```go
// Single-column conflict target
product, err := client.Products().Upsert(ctx, input, <pkg>.ProductConflictSKU)
// → ON CONFLICT ("sku") DO UPDATE SET ...

// Composite conflict target — same API, multiple columns resolved internally
product, err := client.Products().Upsert(ctx, input, <pkg>.ProductConflictRegionSlug)
// → ON CONFLICT ("region", "slug") DO UPDATE SET ...
```

**Generated SQL by dialect:**

| Dialect | Generated SQL |
|---------|--------------|
| PostgreSQL | `ON CONFLICT (col1, col2) DO UPDATE SET col3 = excluded.col3, ...` |
| MySQL | `ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE col3 = VALUES(col3), ...` (conflict target is implicit) |
| SQLite | `ON CONFLICT (col1, col2) DO UPDATE SET col3 = excluded.col3, ...` |

**MySQL note:** MySQL's `ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE` does not accept an explicit conflict target — it triggers on any unique constraint violation. The `conflictKeys` parameter is accepted for API consistency but does not affect the generated MySQL SQL. The consumer should be aware that MySQL may trigger on a different constraint than the one specified. The one case the generator rules out is a target naming a column the INSERT does not write, which carries no conflict clause on any dialect (below).

**Update columns in upsert:** The `DO UPDATE SET` clause includes all non-PK, non-conflict-key columns from the `CreateInput`. Columns that are part of the conflict target or PK are excluded from the SET clause (they are the identity, not the payload).

**Tables with no unique constraints:** If a table has no UNIQUE constraints, `{Table}ConflictPK` is the only conflict target generated.

**The PK conflict target requires schema evidence of an index.** `ON CONFLICT` resolves against a real unique index, so `{Table}ConflictPK` is emitted only when one backs the key: a declared `PRIMARY KEY` constraint always does, and so does a set-equal, non-partial `UNIQUE` (or an inline single-column `UNIQUE`) over the same columns. A primary key declared **only** through `tables.<name>.primary_key.columns` ([8.6](#86-primary-key-strategy)), with neither of those present, is app-enforced uniqueness — the generator emits **no** `{Table}ConflictPK` constant for it rather than a target the database would reject. The guard fails closed deliberately, and anything that takes a conflict target as an argument inherits it: the nested upsert then has no `PK` to pass or default to; it keeps a required `conflictTarget` while a unique target is left, and is omitted when none is ([9.9](#99-nested-mutations), rule **E10**). The flat `upsert<Table>` GraphQL mutation hard-codes `{Table}ConflictPK`, so it is omitted whenever that constant is ([26.5.1](#2651-exposed-resolver-surface)). A table left with no conflict-target constant at all — an app-enforced key with no non-partial UNIQUE beside it — likewise omits `Upsert`, `UpsertMany` and the `{Table}ConflictTarget` type: the only value the argument could take is the zero value, which names no columns, and the statement would be a plain INSERT that duplicates the key.

**Conflict targets that cover every inserted column:** When the exclusions above leave no column to set — the conflict target covers every column the caller supplied — there is nothing to update. PostgreSQL and SQLite emit `DO NOTHING`; MySQL, which has no `DO NOTHING` and rejects an empty `ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE`, assigns a key column to itself. Both leave the conflicting row untouched. This is not limited to pure link tables: a surrogate-PK lookup table upserted on its natural unique key (`tags(id, name UNIQUE)` targeting `name`) reaches it too. See [Section 9.7](#97-pk-resolution-and-entity-return-path) for what PK resolution must do on this branch.

**An input that supplies no column is a plain insert.** A zero `Create<T>Input` on a table with no required field supplies no column ([9.4c](#94c-nil-input-handling)), so the INSERT takes the dialect's all-defaults form (`DEFAULT VALUES`, or `() VALUES ()` on MySQL) and `Upsert` emits **no** conflict clause on any dialect. SQLite accepts no upsert clause after `DEFAULT VALUES`, and the rule is uniform so that one spelling has one outcome. On the common target — a database-generated primary key — nothing can conflict, and the call inserts a new row of column defaults. A conflict on a `UNIQUE` column that has a `DEFAULT` is a unique violation on every dialect (PostgreSQL 23505, SQLite 2067, MySQL 1062) rather than an update. On MySQL this is a deliberate change: `ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE` would otherwise match that row and return it unchanged.

**A conflict target the INSERT does not write is no target.** The same rule holds when the input supplies columns but not every column of the conflict target — `{Table}ConflictPK` on a database-generated key, or a unique column left to its `DEFAULT`. Such a target can match only a value the database chose, never one the caller supplied, so `Upsert` emits no conflict clause and the call is a plain insert. On PostgreSQL and SQLite this changes only a target over a defaulted column (including a sequence-backed key whose next value collides with a row inserted with an explicit key), which no longer updates the row that holds that value. On MySQL, whose `ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE` names no target, it is what stops a primary-key upsert from updating whichever row a different unique column collided with — including a `read_only` column with a constant `DEFAULT` ([32.3](#323-per-surface-behavior)), which the flat `upsert<Table>` mutation ([26.5.1](#2651-exposed-resolver-surface)) always reaches, since it targets the primary key and cannot write that column. `UpsertMany` keeps its own rule for such targets (below).

#### Batch upsert — dedupe, return shape, and key resolution

`UpsertMany` ([9.2](#92-write-operations)) is one statement per sub-batch over the same conflict-target enum `Upsert` takes. Three behaviors the three dialects disagree on are decided here rather than left to whichever one the consumer develops against; each was measured before it was decided.

**1. Inputs are deduped by conflict target before the statement is built, last occurrence wins.** PostgreSQL rejects an `ON CONFLICT ... DO UPDATE` that would affect one row twice (`ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE command cannot affect row a second time`); MySQL and SQLite accept the same statement and keep the **last** duplicate. Deduping last-wins is what makes one spelling produce one outcome on all three — the alternative is a PostgreSQL-only failure on every table whose conflict target does not cover every inserted column, which is every table but a pure link table. The deduped slice keeps first-appearance order and carries the last occurrence's values.

The dedupe needs the conflict target's columns to be ones the statement supplies. When they are not — a target naming a column no `Create{Table}Input` field maps to — there is nothing to key on, and the two key shapes diverge deliberately: a table whose own key is database-generated **refuses** (below), because it could not name its written rows either, while a table with a caller-known key proceeds **undeduped**, since it can still name them. The undeduped path is the one place `UpsertMany` is not dialect-uniform: PostgreSQL rejects an in-statement duplicate there where MySQL and SQLite accept it. It is unreachable on the shapes that matter — every primary-key and unique column a conflict target can name is a `Create{Table}Input` field on a table the generator emits a target for — and the alternative, refusing a write the dialect would accept, trades a rare divergence for a common failure.

A row is exempt from the dedupe when it carries no **definite, non-NULL** value for every conflict column — a `DEFAULT` the database has not yet evaluated, or a NULL. NULL never matches under a unique index on any of the three dialects, so two NULL-keyed rows are two rows; collapsing them would drop a row the caller asked to insert. Row identity is computed from what each value **binds** as, not from how it prints, so a nullable column's pointer keys by its value.

**2. The returned `[]*Entity` carries one entity per deduped input on every dialect, including the `DO NOTHING` branch.** `RETURNING` yields only the rows a statement actually inserted — measured on PostgreSQL and SQLite — so a batch that conflicted would come back short, and the caller could not tell from the result which input was dropped. `UpsertMany` therefore never reads its rows out of `RETURNING`: it resolves the written keys first and re-fetches them through `GetMany`, exactly as `CreateMany` does. Order is `GetMany`'s.

**3. `AffectedPKs` comes from the inputs, or from a read-back — never from the statement.** Two conditions must both hold for the inputs to be trusted, and the second is the one that is easy to miss. The key must be knowable before the write — a composite key, or the `app` / `caller` strategies, which covers every junction table — **and the conflict target must cover every primary-key column**. Where both hold the key is taken from the inputs and the sub-batch costs one statement.

**A conflict target that does not cover the key makes the input's key the wrong key, whatever the strategy.** The key column is excluded from the update half of the clause — a row's identity is not a mutable attribute — so a row that conflicts on some *other* unique constraint keeps the key it already had, and the key the caller supplied names a row that does not exist. `AffectedPKs` would then name absent rows on the cache and event paths, and the terminal `GetMany` would silently return short. Such a target reads its keys back exactly as a database-generated key does. The single-row `Upsert` never has to make this distinction: on a `RETURNING` dialect it resolves the key from the statement on *every* shape, and on MySQL from `LAST_INSERT_ID()`; batched, neither is available, so the distinction becomes explicit. Because the set of conflict targets a table declares is fixed at generation time while the choice among them is not, a table whose targets all cover the key pays no runtime branch and no second statement — every junction table is in this case.

Where the key is not knowable before the write (`db` strategy: `serial`, `AUTO_INCREMENT`, or a `DEFAULT`-backed `uuid` the caller left unset) no dialect can report the batch's keys, on any target:

| Dialect | Why the statement cannot name the rows |
|---------|----------------------------------------|
| MySQL | `LAST_INSERT_ID()` after a batch that mixed inserts with conflicts names the first **newly inserted** row, not the batch's first row. Fabricating keys from the first — which `CreateMany` does for a plain multi-row INSERT, as `firstID + i × auto_increment_increment` ([9.8.5](#985-createmany)) — yields a wrong key for every row |
| PostgreSQL / SQLite | `RETURNING` omits every row that took the `DO NOTHING` branch, and its row order is not contractual |

**Both halves compare values as Go sees them, which the database's own equality can outrun.** Row identity — for the dedupe, and for matching a written row to the row read back for it — is computed from the bound value, while the unique index compares under the column's collation and storage rules. Where the two disagree the Go side is the stricter: a case-insensitive collation (MySQL's default `utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci`), `CHAR(n)` padding, or a timestamp precision the column truncates. Two rows the database would call one are then left undeduped (PostgreSQL rejects the statement, loudly), and on a database-generated key a written row may fail to match its read-back (an error naming the cause, after the write). Neither is silent. A conflict target on a case-sensitively-compared column — which every UUID, integer and default-collation text key is — is unaffected.

Those rows are read back by the conflict target after the sub-batch is written — the batched form of the lookup [9.7](#97-pk-resolution-and-entity-return-path) already specifies for a single-row upsert, and unambiguous for the same reason: an explicit conflict target can only have fired on those columns. It costs a second statement per sub-batch, and it is a key-resolution read, so [25.1](#251-query-count-guarantee)'s write bound is unchanged. Like the single-row lookup it applies neither the soft-delete filter nor a tenant predicate — the unique index matched regardless of either — and the terminal `GetMany` applies the read path's own filters afterwards.

The read-back needs a key, so on such a table a conflict target naming a column the input does not supply is an **error before anything is written**, rather than a batch whose rows cannot be named. A `{Table}ConflictPK` target on an `AUTO_INCREMENT` key is the reachable case: the column is absent from `Create{Table}Input` entirely. The same applies per row to a conflict value that is not definite. Failing closed here matches the `{Table}ConflictPK` rule above — a loud refusal beats a silently wrong primary key on the event and cache paths that consume it.

### 9.6 Per-Call Options

Every generated client method accepts an optional `...func(*CallOptions[{Table}FieldOptions])` as the last parameter. When omitted, default behavior applies — hooks, cache, and events all execute normally. When provided, the function receives a `CallOptions` struct that the caller mutates to override behavior for that single call.

```go
// CallOptions controls per-call behavior overrides — generated once per package.
type CallOptions[FO any] struct {
    SkipCache          bool           // bypass cache read-through and write-through
    SkipEvents         bool           // suppress event publishing for this mutation
    SkipHooks          bool           // bypass all hooks except panic recovery
    SkipTenancy        bool           // bypass tenant filter injection (see Section 29)
    Tenant             *<tenant type> // resolve tenancy to this value (see 29.4.4)
    FieldOptions       *FO            // column selection and relationship loading
    LockMode           LockMode       // row-level locking for read methods (see 9.6a)
    AllowInTransaction bool           // permit Stream inside a transaction (see 9.4a)
}
```

This listing is the struct's full shape and its field order. **Two fields are gated, the rest are unconditional.** `SkipTenancy` is generated only when `tenancy.enabled: true` is set globally ([29](#29-tenancy)), and `Tenant` only when the package additionally has a tenanted entity to take its concrete type from ([29.4.4](#2944-calloptionsskiptenancy-and-calloptionstenant)); non-tenanted projects see the struct without either. `LockMode` and `AllowInTransaction` are emitted for every package even though each is meaningful on only a subset of methods — the methods they serve are generated on every table, so a gate could key only on schema shape, and the struct's shape would then move with the schema rather than with a mode the consumer chose ([9.4a](#94a-streaming-operations)).

**FieldOptions semantics within CallOptions:**

| Value | Meaning | Behavior |
|-------|---------|----------|
| `nil` (default) | Select all columns, no relationships | Full entity returned |
| `&ProductFieldOptions{Name: true, Price: true}` | Select specific columns + relationships | Partial entity returned |
| `&ProductFieldOptions{}` (all false) | Caller doesn't need the result | Skip entity fetch entirely, return `nil` |

The empty FieldOptions short-circuit applies to all mutation methods that return entities. When an empty `&FieldOptions{}` is set, the method performs the write but skips any follow-up queries (ID collection, `Get`/`GetMany`) and returns `nil`. This is useful for fire-and-forget mutations where the caller only needs to know the write succeeded.

**On the read path an all-false selection means "no rows", and the loud spelling is deliberate.** `GetMany` returns an empty slice and `Get` returns **`ErrNotFound`** — the single-row spelling of the same answer, not an inconsistency between the two. The alternative was to let a read short-circuit silently the way a mutation does and return `nil, nil`; that was rejected. On a *read*, an all-false selection is almost always a caller mistake — asking to load a row while selecting nothing from it — and a silent nil hands back a result indistinguishable from a legitimately absent row, so the mistake surfaces later and somewhere else. A clear error shows the problem where it was made. The read path is therefore **not** where the mutation-side `nil, nil` contract above gets spelled, and every entity-returning mutation guards its own trailing read rather than relying on the read to stay quiet. A mutation that forwards an all-false `FieldOptions` into its terminal `Get` unguarded reports `ErrNotFound` for a write that already committed — the defect single-row `Update` carried until [9.2](#92-write-operations)'s escape was added to it.

**Structurally required columns.** A narrowed projection selects what the caller asked for *plus* the columns the call itself has to read back, unioned in and re-sorted before the `SELECT` is built:

| Consumer | Column unioned in | Read by |
|----------|-------------------|---------|
| `Connection` | the entity's `cursor_keys` | `encode<T>Cursor`, which builds each edge's cursor from the returned row |
| `GetMany` with any O2M / M2M relationship selected | the parent's first PK column | the relationship loaders, which collect the parent side of every mapping off the scanned row |
| an O2O relationship | the target's first PK column | the JOIN scan, which distinguishes a LEFT JOIN miss by testing that PK against its zero value |
| an O2M relationship | the child's FK column, declared on the child fetch | the parent-child bucketing, which is keyed on it |
| an M2M relationship | the target's first PK column, declared on the target fetch | the target-to-parent map, which is keyed on it |

This is a pure over-fetch of the entity struct: it never widens what a consumer surface renders, since the GraphQL layer serializes only the fields the request selected ([26.5.2](#2652-field-selection-translation--the-central-mechanism)). Every column it adds is a key, and all but one are kept API-readable by [32.4](#324-validation) for exactly this reason — primary keys under the PK rule, and resolved `cursor_keys` (PK or not) under the cursor-key rule, so a column whose value reaches an edge cursor is never one `access` has restricted. The O2M child FK is the exception, deliberately: [32.5](#325-interactions) allows `access` on an FK column precisely so a config can hide the raw id while leaving the nested relationship object exposable, so a restricted FK still joins the child projection. It is safe for the same reason the rest of the over-fetch is — the loader reads the value to bucket children by parent and nothing serializes it, and the walker emits no `case` for a restricted column, so no request can name it.

The union applies **only** when the caller's selection is non-empty, so an all-false `&FieldOptions{}` still short-circuits its own entity fetch per the table above and a count-only query issues no entity fetch at all. This holds identically at every depth and for both list loaders: an all-false `FieldOptions` on a nested O2M *or* M2M relationship skips that child fetch and leaves the parent's relationship slice nil, rather than returning rows carrying nothing but the mapping key. The short-circuit is a Go-client affordance: below the envelope a GraphQL request cannot express it, because every selection set asks for the row it is written against. The generated walker therefore never hands an all-false value to a read for a row that was requested — it projects the entity's row identity instead ([26.5.2](#2652-field-selection-translation--the-central-mechanism), "Row identity"), and the only GraphQL selection that reaches a client method with an all-false `FieldOptions` is a count-only envelope, which never reaches the entity at all. O2O is the exception in kind rather than in rule: its target is columns on the parent's JOIN rather than a separate fetch, so an all-false O2O `FieldOptions` still contributes the target's key column — the value that separates a real row from a LEFT JOIN miss. `Stream` is exempt entirely: `Stream{Table}FieldOptions` carries no relationships ([9.4a](#94a-streaming-operations)) and `Stream` encodes no cursors.

**Usage:**

```go
// Normal call — no overrides, all hooks/cache/events fire, all columns returned
product, err := client.Products().Create(ctx, input)

// Skip cache for this read (e.g., force a fresh DB read)
product, err := client.Products().Get(ctx, id, func(o *<pkg>.CallOptions[<pkg>.ProductFieldOptions]) {
    o.SkipCache = true
})

// Select specific columns and load company relationship
product, err := client.Products().Get(ctx, id, func(o *<pkg>.CallOptions[<pkg>.ProductFieldOptions]) {
    o.FieldOptions = &<pkg>.ProductFieldOptions{
        Name: true, Price: true,
        Company: &<pkg>.CompanyFieldOptions{Name: true},
    }
})

// Fire-and-forget mutation — skip entity fetch
_, err := client.Products().Create(ctx, input, func(o *<pkg>.CallOptions[<pkg>.ProductFieldOptions]) {
    o.FieldOptions = &<pkg>.ProductFieldOptions{} // empty — skip fetch
})
```

**How each flag affects the pipeline:**

| Flag | Hooks | Cache | Events | Tenancy | DB Operation |
|------|:-----:|:-----:|:------:|:-------:|:------------:|
| (none) | Run | Read/write | Publish | Auto-filter | Execute |
| `SkipCache` | Run | **Bypass** | Publish | Auto-filter | Execute |
| `SkipEvents` | Run | Read/write | **Suppress** | Auto-filter | Execute |
| `SkipHooks` | **Bypass** (except panic recovery) | **Bypass** | **Suppress** | Auto-filter | Execute |
| `SkipTenancy` | Run | Read/write | Publish | **Bypass** | Execute |
| `LockMode != LockNone` | Run | **Bypass** (forced) | Publish | Auto-filter | Execute with `FOR UPDATE`-class clause |

`SkipHooks` implies `SkipCache` and `SkipEvents` because cache and events are implemented as hooks (sections 27, 28). `SkipTenancy` is orthogonal — tenancy runs in the SQL builders, not as a hook, so `SkipHooks` does NOT imply `SkipTenancy` (section 29.4.4). Panic recovery always runs regardless of flags.

**Relationship propagation:**

When `GetMany` loads relationships via `FieldOptions`, the resolved `CallOptions` propagate to all relationship loading queries automatically. The consumer sets options once on the top-level call:

```go
// SkipCache applies to the product query AND all relationship loads (company, reviews, tags)
products, err := client.Products().GetMany(ctx, input, func(o *<pkg>.CallOptions[<pkg>.ProductFieldOptions]) {
    o.SkipCache = true
})
```

The generated relationship loader receives the resolved `CallOptions` from the parent `GetMany` and applies them to each child query. There is no way to set different options per relationship — the options are per-operation, not per-query.

### 9.6a Lock Modes

`LockMode` is a `CallOptions` field that adds a row-level locking clause to read methods (`Get`, `GetMany`, `Connection`). It enables read-modify-write workflows, job queue dispatchers, and other concurrency primitives that require holding a database lock on the selected rows for the duration of the enclosing transaction.

LockMode applies to read methods only. Write methods (`Create`, `Update`, `Upsert`, `*Delete*`) acquire row locks implicitly via the `INSERT`/`UPDATE`/`DELETE` itself; LockMode is ignored on those methods.

#### Lock Mode Constants

```go
type LockMode int

const (
    LockNone                  LockMode = iota // default — no lock clause emitted
    LockForUpdate                             // FOR UPDATE — exclusive lock; blocks other readers/writers
    LockForShare                              // FOR SHARE / LOCK IN SHARE MODE — shared lock; allows other shared readers
    LockForUpdateNoWait                       // FOR UPDATE NOWAIT — error immediately if any conflicting lock held
    LockForUpdateSkipLocked                   // FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED — skip rows currently locked by another tx
)
```

#### Generated SQL by dialect

| Mode | PostgreSQL | MySQL | SQLite |
|------|------------|-------|--------|
| `LockNone` | (no clause) | (no clause) | (no clause) |
| `LockForUpdate` | `FOR UPDATE` | `FOR UPDATE` | unsupported — runtime error |
| `LockForShare` | `FOR SHARE` | `LOCK IN SHARE MODE` | unsupported — runtime error |
| `LockForUpdateNoWait` | `FOR UPDATE NOWAIT` | `FOR UPDATE NOWAIT` (8.0+) | unsupported — runtime error |
| `LockForUpdateSkipLocked` | `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` | `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` (8.0+) | unsupported — runtime error |

The clause is appended to the `SELECT` statement after the `ORDER BY`/`LIMIT`/`OFFSET` clauses by the dialect-specific `BuildSelect` implementation.

**SQLite limitation.** SQLite has no per-row locking — its concurrency model uses whole-database write locks via `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` / `BEGIN EXCLUSIVE`. Setting any `LockMode` other than `LockNone` against the SQLite dialect returns a sqlgen error at the runtime guard (see "Transaction precondition" below); no SQL is issued. Cross-dialect codebases must branch their concurrency design at the application layer for SQLite.

**MySQL version requirement.** `NOWAIT` and `SKIP LOCKED` modifiers require MySQL 8.0+. On older MySQL versions, the runtime rejects these modes — the generator emits a version-aware guard that returns an error at call time. The MySQL client probes the server with `SELECT VERSION()` lazily on the first `LockForUpdateNoWait`/`LockForUpdateSkipLocked` call, gated by `sync.Once` so the probe runs at most once per client lifetime; the probe result (success or error) is cached so a transient probe failure surfaces immediately to every caller. PostgreSQL and SQLite client structs do not carry the version cache. MariaDB (`10.x-MariaDB` version strings) parses to major version 10 and trivially clears the `< 8` check — MariaDB 10.6+ supports `NOWAIT` / `SKIP LOCKED`.

#### Transaction precondition

Row locks are meaningless outside a transaction. The generated method body checks for an active transaction before issuing the SELECT and returns a sqlgen-flavored error if none is present:

```go
if options.LockMode != LockNone {
    if !database.InTransaction(ctx) {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("get %s: LockMode requires an active transaction (use Begin or WithTx)", c.table.Name)
    }
    options.SkipCache = true // forced — reading from cache would skip the actual DB lock
}
```

`database.InTransaction(ctx context.Context) bool` is a new exported helper in the `database` runtime package; it wraps `FromContext(ctx) != nil && !tx.IsClosed()`.

The forced `SkipCache = true` is non-negotiable. A cache hit without acquiring the actual row lock is a silent correctness bug. The cache hook's existing `SkipCache` short-circuit (Section 27) handles the bypass — no new op-type dispatch needed in the cache template.

#### Transaction flow integration

LockMode plugs into the existing transaction surface (`Begin`, `Commit`, `Rollback`, `WithTx`, Section 20.4) without changes. Generated methods already route through `database.Conn(ctx, c.querier)` which auto-detects an active `*Tx` in the context. LockMode only adds the precondition check and the SELECT-clause suffix — the connection routing is unchanged.

**Pattern 1 — `WithTx` (recommended):**

```go
err := c.WithTx(ctx, "withdraw", func(ctx context.Context) error {
    account, err := c.Accounts.Get(ctx, accountID, func(o *CallOptions[AccountFieldOptions]) {
        o.LockMode = LockForUpdate
    })
    if err != nil { return err }

    if account.Balance < amount {
        return errors.New("insufficient funds")
    }
    _, err = c.Accounts.Update(ctx, accountID, &UpdateAccountInput{
        Balance: omittable.Set(account.Balance - amount),
    })
    return err
}) // commit releases the lock; rollback also releases
```

**Pattern 2 — explicit `Begin`/`Commit`:**

```go
txCtx, err := c.Begin(ctx, "withdraw")
if err != nil { return err }
defer c.Rollback(txCtx) // no-op if already committed

account, err := c.Accounts.Get(txCtx, id, func(o *CallOptions[AccountFieldOptions]) {
    o.LockMode = LockForUpdate
})
// ... read-modify-write logic ...
return c.Commit(txCtx)
```

**Pattern 3 — job queue with `LockForUpdateSkipLocked`:**

```go
err := c.WithTx(ctx, "claim_jobs", func(ctx context.Context) error {
    jobs, err := c.Jobs.GetMany(ctx, &GetJobsInput{
        Filter: &JobFilter{Status: &comparator.String{Eq: ptr("pending")}},
        Limit:  ptr(10),
        Sorts:  []sql.Sort{{Column: "created_at", Desc: false}},
    }, func(o *CallOptions[JobFieldOptions]) {
        o.LockMode = LockForUpdateSkipLocked
    })
    if err != nil { return err }

    for _, j := range jobs {
        if err := processJob(ctx, j); err != nil { return err }
        _, err := c.Jobs.Update(ctx, j.ID, &UpdateJobInput{
            Status: omittable.Set("done"),
        })
        if err != nil { return err }
    }
    return nil
})
```

Multiple workers running the same `WithTx` block concurrently each grab a disjoint set of pending jobs — `SKIP LOCKED` skips rows already held by sibling workers. No external queue infrastructure required.

#### Lock release semantics

Row locks are released only by `Commit` or `Rollback` of the **outermost** transaction. They are **not** released when a savepoint (nested `WithTx` / `Begin`) is rolled back or released:

```go
c.WithTx(ctx, "outer", func(ctx context.Context) error {
    c.Accounts.Get(ctx, id, func(o *CallOptions) { o.LockMode = LockForUpdate })
    // → row lock acquired

    c.WithTx(ctx, "savepoint_inner", func(ctx context.Context) error {
        return errors.New("force inner rollback")
    })
    // → savepoint_inner rolled back; the row lock from above is STILL held

    return nil // outer commit — row lock finally released here
})
```

This matches PostgreSQL and MySQL semantics; sqlgen does not introduce new behavior. Document this when LockMode lands so consumers don't expect savepoint-scoped locks.

#### Hook chain interaction

LockMode runs inside the existing query-hook chain. Order of operations at call time:

1. `resolveCallOptions(opts)` produces the options struct including LockMode.
2. Method body checks `database.InTransaction(ctx)`; errors if LockMode != LockNone and no tx is active.
3. Method body forces `options.SkipCache = true` if LockMode != LockNone.
4. Hook chain runs: tenancy adds WHERE conditions, soft-delete adds its predicate, custom user hooks fire.
5. Cache hook short-circuits via the `SkipCache` flag (same path as Stream, Section 9.4a).
6. Inner function builds the `SELECT` (with the lock-clause suffix appended by the dialect-specific `BuildSelect`) and runs it through `database.Conn(ctx, c.querier)` — which returns the tx-bound querier.
7. Lock is held; rows are scanned; method returns.
8. Lock released only when the consumer's outer `Commit` or `Rollback` executes.

Tenancy filters narrow which rows get locked (correct — only rows in the consumer's tenant are locked). Soft-delete filters exclude soft-deleted rows from the locked set (correct — those rows aren't visible to the application).

#### Chained internal calls do not inherit LockMode

`Create`/`Update`/`Upsert`/`Restore`/`SoftDelete*` chain an internal `Get`/`GetMany` for the entity-return path (Section 9.7). When the caller sets `LockMode` on a write method, the chained read does **not** inherit it — the write itself already acquired an implicit row lock that survives until commit, so re-locking via the chained read adds nothing. The internal call already uses `SkipHooks: true`; the generator extends that to also force `LockMode: LockNone` on the chained call.

**Read-method internals propagate LockMode.** `Get` chains an internal `GetMany` (Section 9.8.2) and `Connection` chains an internal `GetMany` (Section 9.8.7). When the caller sets `LockMode` on `Get` or `Connection`, the inner `GetMany` MUST carry the same `LockMode` so the actual SELECT emits the lock clause. The inner runtime guard re-runs but is idempotent (same ctx, same tx, same forced `SkipCache`). The "do not inherit" rule above is scoped to write-method chained reads only.

#### Validation rules

The runtime guard added to read-method bodies enforces:

| Condition | Behavior |
|-----------|----------|
| `LockMode != LockNone` outside a transaction | Returns sqlgen error before SQL roundtrip |
| `LockMode != LockNone` on SQLite dialect | Returns sqlgen error before SQL roundtrip |
| `LockNoWait` / `LockSkipLocked` on MySQL < 8.0 | Returns sqlgen error before SQL roundtrip |
| `LockMode != LockNone` with active tx on PG / MySQL 8.0+ | Forces `SkipCache = true`; emits lock clause; executes |

#### Codegen surface

Total surface change is small:

| File | Change |
|------|--------|
| `database/transaction.go` | Add exported `InTransaction(ctx) bool` helper |
| Runtime `sql/select.go` | Add `LockMode` field to `SelectOptions` |
| Per-dialect `BuildSelect` | Append lock-clause suffix based on `LockMode` |
| Generated `CallOptions[FO]` | Add `LockMode LockMode` field |
| Generated read methods (`Get`, `GetMany`, `Connection`) | Add precondition guard + `SkipCache` force + thread `LockMode` into `SelectOptions` |
| Generated chained-Get sites in write methods | Force `LockMode = LockNone` on the internal call (alongside existing `SkipHooks = true`) |

Tests required: per-dialect SQL emission tests for each LockMode constant, runtime-guard tests for outside-transaction and SQLite-dialect rejection paths, integration test for `LockForUpdateSkipLocked` job-queue pattern using two concurrent transactions in a testcontainer.

---

### 9.7 PK Resolution and Entity Return Path

All write methods that return entities (`Create`, `Update`, `Upsert`) follow a unified pattern across all dialects: perform the write, resolve the PK, then call `Get(ctx, pk, opts...)` to return the full entity with relationship loading via `FieldOptions`. There is no special MySQL workaround — the only dialect-specific logic is how the PK is resolved after INSERT.

**PK resolution by dialect and strategy:**

| Dialect | PK Strategy | PK Resolution | Then |
|---------|-------------|--------------|------|
| PostgreSQL/SQLite | `db` (UUID + DEFAULT) | `INSERT ... RETURNING "id"` → scan PK | `Get(ctx, id, opts...)` |
| PostgreSQL/SQLite | `db` (auto-increment) | `INSERT ... RETURNING "id"` → scan PK | `Get(ctx, id, opts...)` |
| PostgreSQL/SQLite | `app` / `caller` | PK known before INSERT | `Get(ctx, id, opts...)` |
| MySQL | `db` (AUTO_INCREMENT) | `Exec()` → `LastInsertId()` | `Get(ctx, id, opts...)` |
| MySQL | `app` (UUID) | PK known before INSERT (app-generated) | `Get(ctx, id, opts...)` |
| MySQL | `caller` | PK known before INSERT (caller-provided) | `Get(ctx, id, opts...)` |
| Composite PK (all dialects) | `caller` | PK always known from input | `Get(ctx, pk, opts...)` |

The generator emits only the variant matching the table's dialect and PK strategy. See [Section 9.8.4](#984-create) for full implementation examples including `insertAndResolveID`.

**Key design points:**
- `RETURNING` is only used for PK resolution (`RETURNING "id"`), never for full entity scanning. The follow-up `Get` handles relationship loading and FieldOptions.
- Composite PK tables never need `insertAndResolveID` — the PK is always known from the input.
- `UpdateMany`, `SoftDeleteMany`, and batch operations collect IDs then use `GetMany` for the return path.

**Upsert invariant: a conflict that changes nothing still resolves a PK.** An idempotent upsert — same conflict key, same column values — must return the conflicting row, not a not-found error. The row exists and the write succeeded; reporting failure rolls back the caller's transaction, maps to `NOT_FOUND` on GraphQL, and leaves any nested write with no parent PK to key on. Each dialect loses the PK on this branch for its own reason, so each is pinned separately:

| Dialect | How the PK is lost | Required mechanism |
|---------|-------------------|--------------------|
| MySQL | The OK packet carries `insert_id = 0` for an `ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE` that modifies no row, so `LastInsertId()` returns 0 | The set list opens with `` `pk` = LAST_INSERT_ID(`pk`) ``, republishing the id into the OK packet without touching the row. It must lead the list so no later `VALUES(...)` assignment overwrites it |
| PostgreSQL / SQLite | `DO NOTHING` (Section 9.5) returns no row, so `RETURNING` yields nothing to scan | The caller reads the result set rather than a single row, and on an empty set resolves the PK with a follow-up `SELECT` on the conflict columns. The lookup is unambiguous because an explicit `ON CONFLICT` target can only have fired on those columns |

The follow-up `SELECT` must **not** apply the soft-delete filter: the unique index matched regardless of the soft-delete column, so a soft-deleted row is still the row whose PK it resolves. (The terminal `Get` then applies the read path's own soft-delete filter, exactly as it does on the `DO UPDATE SET` branch — so an upsert conflicting with a soft-deleted row still returns `ErrNotFound`. That is existing behavior, not a property of this fallback.) Because it is a second statement, a concurrent delete between the two returns `ErrNotFound`; callers needing the pair to be atomic run the upsert in a transaction.

The follow-up `SELECT` requests more than one column when the table is tenanted, and `BuildSelect` **sorts** its column list where `RETURNING` does not. Scan targets on that path are therefore bound by column name, never by position: a tenant column that sorts before the PK (`account_id`, `company_id`) would otherwise bind to the wrong target, silently when the two share a Go type.

**Batched, the same lookup is the only mechanism.** `UpsertMany` ([9.2](#92-write-operations)) cannot use either row of the table above: `LAST_INSERT_ID()` after a batch that mixed inserts with conflicts names the first *newly inserted* row rather than the batch's first, and `RETURNING` omits every `DO NOTHING` row while promising nothing about the order of the rest. A table whose key is known before the write takes it from the inputs **on a conflict target that covers every primary-key column**; on any other target, and on a table whose key is database-generated, it reads the sub-batch back by the conflict columns it targeted — the batched form of the lookup above, resolving every row rather than one, and applying neither the soft-delete filter nor a tenant predicate for the same reason. The extra condition is not a `db`-strategy quirk: a conflict on a non-key unique constraint leaves the existing row's key in place on every strategy, so an input-sourced key would name a row that does not exist ([9.5 Batch upsert](#batch-upsert--dedupe-return-shape-and-key-resolution)). Because it resolves keys rather than writing, it leaves [25.1](#251-query-count-guarantee)'s write bound unchanged, exactly as the trailing `Get` / `GetMany` does. See [9.5 Batch upsert](#batch-upsert--dedupe-return-shape-and-key-resolution).

A `DO UPDATE SET pk = pk` self-assignment would also make `RETURNING` yield a row, but it converts a logical no-op into a physical row write — tuple rewrite, row lock, and `UPDATE` triggers firing on a row nothing changed — and is therefore not used.


### 9.8 Generated Method Patterns

This section provides concrete Go implementation examples for each generated method. These are the **reference targets** that code generation templates produce. All examples use the reference schema below with PostgreSQL (pgx driver) unless noted otherwise. MySQL and SQLite variations are documented where behavior differs.

#### Design Principles

**1. Method Independence.** Each generated method is self-contained — no public method on an entity client calls another public method on the same client, with well-defined exceptions for `Get`, `GetMany`, and `Count`.

Generation is schema-driven: every method the schema allows is generated, and the only gates are the schema facts listed in [4.6 Operations](#operations). `Get`, `GetMany`, and `Count` are foundational — other methods depend on them, and no schema fact on a table removes them:

- **Write method return path**: `Create`, `Update`, and `Upsert` all call `Get` after performing the write to return the resulting entity. This is the same pattern across all dialects — no special MySQL workaround needed. It also enables relationship loading on write results via `FieldOptions`.
- **Empty update path** (Section 9.5): `Update` calls `Get` when no fields are set, to return the current entity unchanged — unless the call carries a non-nil `FieldOptions` selecting nothing, which suppresses the `Get` on this path and on the normal one alike ([9.2](#92-write-operations), [9.6](#96-per-call-options)).
- **Cross-entity relationship loading**: `GetMany` calls related entity clients' `GetMany` for O2M/M2M relationship loading.
- **Pagination**: `Paginate` delegates to `Count` for total count and `GetMany` for page data, ensuring FieldOptions, relationship loading, and soft delete filtering are handled consistently.

No other inter-method dependencies exist, so a schema fact that removes a method (a missing soft-delete column, incrementable column or conflict target) never breaks another one.

**2. Shared Scan Function.** Each table has one generated scan function: `scan{Table}s(rows database.Rows, columns []string) ([]*{Table}, error)`. All methods that read entities — `Get`, `GetMany`, `Paginate`, `Connection` — use this same function. Write methods (`Create`, `Update`, `Upsert`) delegate to `Get` for their return value.

**3. Unified per-call options via `CallOptions[FO]`.** Every method accepts an optional trailing `...func(*CallOptions[FO])` parameter where `FO` is the table's FieldOptions type. This single extensibility point bundles behavioral overrides (`SkipCache`, `SkipEvents`, `SkipHooks`) and field selection (`FieldOptions`) into one mechanism.

```go
// Shared — generated once per package. Abbreviated to the four fields this
// principle is about; see 9.6 for the struct's full shape and field order.
type CallOptions[FO any] struct {
    SkipCache    bool // bypass cache read-through and write-through
    SkipEvents   bool // suppress event publishing for this mutation
    SkipHooks    bool // bypass all hooks except panic recovery
    FieldOptions *FO  // column selection and relationship loading
}
```

**FieldOptions semantics within CallOptions:**

| Value | Meaning | Behavior |
|-------|---------|----------|
| `nil` (default) | Select all columns, no relationships | Full entity returned |
| `&ProductFieldOptions{Name: true, Price: true}` | Select specific columns + relationships | Partial entity returned |
| `&ProductFieldOptions{}` (all false) | Caller doesn't need the result | Skip entity fetch entirely, return `nil` |

The empty FieldOptions short-circuit applies to all mutation methods that return entities. When an empty `&FieldOptions{}` is set, the method performs the write but skips any follow-up queries (ID collection, `Get`/`GetMany`) and returns `nil`. This is useful for fire-and-forget mutations where the caller only needs to know the write succeeded.

**4. Soft delete scoping via comparator.** When a table has a soft delete column, the filter struct includes a regular comparator field for that column (e.g., `DeletedAt *comparator.NullableTime`). There is no `IncludeDeleted` or `IsSoftDeleted` — the comparator is the single mechanism for controlling soft delete filtering.

When `exclude_deleted` is enabled (default when a soft delete column exists), each method checks whether the user set the soft delete comparator on the filter:
- **User didn't set it** → method injects the default "is not deleted" condition (e.g., `deleted_at IS NULL` for timestamp, `is_deleted = false` for bool, `deleted = 0` for integer)
- **User set it** → method uses the user's comparator, no default injected

Exceptions:
- **`SoftDelete*`** — always adds "is not deleted" condition (only soft-delete active rows)
- **`Restore*`** — always adds "is deleted" condition (only restore deleted rows)
- **`Get` / `Exists`** — PK methods with no filter; always inject the default when `exclude_deleted` is enabled

When `exclude_deleted` is disabled, no default condition is injected for any method. The user's comparator is respected if set.

**Shared generic input types:**

```go
// PaginateInput — shared across all tables via generics
type PaginateInput[F any] struct {
    Filter *F
    Limit  int
    Offset int
}

// ConnectionInput — shared across all tables via generics
type ConnectionInput[F any] struct {
    Filter *F
    First  *int
    Last   *int
    After  *string
    Before *string
}

// IncrementInput — shared across all tables via generics
type IncrementInput[C ~string] struct {
    Column C
    Amount int
}

// PaginateResult — returned by Paginate()
type PaginateResult[T any] struct {
    Items           []*T  // entities for the current page
    TotalCount      int64 // total matching rows across all pages
    TotalPages      int   // ceil(TotalCount / PageSize)
    PageSize        int   // the limit used for this query
    CurrentPage     int   // 1-indexed page number derived from offset/limit
    HasNextPage     bool  // true if there are pages after this one
    HasPreviousPage bool  // true if there are pages before this one (CurrentPage > 1)
}

// resolveCallOptions — shared helper, applies option functions and returns the resolved struct.
// SkipHooks implies SkipCache and SkipEvents because cache and events are implemented as hooks.
func resolveCallOptions[FO any](opts []func(*CallOptions[FO])) CallOptions[FO] {
    var options CallOptions[FO]
    for _, fn := range opts {
        fn(&options)
    }
    // SkipHooks implies SkipCache and SkipEvents — cache and events are hooks.
    if options.SkipHooks {
        options.SkipCache = true
        options.SkipEvents = true
    }
    return options
}

// toAnySlice — shared helper, converts a typed slice to []any for variadic In() calls.
func toAnySlice[T any](s []T) []any {
    result := make([]any, len(s))
    for i, v := range s {
        result[i] = v
    }
    return result
}

// unionColumns — shared helper, adds the columns a call structurally requires to a
// narrowed projection (Section 9.6) and re-sorts, because the builder emits columns
// sorted and the scan functions match positionally against this slice.
func unionColumns(columns []string, required ...string) []string {
    var missing []string
    for _, r := range required {
```
