That half is a generator limitation rather than a schema fact, so it is **reported** for an edge the config lists by name instead of being dropped silently the way a verb the `nested_mutations.verbs` mask turned off is. On a **has-one** edge, `create` and `connect` also require the two terms the occupancy read ([9.9.3](#993-the-eligibility-matrix)) filters on: the traversed FK's `= parent` term and, on a polymorphic edge, the discriminator's equality term. An edge that cannot render them loses `create`, rather than writing a child it cannot check for. It has already lost the other verbs to the same terms, so the edge carries nothing. This clause is a generator limitation too, and is reported the same way. |
| **E9** | *Retired.* It required `upsert_many` and `hard_delete` on the junction table. The client has no toggles ([4.6](#46-generationconfig)): `HardDeleteMany` and `HardDeleteWhere` are generated on every table, and `UpsertMany` on every junction **E13** admits, so the [9.9.6](#996-execution-order) link step and both unlink verbs always have their method. |
| **E10** | `UpsertWithRelated` requires the existence of a generated `<Table>ConflictTarget` constant to pass it. A table whose uniqueness is app-enforced through `primary_key.columns` emits no `<Table>ConflictPK` ([9.5](#95-edge-case-behaviors)), and, with no unique target left either, the nested upsert surface is omitted. |
| **E11** | M2M `disconnect` and `clear` require the junction to have **no soft-delete column**. With one, neither mechanism is correct: a hard delete destroys a row the schema marked soft-deletable, and a soft delete leaves the link visible, because the M2M loader's junction query is a bare `SELECT` carrying only the parent-id `IN` condition, with no soft-delete predicate ([13.2](#132-loading-strategy)). Refusing the verb is the fail-closed direction. `create` and `connect` on such an edge are unaffected. |
| **E12** | On a **self-referential** edge, a `connect` or `disconnect` naming the parent's own primary key is refused with `ErrNestedVerbConflict` in that edge's validate step, before any statement on the edge runs; the parent write and any earlier edge have already run and roll back with the transaction or savepoint. No other guard catches it — an unparented self is an adoptable orphan under `connect`'s own rule — and left unguarded it writes a row that is its own parent, which every recursive read walks forever. A longer cycle (connecting a row to its own ancestor) is **not** detected; see [26.12](#2612-known-limitations). |
| **E13** | An M2M edge requires the junction to emit a PK-covering `<Junction>ConflictTarget` constant, which the [9.9.6](#996-execution-order) link step passes to `UpsertMany`. This is **E10**'s rule one level down: a table whose uniqueness is app-enforced through `primary_key.columns` emits no `<Table>ConflictPK` ([9.5](#95-edge-case-behaviors)), and a junction in that shape has nothing the link step can name. Such a junction also has its `UpsertMany` omitted with the constant ([4.6 Operations](#operations)). |

**A parent with zero eligible edges gets no nested surface at all** — no Go method, no wrapper input type, no GraphQL mutation. A wrapper carrying only the flat input would be the base operation with extra steps. The rule is per parent on the Go surface, which keeps the uniform method set: a parent whose edges carry only update-side verbs (`disconnect`, `clear`) still gets `CreateWithRelated`, with empty create-side blocks. The GraphQL surface applies it per family as well, after **E7**'s narrowing: `create<T>WithRelated` is dropped when no surviving edge carries `create` or `connect`, and the update and upsert mutations when no edge survives at all.

#### 9.9.5 Generated surface

Six type families per eligible parent. Every name is registered with the codegen name resolver ([8.5](#85-naming-rules)); these names key on the **(parent, edge)** pair rather than on a table, so a collision between a generated nested name and a real table's name is a codegen error naming both, not a `go build` failure.

| Type | Shape |
|---|---|
| `Create<Parent>WithRelatedInput` | `Create<Parent>Input` + one optional `<Parent><Edge>CreateNested` per eligible edge |
| `Update<Parent>WithRelatedInput` | `Update<Parent>Input` + one optional `<Parent><Edge>UpdateNested` per eligible edge |
| `Upsert<Parent>WithRelatedInput` | `Create<Parent>Input` + the **same** `<Parent><Edge>UpdateNested` blocks |
| `<Parent><Edge>CreateNested` | the per-edge verb block: `create` and `connect` only |
| `<Parent><Edge>UpdateNested` | the per-edge verb block: `create`, `connect`, `disconnect`, `clear` |
| `<Parent><Edge>CreateInput` | the child's create input **minus** the traversed FK and **minus** the edge's discriminator column — shapes 2 and 3 only |

On an **M2M** edge the `create` verb takes the target's ordinary `Create<Target>Input` unchanged: there is no traversed FK on the target to elide, because the link lives in the junction row the executor writes afterwards.

**That is also why an M2M edge carrying a `discriminator:` is not write-eligible** ([9.9.4](#994-eligibility-rules) E2). The two rules cannot both hold on that shape. Taking the target's input unchanged means the discriminator column stays a field the caller fills in, so a nested `create` inserts a row the edge's own loader then filters out — a link the caller can never read back, reported as success. Setting it from the edge instead overwrites a field the input type still advertises, which is the accept-and-drop failure the separate input types in [9.2](#92-write-operations) exist to prevent. Narrowing the M2M input the way shapes 2 and 3 are narrowed would resolve it and is deliberately **not** done in v1: no schema yet declares such an edge, and refusing the write surface is the fail-closed direction that keeps the failure loud. The read surface is untouched — the loader applies the predicate exactly as it does on any other polymorphic edge.

**The wrapper contains the flat input; it never restates its fields.** `Create<Parent>WithRelatedInput` holds a `Create<Parent>Input`, so the access projection, the column-map overrides, the increment operators and every future create-input change are inherited for free.

**The create-side block is a narrower type, not the same type with rules.** `disconnect` and `clear` are meaningless on a row that does not exist yet, so they are not expressible on `CreateWithRelated` rather than accepted and ignored.

**`UpsertWithRelated` reuses the update-side block verbatim**, and needs no insert-vs-update branch detection. Each verb means the same thing on either branch, and only the state the parent brings to it differs. On a freshly inserted parent, `create` and `connect` behave exactly as they do on the create side, and `disconnect` / `clear` match zero rows and are no-ops. On the conflict branch they behave exactly as they do on `UpdateWithRelated`. One block is therefore correct on both branches, and the generator emits **one executor per edge** shared by all three families, so the three cannot drift.

**That does not make a repeated upsert a no-op.** `connect`, `disconnect` and `clear` are idempotent set operations. `create` is not: it inserts on every call. Repeating an `UpsertWithRelated` that carries `create` takes the conflict branch and inserts again: another O2M child, another M2M target and its link. On a has-one that already holds a child it is refused, with `ErrAlreadyRelated` from the occupancy read ([9.9.3](#993-the-eligibility-matrix)).

**The traversed FK is elided from the nested child input.** `<Parent><Edge>CreateInput` is the child's create input with the FK column removed, because that column is always set from the parent's primary key. Leaving it would force the caller to supply a value that is then overwritten — and on GraphQL a non-null FK field would force the client to invent an id.

**Every nested name carries the `<Parent><Edge>` prefix, and none of them joins the `Create<T>Input` family.** This is the one place where the obvious spelling is wrong. `Create<Parent><SingularEdge>Input` — the name this table carried until 27.7 — reconstructs the *target's own* create input exactly whenever the child table is named `<parent>_<edge>`, which is the conventional name for a dependent table: `users.Profile` over `user_profiles` and `binary_keys.Events` over `binary_key_events` both resolve to `CreateUserProfileInput` / `CreateBinaryKeyEventInput`, the names those two tables already declare. The two types are not interchangeable — the nested one has the FK removed — so the collision is a redeclaration, and it is systematic rather than incidental. Moving the family marker to a suffix puts the nested names in a namespace no table's derived name occupies. The collision is still *checked* ([8.5](#85-naming-rules)), because no identifier scheme is collision-free; what changed is that the check no longer fires on the common case.

**Edges are processed in byte-wise order of the relationship's Go field name**, the `Edge` spelling [9.9.8](#998-error-attribution) attributes errors with — not the declared `name`, which may be the snake form an auto-detected edge carries. The order is total (every edge has a name, unique per parent), independent of whether the optional `tables.<t>.nested_mutations.relationships` block is present, and deterministic across regenerations. It is observable in three places and is contractual in all three: the order of error attribution when two edges would both fail ([9.9.8](#998-error-attribution)), the order in which the inner calls' events are enqueued ([9.9.9](#999-observability)), and the order of the generated members.

**A nil `FieldOptions` returns the parent with its relationship members unpopulated**, on the edges the call just wrote as well as every other. This follows from the execution order below — the terminal read is gated on the caller having *selected* a relationship, and a nil selection selects none — and it matches the flat path, where a nil `FieldOptions` selects all columns and no relationships ([9.6](#96-per-call-options)). It is stated explicitly because "nil means everything" is the right mental model for *columns* and the wrong one here, and the surprise lands on the caller who just created those rows.

#### 9.9.6 Execution order

The parent is always written first — v1 nests only where the parent's PK flows down — so there is no topological sort and no cycle.

```
BEGIN, or SAVEPOINT when ctx already holds a transaction (18.3)

  1. parent := Create | Update | Upsert (ctx, …, FieldOptions with relationships stripped)
         Relationship members MUST be stripped here: loading them would run before
         the nested rows exist and return a stale set.

  2. per eligible edge, in byte order of the relationship's Go field name:

       validate     no target named under two verbs on one edge (see below)
                    not both create and connect on a has-one edge (see below)
                    no self-reference on a self-referential edge (E12)

       clear     →  FIRST, and the ordering is load-bearing: running it after
                    create / connect would unlink what they had just linked
                    O2M: <Target>().UpdateWhere(fk = parent [AND disc], SET fk = NULL) — 1 write
                    M2M: <Junction>().HardDeleteWhere(local_fk = parent)               — 1 write

       occupied  →  has-one only, when create or connect is set (9.9.3):
                    <Target>().GetMany(fk = parent [AND disc], Limit: new(0))  — the occupancy read
                    any row other than the connect target → ErrAlreadyRelated naming it

       create    →  O2M:     <Target>().CreateMany(children with fk = parent [, disc])
                    has-one: <Target>().Create(child with fk = parent [, disc])
                    M2M: CreateMany the targets, PK-only FieldOptions

       connect   →  <Target>().GetMany(id IN … [AND disc], Limit: new(0))  — the visibility read
                    any requested id absent            → ErrNotFound naming it
                    O2M: partition the visible rows by their current FK
                         fk = parent  → no-op, the requested end state holds
                         fk = other   → ErrAlreadyRelated naming it
                         fk IS NULL   → UpdateWhere(id IN … AND fk IS NULL [AND disc],
                                          SET fk = parent)
                                        then GetMany(id IN … AND fk = parent [AND disc])
                                          — the verify read; fewer rows than ids
                                          → ErrAlreadyRelated

       link      →  M2M only: <Junction>().UpsertMany(dedup(created ∪ connected))

       disconnect → SKIPPED ENTIRELY when clear ran on this edge
                    O2M: <Target>().UpdateWhere(id IN … AND fk = parent [AND disc], SET fk = NULL)
                    M2M: <Junction>().HardDeleteMany(pairs)

       [AND disc] / [, disc] — present exactly when the edge declares a
       `discriminator:`, absent otherwise. See "every statement on a
       polymorphic edge is scoped to that edge" below.

  3. IF the caller's FieldOptions selects any relationship:
       parent = Get(ctx, parent.PK, caller's FieldOptions, SkipHooks)

COMMIT, or RELEASE SAVEPOINT
```

**Every statement on a polymorphic edge is scoped to that edge, not to the foreign key it traverses.** An edge declaring a `discriminator:` ([13.4.1](#1341-discriminator--the-structured-form-of-a-polymorphic-edge)) is `fk = parent AND <column> = <value>`, and sibling edges over the same foreign key differ only in the second term — so every statement above carries it: a `create` SETs it, the `connect` visibility read filters on it, and the `connect` adoption, `disconnect` and `clear` all add it to their `WHERE`. Dropping it from a *write* is not a wider match but a wrong one. A `clear` that carries only `fk = parent` unlinks every sibling edge's rows as well, reports success, and names none of them — rows the caller never mentioned, on an edge they were not writing to. An adoption that omits it while the read carries it is the same disagreement one statement later: the row the read approved is not the row the `UPDATE` is allowed to touch, so a target whose value changed in between is adopted into an edge that can never return it. The rule has no M2M half, because [9.9.4](#994-eligibility-rules) **E2** makes an M2M edge declaring a `discriminator:` not write-eligible at all.

A verb whose scope cannot be rendered is refused rather than emitted unscoped, on the same fail-closed reasoning: the discriminator's column has to carry an equality comparator on the target's filter ([11.2](#112-comparator-types)), and an edge whose column does not keeps `create` — which sets the column rather than filtering on it — and loses the rest. A has-one edge loses `create` too, because its occupancy read filters on the column (**E8**). Through built-in bindings neither case arises: **E2** refuses an edge whose discriminator column cannot take the declared value, and every binding that can carries an equality comparator ([9.9.4](#994-eligibility-rules)); the rule stays as defence.

**`clear` runs first and takes no id list.** It unlinks every currently-linked row *on this edge*, is a single write statement on either shape (on MySQL preceded by the pre-SELECT that names its rows, [9.9.7](#997-query-count)), needs no visibility read, and is parent-scoped by construction. It is what makes "replace the whole set" expressible without a `set` verb: `{clear: true, connect: [7, 9]}` *is* "the set is now exactly 7 and 9". When `clear` is true, `disconnect` on the same edge is **ignored rather than rejected** — every id it names is already unlinked, so the caller's requested end state holds.

**On a has-one edge, replacing the child is `clear` plus `create` or `connect`.** `clear` runs before the occupancy read, so the read finds the edge empty and the new child is written. `{disconnect: <current>, create: …}` and `{disconnect: <current>, connect: <other>}` do **not** replace: `disconnect` runs last, so the occupancy read still finds the current child and the call returns `ErrAlreadyRelated`. A has-one on a NOT NULL FK has no `clear` (**E8**), so its child cannot be replaced through the nested block at all. Delete it through the target's own client, then `create`.

**`connect` performs a visibility read; `disconnect` does not.** The asymmetry is structural, not stylistic. A `disconnect` is keyed on the parent's own primary key — the junction pair embeds it, the O2M filter carries `fk = parent` — so it is incapable of touching another parent's rows, and a miss is a no-op. A `connect` is keyed on a **caller-supplied target id** with no such anchor: without the read it is an existence oracle across tenants and access boundaries, and on O2M the `UPDATE`'s row count alone cannot separate *no such row* from *already parented*. See [29.4](#294-generated-behavior) for the tenancy half of this rule.

**`Limit: new(0)` on the visibility read is normative.** A `*Limit` of `0` means *emit no `LIMIT` clause* and *skip the client's default `query_limit`* ([4.6](#46-generationconfig)); a nil `Limit` would let `query_limit` truncate the read, so a `connect` naming more targets than the client's page size would find the tail of its own list absent and report real, visible rows as `NOT_FOUND`. The failure scales with the caller's input size.

**O2M `connect` adopts only unparented rows.** The guard filter carries `fk IS NULL`, and the visibility read decides which of three outcomes the caller gets: not visible → `ErrNotFound` naming the id; parented to a different row → `ErrAlreadyRelated` naming the id; already parented to this parent → **no-op**, because the requested end state holds. Re-parenting — moving a row from another parent — is a different operation with its own authorization question and is opt-in per edge via `allow_reparent: true` ([4.8](#48-tableconfig-per-table)). The three-way split is not decoration: collapsing it to "fewer rows updated than requested → conflict" reports a typo'd or cross-tenant id as an existing relationship, and disagrees with M2M `connect`, which maps the identical caller mistake to `NOT_FOUND`.

**The shortfall check counts a verify read, and it holds on every dialect.** After each chunk's `UPDATE`, the adoption reads the chunk's ids back filtered on `fk = parent`, plus the discriminator on a polymorphic edge, and counts the rows that come back. The read is a plain one inside the transaction, so it sees the transaction's own writes: every row the `UPDATE` adopted is counted. A row another connection parented elsewhere between the visibility read and the `UPDATE` was skipped by the `fk IS NULL` term, so it is not under this parent and is not counted, and the call returns `ErrAlreadyRelated`. The read carries no locking clause, so below SERIALIZABLE it takes no lock. It costs no extra statement either: the adoption's `UpdateWhere` selects nothing, so the read that would hand its rows back is never issued, and the verify read takes its place ([9.9.7](#997-query-count)). The check deliberately does not count what `UpdateWhere` reports. On MySQL those rows come from a pre-SELECT that can disagree with the write ([9.8.6b](#986b-updatewhere)). Under REPEATABLE READ that pre-SELECT answers from the transaction's snapshot, where the contested row is still unparented, so it would count the row the `UPDATE` skipped, and the call would report success with the row still under the other parent. One interleaving can go either way: a row another connection parents to *this* parent inside the same window is counted when the read can see that commit and reported as the shortfall when it cannot. The caller's end state holds either way, and the error is the conservative answer.

**`allow_reparent: true` removes the `fk IS NULL` term, and that changes what a shortfall means.** The guard is what makes the default adoption atomic against a concurrent `connect`; an edge that opts into adopting a parented row is opting out of the guard, so the statement carries the id list alone. Two consequences follow and neither is derivable from the flag's name. The middle outcome disappears — a visible target parented elsewhere is adopted rather than `ErrAlreadyRelated`, leaving `connect` two-way: not visible → `ErrNotFound`, already ours → no-op, anything else → adopted. And the shortfall changes sentinel: with no `fk IS NULL` term, a row the visibility read returned that the verify read does not count has stopped being visible in between — deleted, or soft-deleted — so it reports `ErrNotFound`, not `ErrAlreadyRelated`. Reporting a conflict there would name a relationship that does not exist, which is the failure the three-way split exists to prevent, reappearing on the opt-in path. The same-parent interleaving above is the one exception to "stopped being visible", and it fails the same conservative way.

**Naming one target under two verbs on one edge is a validation error**, returned before any statement *on that edge* runs (the parent write and earlier edges have already run, and roll back with the transaction or savepoint): the order would decide the outcome and there is no defensible default. Concretely this is `connect` ∩ `disconnect`, and `create` ∩ `disconnect` where a `create` entry carries an explicit primary key. The check is skipped for `disconnect` when `clear` is set on the same edge, since `disconnect` is then ignored and cannot contradict anything. **A has-one block that sets both `create` and `connect` is refused the same way**, with `ErrNestedVerbConflict` attributed to `connect`: the edge holds one child and the block asks for two. On `CreateWithRelated` this check is the only guard, because the parent has no child yet for the occupancy read to find.

**The unlink assignment sets the FK to NULL; it does not omit it.** On a nullable FK bound to a pointer type, "set this column to NULL" and "leave this column out of the `SET` list" are both expressible in the same position and only the first unlinks anything. The second matches its rows, reports success and changes nothing — the one failure shape a rows-affected check cannot catch, because the rows do match.

**Intermediate writes take the skip-refetch escape.** Every inner call that does not need its result back passes a non-nil, nothing-selected `FieldOptions` ([9.6](#96-per-call-options)), so it skips the read that would hand its rows back. This is why the escape on single-row `Update` ([9.8.6](#986-update)) is a requirement rather than an optimization.

**The terminal re-read and the adoption's verify read run with hooks skipped, and they are the only inner calls that do.** Every other call in the sequence inherits the caller's `SkipHooks` and fires its own chain ([9.9.9](#999-observability)). Neither of these two is a read the caller asked for. The terminal re-read is the method assembling its own return value, and the verify read is the adoption checking its own write, so surfacing either as a query-hook event would report a read that is an implementation detail of the write. It follows that neither is ever served from or written to the cache — `SkipHooks` implies `SkipCache` ([9.6](#96-per-call-options)). For the terminal read that is the same end state [9.9.9](#999-observability)'s "a relationship-loaded parent is never cached" reaches through [27.6](#276-cache-invariant). For the verify read it is a requirement: a cached answer would not reflect the `UPDATE` that just ran. Tenancy is unaffected, since it runs in the SQL builders rather than as a hook ([9.6](#96-per-call-options)), so the verify read is tenant-scoped exactly as the visibility read is.

**On MySQL the link step's keys are derived, and the transaction is what makes them exact.** MySQL has no `RETURNING`, so the M2M `create`'s `CreateMany` derives its targets' keys from `LAST_INSERT_ID()` and the session's `auto_increment_increment` ([9.8.5](#985-createmany)). The step is a session variable. The nested transaction is one session, so the step is read where the `INSERT` ran. A key derived with the wrong step links the parent to a row this call did not write and reports success. The link step is where a wrong key becomes a persisted row, which is why it is pinned by name, under a step of 2, in the MySQL example.

**Soft-deleted children follow from routing through the target's own client.** A `connect` whose target is soft-deleted is `ErrNotFound` — the visibility read applies the target's soft-delete default, so it is indistinguishable from a target that does not exist, which is the fail-closed direction. A `disconnect` naming a soft-deleted child still unlinks it — O2M and has-one unlink through the target's `UpdateWhere`, which applies no soft-delete default, and M2M deletes the junction pair without reading the target — and `clear` does the same for every soft-deleted child on the edge. While the child stays soft-deleted the difference is unobservable, since it is absent from every read of the relationship; a later `Restore` returns it unlinked, which is what the `disconnect` asked for.

#### 9.9.7 Query count

The write-side bound is stated with [25.1](#251-query-count-guarantee)'s read-side guarantee: **`ceil(N / batch_size)` statements per participating table per verb, plus a bounded set of reads — never a per-row read.** `clear` is the one verb that is never more than one write statement, because it names no ids.

The bound is per *verb*, not per table, because `connect` and `disconnect` on one edge genuinely cannot merge: on O2M they are two `UPDATE`s with different `SET` values and guards, and on M2M one is the junction upsert and the other a `DELETE`. A three-verb M2M block is 3 statements at batch scale, not 3 × N.

**On MySQL, a verb that routes through a `*Where` method costs one more statement per chunk.** PostgreSQL and SQLite report the rows a write touched through `RETURNING`, inside the write. MySQL has no `RETURNING`, so `UpdateWhere` and the delete-by-filter methods name those rows with a pre-SELECT issued first ([9.8.6b](#986b-updatewhere)). The verbs affected are the O2M / has-one `connect` adoption, O2M / has-one `disconnect`, and `clear` on either shape. Each write costs two statements per chunk on MySQL where the other dialects spend one, and `clear` is at most two there: one read, then one write unless the read found nothing, since MySQL's `*Where` methods skip the write when nothing matches. The bound keeps its shape — per chunk, never per row — and the read is listed below.

Every read earns its place:

| Read | When | Why it is unavoidable |
|---|---|---|
| parent PK resolution | always | children key on the parent's PK, and `Create` / `Upsert` surface a generated PK only through the return value |
| M2M target PKs | per edge with a non-empty `create` | junction rows need the generated target PKs |
| `connect` visibility | per edge with a non-empty `connect`, O2M and M2M alike | the FK constraint proves a row exists, not that the caller may see it; on O2M it is also the only thing separating *absent* from *already parented* |
| has-one occupancy read | per has-one edge with `create` or `connect` set, every dialect | a has-one holds one child, and only a UNIQUE FK makes the database refuse a second one; this read is what finds the child the parent already holds ([9.9.3](#993-the-eligibility-matrix)). It is a plain `SELECT`, so MySQL spends no extra statement on it |
| O2M / has-one `connect` verify read | per chunk the adoption `UPDATE` runs on, every dialect | the [9.9.6](#996-execution-order) shortfall check counts it — the chunk's ids now under this parent, which is the only count that separates an adopted row from one a concurrent `connect` took first |
| MySQL `*Where` pre-SELECT | MySQL only: per chunk of the O2M / has-one `connect` adoption and `disconnect`, and once per `clear` | MySQL has no `RETURNING`, so this read is what names the rows the write changes, for cache invalidation and events. The adoption's shortfall check does not count it ([9.8.6b](#986b-updatewhere)) |
| MySQL key step | MySQL only: per target `CreateMany` statement of two or more rows | MySQL has no `RETURNING`, so a batch's keys are derived from `LAST_INSERT_ID()`, spaced by `auto_increment_increment`, a session variable only the `INSERT`'s own session can report ([9.8.5](#985-createmany)). Inside the nested transaction it is one statement on that session, never a `BEGIN` |
| terminal re-read | only when the caller selected a relationship | step 1 stripped them |

#### 9.9.8 Error attribution

Errors are attributed **per edge and per verb**, wrapping [22.3](#223-error-wrapping-convention)'s convention:

```
update user with related: Categories: connect: 7: sqlgen: resource not found
update user with related: Events: disconnect: <wrapped>
update user with related: Categories: clear: <wrapped>
```

**The edge is spelled as the relationship's Go field name, and the id renders plainly.** Both follow from [22.2](#222-constraint-errors), which is the normative definition: `Edge` is "the relationship field name, e.g. `Categories`", and `ID` is the bare target id with no room for a per-target noun. The structured error and the message are built from the same two values, so a lowercased edge in the message would be a third spelling of a fact the struct already fixes — and `extensions.path` carries `Edge` verbatim ([26.5.5](#2655-error-mapping)), so the wire format would disagree with the log line. `*NestedMutationError.Error()` renders `<Edge>: <verb>[: <id>]: <cause>`, dropping the id segment when the failure is not id-scoped.

Attribution is not per *row*: a batched statement reports one violation for the whole statement and the offending index is not recoverable from any driver. The wrapped error is untouched, so `errors.Is(err, ErrConstraintViolation)` and the `*ConstraintError` dispatch keep working — a child FK violation is still a foreign-key violation and a duplicate is still a unique violation.

Two failures have no existing sentinel and get one, both carried by the structured `*NestedMutationError{Edge, Verb, ID}` wrapper ([22.1](#221-generated-error-types), [22.2](#222-constraint-errors)):

| Condition | Error | GraphQL code |
|---|---|---|
| `connect` target not visible — O2M and M2M alike | `ErrNotFound` naming the id | `NOT_FOUND` — **never** `BAD_REFERENCE` |
| `connect` target already parented to **another** row (O2M) | `ErrAlreadyRelated` naming the id | `CONFLICT` — unreachable on an `allow_reparent: true` edge, which adopts it instead ([9.9.6](#996-execution-order)) |
| `connect` target already parented to **this** parent (O2M) | none — no-op | n/a |
| has-one `create` or `connect` when the parent already holds a **different** child | `ErrAlreadyRelated` naming the child the edge holds, attributed to `connect` when the block sets it and to `create` otherwise | `CONFLICT` — on every has-one edge, `allow_reparent: true` included: the flag lets a target change parents, not a parent hold two children |
| two verbs naming one target on one edge, a has-one block setting both `create` and `connect`, or a self-reference on a self-referential edge | `ErrNestedVerbConflict` | `INVALID_INPUT` |

The `NOT_FOUND` mapping for a visibility miss is pinned, not incidental: mapping it to `BAD_REFERENCE` would tell the caller the row exists and they may not have it, which is the existence oracle the visibility read was added to close.

#### 9.9.9 Observability

Nested methods have **no `hook.MutationOp` of their own** ([21.2](#212-hook-types)). They write nothing directly — every inner call fires its own hook chain under its own op — so giving them one would double-count every nested mutation in hooks, events and cache invalidation. Four consequences, each observable and none deducible from the flat path:

- **What fires, and in what order.** One hook chain, one event and one cache-invalidation dispatch per inner call, in the execution order of [9.9.6](#996-execution-order) — parent first, then per edge in Go-field-name order, `clear` before `create` before `connect` before `link` before `disconnect`. Events and invalidation register as `OnCommit` callbacks and flush FIFO after the **root** transaction commits ([18.6](#186-deferred-side-effects)), not after the nested method returns.
- **A rolled-back savepoint emits nothing.** When a nested mutation runs at depth and its savepoint rolls back, the callbacks accumulated at that depth are discarded rather than promoted, so no event and no invalidation fires for work the database threw away.
- **A relationship-loaded parent is never cached.** The terminal read selects relationships, and any relationship flag on `FieldOptions` bypasses the cache entirely ([27.6](#276-cache-invariant), [27.7](#277-cache-behavior-by-operation)). A nested write therefore cannot leave a stale composite entity in the cache.
- **Nested creates do not warm the cache**, although flat `Create` / `CreateMany` do. Warming would cost back the very read the skip-refetch escape exists to avoid: the inner calls pass a nothing-selected `FieldOptions`, so there is no entity to write through. This is a deliberate asymmetry between two write paths and is recorded here so it is not read as a defect.

#### 9.9.10 Tenancy and column access

Both are inherited, with one rule that is genuinely new:

- **A `connect` is tenant-checked by reading the target through its own client**, which applies the target's tenant filter. The FK constraint proves the row exists; only the read proves the caller may see it. A target in another tenant is `ErrNotFound`, identical to a target that does not exist. See [29.4](#294-generated-behavior).
- **`SkipTenancy` propagates to every nested child**, and under it the tenant column is not auto-set — the caller must populate it on each nested child input, exactly as on the flat path. See [29.10](#2910-relationship-propagation).
- **The [§32](#32-column-access-control) access projection governs nested inputs.** A column the projection drops from a child's create input is absent from the nested child input too, and an entity hidden from the API gets no nested member on the API surface. See [32.5](#325-interactions).

---

## 10. Omittable Package

The `omittable` package provides a generic wrapper type used throughout generated input structs to distinguish three states: **not provided**, **set to a value**, and **set to zero/nil**.

### 10.1 The Problem

Go zero values are ambiguous in update operations. If a `CreateUserInput` has `Name string` and the caller doesn't set it, Go initializes it to `""`. The generated code cannot distinguish "the caller wants to set the name to empty string" from "the caller didn't provide a name at all."

For **create** inputs, some fields are required and some are optional — optional fields need the omittable wrapper.

For **update** inputs, **every** field must be omittable — a partial update should only modify fields the caller explicitly sets.

### 10.2 API

```go
package omittable

// Value wraps a value of type T with presence tracking.
type Value[T any] struct {
    value T
    set   bool
}

// Set creates a Value that is present with the given value.
func Set[T any](v T) Value[T]

// Omit creates a Value that is not present (zero state).
func Omit[T any]() Value[T]

// Get returns the value and whether it was set.
func (o Value[T]) Get() (T, bool)

// IsSet returns true if the value was explicitly provided.
func (o Value[T]) IsSet() bool

// MustGet returns the value, panicking if not set.
func (o Value[T]) MustGet() T

// MarshalJSON implements json.Marshaler. Marshals the wrapped value.
func (o Value[T]) MarshalJSON() ([]byte, error)

// UnmarshalJSON implements json.Unmarshaler. Marks the value as set.
// A JSON null sets the zero value for T (nil for pointer types).
func (o *Value[T]) UnmarshalJSON(data []byte) error

// IsZero reports whether the value is unset. Enables the omitzero
// JSON struct tag to omit unset fields during marshaling.
func (o Value[T]) IsZero() bool
```

### 10.3 Usage in Generated Code

**Create inputs** — field classification determines whether a column is required, omittable, or excluded:

| Column Property | CreateInput Treatment | Rationale |
|----------------|----------------------|-----------|
| NOT NULL, no DEFAULT | Required (bare type) | Caller must provide |
| Nullable (no DEFAULT) | `omittable.Value[*T]` | Caller may omit; DB inserts NULL |
| Has DEFAULT (nullable or not) | `omittable.Value[T]` | Caller may omit; DB applies default |
| PK (strategy `db`, UUID) | `omittable.Value[T]` | Caller may override; DB applies default if omitted |
| PK (strategy `app`) | `omittable.Value[T]` | Caller may override; app generates UUID if omitted |
| PK (strategy `db`, auto-increment/serial/identity) | Excluded | Sequence-based — caller cannot provide |
| PK (strategy `caller`) | Required (bare type) | Caller must provide |
| `GENERATED ALWAYS AS (...)` | Excluded | Computed by DB, never writable |
| Soft delete columns (`deleted_at`, etc.) | `omittable.Value[T]` | Caller may omit (default NULL/false/0); supports data backfilling |
| Columns in `update_columns` list (`updated_at`, etc.) | `omittable.Value[T]` | Caller may omit; DB applies default on CREATE, `time.Now()` auto-set on UPDATE |

When a field is omittable in CreateInput and the caller doesn't set it, the SQL builder **omits the column entirely** from the INSERT statement, allowing the database to apply its DEFAULT. The generator never duplicates DEFAULT expressions in Go code.

For `CreateMany`, all rows in a multi-row INSERT must share the same column list. When omittable fields differ per row, `sql.Default` is used as a sentinel value — `BuildMultiInsert` emits the SQL `DEFAULT` keyword instead of a placeholder for that position. This works on PostgreSQL and MySQL. **SQLite does not support the `DEFAULT` keyword in VALUES clauses**, so the code generator emits `sql.DefaultExpr` instead — a sentinel carrying the raw SQL default expression (parsed from the DDL) or `NULL` for nullable columns without a default. `BuildMultiInsert` writes the expression inline. A table with no writable column (its only non-generated column is a `db`-strategy auto-increment key) still names that key in each `CreateMany` row, because a multi-row INSERT cannot name no column: PostgreSQL and MySQL send `DEFAULT`, and SQLite sends `NULL` for the NOT NULL `INTEGER PRIMARY KEY`, which SQLite fills with the next rowid.

```go
type CreateProductInput struct {
    Name      string                         // Required — NOT NULL, no DEFAULT
    Price     float64                        // Required — NOT NULL, no DEFAULT
    CompanyID omittable.Value[*string]       // Optional — nullable FK
    Status    omittable.Value[string]        // Optional — has DEFAULT 'active'
    // id: excluded (PK, strategy app — auto-generated)
    // created_at: excluded (has DEFAULT NOW())
    // total: excluded (GENERATED ALWAYS AS price * quantity)
}
```

**Update inputs** — all mutable fields use `omittable.Value[T]`. PK and computed columns are excluded. `update_columns` (e.g., `updated_at`) are included as omittable — the caller may override, otherwise `time.Now()` is auto-set in the generated Update method after the empty-update check:

```go
type UpdateProductInput struct {
    Name      omittable.Value[string]  // Set to update, omit to leave unchanged
    Price     omittable.Value[float64]
    CompanyID omittable.Value[*string] // Set to nil to NULL, omit to leave unchanged
    Status    omittable.Value[string]  // Set to override default
    UpdatedAt omittable.Value[time.Time] // Set to override auto-set, omit for time.Now()
    // id: excluded (PK — never updated)
    // created_at: excluded (immutable)
    // total: excluded (GENERATED ALWAYS — computed by DB)
}
```

**Generated SQL logic** — the generated client code builds the SET clause directly by checking `IsSet()` on each `omittable.Value[T]` field. No reflection is used — the generator knows all field names and column mappings at generation time and produces explicit checks:

```go
// Generated code (simplified) — no reflection, explicit per-field checks
func (c *productClient) Update(ctx context.Context, id string, input *UpdateProductInput) (*Product, error) {
    table := sql.Table{Schema: "public", Name: "products"}
    builder := sql.NewUpdateBuilder(dialect, table)
    builder.Where(sql.Where("id").Eq(id))

    if input.Name.IsSet() {
        builder.Set("name", input.Name.MustGet())
    }
    if input.Price.IsSet() {
        builder.Set("price", input.Price.MustGet())
    }
    if input.CompanyID.IsSet() {
        builder.Set("company_id", input.CompanyID.MustGet())
    }
    if input.Status.IsSet() {
        builder.Set("status", input.Status.MustGet())
    }
    // ... one check per mutable field

    result := builder.Build()
    // result.Statement contains only SET clauses for fields where IsSet() == true
    // Produces: UPDATE "public"."products" SET ... WHERE "id" = $1
    // ...
}
```

Each field is checked individually in generated code — the `IsSet()` / `MustGet()` calls are direct method calls on the `omittable.Value[T]` type, not reflection-based introspection. If no fields are set, the builder produces an empty SET clause and the method returns the current entity unchanged (Section 9.5).

**Caller usage:**

```go
// Only update the price — name is untouched
client.Products().Update(ctx, productID, &<pkg>.UpdateProductInput{
    Price: omittable.Set(49.99),
})

// Set nullable FK to nil (NULL in DB)
client.Products().Update(ctx, productID, &<pkg>.UpdateProductInput{
    CompanyID: omittable.Set[*string](nil),
})
```

### 10.4 JSON Serialization

`Value[T]` implements `json.Marshaler` and `json.Unmarshaler` so that update inputs can be deserialized from API requests. An absent JSON field produces an unset `Value`, a `null` JSON field produces `Set(nil)` for pointer types, and a present JSON field produces `Set(value)`.

`Value[T]` also implements `IsZero() bool`, returning `true` when the value is unset. Generated struct fields use the `omitzero` struct tag (not `omitempty`) to omit unset values during JSON marshaling. Go 1.24+ `encoding/json` calls `IsZero()` only via `omitzero`; the legacy `omitempty` tag does not invoke `IsZero()` on struct types.

## 11. Filtering & Comparators

### 11.1 Generated Filter Struct

Each table gets a `{Table}Filter` struct with:
- One comparator field per column (type determined by column Go type — includes the soft delete column as a regular comparator, e.g., `DeletedAt *comparator.NullableTime` for timestamp strategy)
- One `*{Target}Filter` field per **list** relationship (O2M / M2M) — filter the parent by its children, compiled to a correlated `EXISTS` (see [Relationship filters](#relationship-filters) below)
- `And []*{Table}Filter` — each member's own fields are AND'd, and the members are AND'd together
- `Or []*{Table}Filter` — each member's own fields are AND'd, and the members are **OR'd** together, i.e. `Or: [A, B]` compiles to `(A OR B)`. A filter object's own fields are always conjunctive; only `Or`-list membership is disjunctive
- For composite PK tables: `PKs []{Table}PK` — batch composite PK match via tuple IN or expanded OR

Each filter struct has a generated `ToConditions(dialect)` method that converts the filter to SQL conditions **without reflection**. The generator produces explicit nil-checks per comparator field:

```go
// Generated per table — converts filter struct to SQL conditions.
// Packages with relationship filter members extend the signature with a
// variadic `opts ...FilterOption`; see "FilterOption" under Relationship
// filters below.
func (f *ProductFilter) ToConditions(dialect sql.Dialect) []sql.Condition {
    // A nil receiver contributes no conditions. The *Where methods dereference
    // their filter only here, so this is what makes a nil filter reach
    // ErrEmptyFilter (Section 10) rather than dereference nil; it also lets a
    // nil entry inside And/Or be skipped.
    if f == nil {
        return nil
    }

    var conds []sql.Condition

    // Per-column comparators — one nil-check per field
    if f.ID != nil {
        conds = append(conds, f.ID.Parse(dialect.QuoteIdentifier("id"), dialect)...)
    }
    if f.Name != nil {
        conds = append(conds, f.Name.Parse(dialect.QuoteIdentifier("name"), dialect)...)
    }
    if f.Price != nil {
        conds = append(conds, f.Price.Parse(dialect.QuoteIdentifier("price"), dialect)...)
    }
    if f.CreatedAt != nil {
        conds = append(conds, f.CreatedAt.Parse(dialect.QuoteIdentifier("created_at"), dialect)...)
    }

    // And/Or composition — recursive on the same generated method.
    //
    // A filter object's own fields are ALWAYS conjunctive; only membership in
    // the `Or` list is disjunctive. So each `Or` member contributes
    // sql.And of its own conditions, and the members are OR'd together as ONE
    // group condition appended to conds. Appending a per-member sql.Or instead
    // would append N conditions, which the caller joins with AND — collapsing
    // `Or: [A, B]` into `A AND B`.
    //
    // The group is appended only when some member compiled to something: an
    // empty sql.Or expands to a literal "()", which the builder keeps because
    // it is not the empty string, yielding invalid SQL.
    for _, sub := range f.And {
        subConds := sub.ToConditions(dialect)
        if len(subConds) > 0 {
            conds = append(conds, sql.And(subConds...))
        }
    }
    var orGroup []sql.Condition
    for _, sub := range f.Or {
        subConds := sub.ToConditions(dialect)
        if len(subConds) > 0 {
            orGroup = append(orGroup, sql.And(subConds...))
        }
    }
    if len(orGroup) > 0 {
        conds = append(conds, sql.Or(orGroup...))
    }

    // Soft delete column — regular comparator field, no special handling.
    // Soft delete scoping (injecting default "is not deleted" conditions) is
    // handled by the generated methods, not the filter. ToConditions produces
    // only explicit caller-set conditions.
    if f.DeletedAt != nil {
        conds = append(conds, f.DeletedAt.Parse(dialect.QuoteIdentifier("deleted_at"), dialect)...)
    }

    return conds
}
```

This follows the same reflection-free pattern as scan targets (Section 19.1) and update builders (Section 10.3) — the generator knows all fields at generation time and produces explicit per-field code. The `And`/`Or` recursion calls the same generated method on nested filter instances.

**Soft delete scoping** is handled by the generated methods, not the filter. When `exclude_deleted` is enabled (default when a soft delete column exists), each method checks whether the caller set the soft delete comparator on the filter — if not, the method injects a default "is not deleted" condition (e.g., `deleted_at IS NULL`). If the caller sets the comparator, no default is injected. This keeps `ToConditions` purely a condition converter with no implicit behavior. See [Section 9.8](#98-generated-method-patterns) for implementation details.

#### Relationship filters

A filter can constrain a row by its **related** rows. Each **list** relationship on the table — O2M and M2M — contributes one `*{Target}Filter` field, and a non-nil value compiles to a correlated `EXISTS` subquery. The subquery is built from the join metadata the relationship already carries: the FK column on the target for O2M, the junction table plus both its FKs for M2M.

A **to-one** relationship (O2O / belongs-to) contributes **no** filter member. Its FK column is directly filterable on the parent, and the inverse list direction on the target expresses the same predicate, so an `EXISTS` compilation for to-one relationships would add a third spelling of a predicate the filter already carries twice.

```go
type TaskFilter struct {
    Status    *comparator.Enum[TaskStatus] `json:"status"`
    Assignees *UserFilter                  `json:"assignees"`  // M2M via task_assignees
    Labels    *LabelFilter                 `json:"labels"`     // M2M via task_labels
    And []*TaskFilter `json:"and"`
    Or  []*TaskFilter `json:"or"`
}
```

`ToConditions` emits one `EXISTS` per non-nil relationship member and delegates the subquery's `WHERE` to the target's own `ToConditions`, so nesting composes recursively and a relationship filter combines freely with column filters and with `and` / `or`:

```sql
-- filter: { status: {eq: 'done'}, assignees: { id: {eq: $2} } }
SELECT ... FROM "tasks" WHERE "status" = $1 AND EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM "task_assignees" ja
  JOIN "users" tgt ON tgt."id" = ja."user_id"
  WHERE ja."task_id" = "tasks"."id" AND tgt."id" = $2
    AND tgt."deleted_at" IS NULL          -- target's soft-delete rule
    AND tgt."workspace_id" = $3           -- target's tenant rule, when tenanted
)
```

The subquery's **structure** is identical on all three dialects — only identifier quoting and placeholder style differ (`$N` on PostgreSQL, `?` on MySQL and SQLite), as for any other generated condition.

Three invariants:

1. **The target's own scoping applies inside the subquery.** Its soft-delete predicate ([§17.3](#173-generated-behavior)) and, when the target is tenanted, its tenant predicate ([§29.4.1](#2941-reads)) are injected into the `EXISTS`. A relationship filter is a read of the target, so it must not become a path around either rule — without the tenant injection it would be a cross-tenant existence probe.
2. **The parent-side correlation reference carries no qualifier at generation time.** The plain read path emits `FROM "tasks"` (unqualified) while the O2O-join path emits `FROM "tasks" t` and alias-prefixes every filter condition, so the correlation must render as `"tasks"."id"` in the first case and `t."id"` in the second. The generator therefore emits the structured `Exists` condition ([§11.5](#correlated-exists-and-qualifier-resolution)), which carries only the correlation **column**; the builder resolves the qualifier against the enclosing statement, and `PrefixConditions` passes the condition through untouched because it is not a leaf clause.
3. **One hop per level.** Depth comes from nesting a relationship filter inside a relationship filter; there are no aggregate predicates (`count > 3`) — those need a `GROUP BY` / `HAVING` shape and their own operator vocabulary.

An unset (nil) relationship member contributes no SQL, preserving the "nil filter ⇒ no WHERE clause" contract.

##### `FilterOption` — how the tenant reaches `ToConditions`

Invariant 1 needs a value `ToConditions(dialect)` cannot reach. The subquery's tenant predicate is a **bound parameter**, not a correlated column, and the tenant is resolved from `ctx` by the client method — so a filter converted with the dialect alone has nothing to bind. `ToConditions` therefore takes a variadic option set:

```go
func (f *TaskFilter) ToConditions(dialect sql.Dialect, opts ...FilterOption) []sql.Condition
```

The parameter is emitted **only when the package contains at least one relationship filter member**; a project with no list relationship keeps the bare `ToConditions(dialect)` and regenerates byte-identically. When it is emitted, every filter in the package carries it — including views, which have no relationships — so recursion through `and` / `or`, recursion into a relationship member, and every generated call site have one uniform signature. `ToConditions(dialect)` remains a valid call in either form.

Two things travel in the option set, and both must reach an arbitrarily nested member:

- **The resolved tenant**, via the exported `WithFilterTenant(tenant T)`. Generated read and filter-accepting mutation methods pass it automatically from the same resolution the outer `WHERE` uses; converting a filter without it produces subqueries scoped as if `CallOptions.SkipTenancy` were set, which is exactly what `SkipTenancy` itself needs.
- **The subquery nesting depth**, which names the target alias (`tgt0`, `tgt1`, …). A self-referential relationship filter nested inside itself ([§13.5](#135-self-referential-relationships)) would otherwise alias both levels the same, and the inner alias would shadow the outer one — the correlation would silently compare the related row to itself.

**Emission is limited to shapes `Exists` can express.** It carries exactly one correlation column, so a parent without a single-column primary key contributes no relationship filter members, and an M2M whose target has no single-column primary key contributes none for that edge. A relationship whose Go field name is already taken by a column comparator is likewise skipped — the column wins, as it does on the model struct.

**MySQL error 1093.** MySQL rejects an `EXISTS` naming the table an `UPDATE` or `DELETE` is mutating. A relationship filter whose target *is* the mutated table — a self-referential edge — is therefore a read-path predicate on MySQL, not one to pass to `UpdateWhere` / `SoftDeleteWhere` / `HardDeleteWhere` / `Increment`. PostgreSQL and SQLite accept it.

### 11.2 Comparator Types

#### Universal Comparators (all dialects)

| Comparator | Go Constraint | Operators |
|------------|---------------|-----------|
| `ID` | string-based IDs | `Eq`, `Neq`, `In`, `Nin`, `Gt`, `Gte`, `Lt`, `Lte`, `Custom` |
| `NullableID` | nullable string IDs | All of ID + `Null` |
| `String` | string columns | `Eq`, `Neq`, `Contains`, `StartsWith`, `EndsWith`, `Like`, `NLike`, `In`, `Nin`, `Gt`, `Gte`, `Lt`, `Lte`, `Custom` |
| `NullableString` | nullable strings | All of String + `Null` |
| `Number[T]` | any numeric `T` | `Eq`, `Neq`, `In`, `Nin`, `Gt`, `Gte`, `Lt`, `Lte`, `Between`, `NBetween`, `Custom` |
| `NullableNumber[T]` | nullable numeric | All of Number + `Null` |
| `Bool` | boolean columns | `Eq`, `Neq`, `Custom` |
| `NullableBool` | nullable booleans | All of Bool + `Null` |
| `Time` | `time.Time` | `Eq`, `Neq`, `In`, `Nin`, `Gt`, `Gte`, `Lt`, `Lte`, `Between`, `NBetween`, `Custom` |
| `NullableTime` | nullable time | All of Time + `Null` |
| `Enum[T]` | any enum `T` | `Eq`, `Neq`, `In`, `Nin`, `Custom` |
| `NullableEnum[T]` | nullable enum | All of Enum + `Null` |
| `Opaque[T]` | any `T` — no constraint | `Eq`, `Neq`, `In`, `Nin`, `Gt`, `Gte`, `Lt`, `Lte`, `Custom` |
| `NullableOpaque[T]` | nullable opaque | All of Opaque + `Null` |

**`Opaque[T]` — the family for columns whose Go type is neither text nor a Go
numeric.** `bytea` / `blob`, `inet`, `cidr` and `macaddr` resolve to `[]byte`,
`net.IP`, `net.IPNet` and `net.HardwareAddr`. Each is equality- and
order-comparable **in SQL**, but none is a Go `string` and none satisfies
`comparator.Numeric`, so without this family they fall through to
`comparator.String`, and the generated filter compares a binary or network column
against a text parameter. The operand is the column's own Go type, so
the driver encodes it natively — `payload = $1` binds a `[]byte`, not a base64
or hex rendering of one.

The type parameter is `any`, **not `comparable`**: `[]byte`, `net.IP` and
`net.IPNet` are not comparable, and the constraint would buy nothing — the
family never compares in Go, it only emits `sql.Condition` values whose operands
go straight to the driver. (`Enum[T]`'s `comparable` constraint is likewise
nominal; it is kept there because enum Go types are always comparable and the
constraint documents intent.)

The **text** operators — `Contains`, `StartsWith`, `EndsWith`, `Like`, `NLike` —
are deliberately absent. `interval`, `inet` and `macaddr` have no `LIKE`
operator at all (PostgreSQL raises SQLSTATE 42883), and on `bytea` / `blob`
pattern matching runs against raw bytes, which is not what a caller filtering a
signature or a MAC address means.

#### JSON Comparator (PostgreSQL and MySQL)

Generated for `json`/`jsonb` columns on PostgreSQL and MySQL. Produces dialect-specific SQL.

| Comparator | Operators |
|------------|-----------|
| `JSON` | `Contains`, `HasKey`, `Custom` |
| `NullableJSON` | All of JSON + `Null` |

**Dialect-specific SQL generation:**

| Operator | PostgreSQL | MySQL |
|----------|-----------|-------|
| `Contains` | `col::jsonb @> $` | `JSON_CONTAINS(col, $)` |
| `HasKey` | `col::jsonb ? $` | `JSON_CONTAINS_PATH(col, 'one', $)` |

The `JSON` comparator's `Parse()` method accepts the dialect and produces the correct SQL for each database.

**SQLite is not covered, and the column is non-filterable there rather than silently unfiltered.** `Parse` has no `sqlite` arm, so on SQLite both operators fall through and the comparator contributes zero conditions. A filter field that parses, dispatches into a real translator and emits no SQL is the accept-and-ignore class [§26.4](#comparator-input-projection) exists to remove, so the generator does not emit one: a column resolving to `types.JSON` under `input.dialect: sqlite` — reachable only through `type_map` / `overrides.types` / `column_map.type`, since the SQLite parser types a `JSON` column, a declared type it does not recognize, as `blob`, and [7.2](#72-built-in-type-mappings) maps `blob` to `[]byte` — is filterable on **neither** the model side nor the GraphQL side. It keeps its Go type, its column, and every other surface; only the filter field is absent.

The gap is `Contains`, not the dialect — measured against SQLite 3.51.3, PostgreSQL 16 and MySQL 8.0. SQLite has a faithful `HasKey` — `json_type(col, $) IS NOT NULL` agrees with `JSON_CONTAINS_PATH` on every probed path, including a key whose value is `null`, which the more obvious `json_extract(col, $) IS NOT NULL` gets wrong. It has no containment operator, and every emulation it can express is path-based and therefore position-sensitive, where `@>` and `JSON_CONTAINS` compare array elements order-independently: `{"tags":["y"]}` is contained in `{"tags":["x","y"]}` on both supported dialects and is not under any SQLite form. Shipping that would trade an over-broad no-op for a plausible, silently wrong subset. `comparator.JSON` is a dialect-agnostic Go struct, so `Contains` cannot be withheld from one dialect while `HasKey` ships; the family goes as a unit. Two further SQLite-only facts weigh the same way: SQLite has no JSON column type, so nothing validates the stored text, and a single malformed row anywhere in the scanned set fails the whole query with `malformed JSON` — including rows the filter would not have matched.

Filterability on both surfaces derives from the same comparator resolution, so a `sqlite` arm in `Parse` is the single point that governs the dialect.

**The PostgreSQL cast is required, and it is free.** Containment (`@>`) and existence (`?`) are defined for `jsonb` alone — PostgreSQL gives the `json` type only `->`, `->>`, `#>` and `#>>` — so the uncast form fails at request time with `operator does not exist: json @> unknown` (SQLSTATE 42883). Casting is therefore not an optimization to weigh but the operator's precondition. Where the column is already `jsonb` the cast costs nothing: the planner elides a same-type cast, so a GIN index still matches (`meta::jsonb @> $1` plans as `Index Cond: (meta @> …)`). That is what lets one arm serve both column types, which it must — `Parse` receives a column name and a dialect, never the column's SQL type. Nor is there an index to lose on the `json` side: PostgreSQL has no GIN opclass for `json` at all, while `CREATE INDEX … USING GIN ((col::jsonb))` matches the cast form exactly.

Two limits follow from the cast and are accepted rather than worked around:

- **A `json` value holding a `\u0000` escape cannot be cast.** `json` stores it; `jsonb` cannot represent it. A filter whose scan reaches such a row fails with `unsupported Unicode escape sequence`. This is unavoidable while keeping the operators, since containment on `json` has no json-native form; the alternative is dropping the operators entirely.
- **`HasKey`'s operand is dialect-specific.** PostgreSQL's `?` takes a bare key name (`region`); MySQL's `JSON_CONTAINS_PATH` takes a JSON path (`$.region`). One `hasKey` input therefore means different things on the two dialects. The comparator does not translate between the forms — a portable filter must spell the operand for its own dialect.

`Null` tests the column itself and takes no cast on either dialect (`col IS NULL`).

#### PostgreSQL-Only Comparators

These comparators are only generated when `input.dialect` is `postgres`. Using them with other dialects is a configuration error caught at generation time.

| Comparator | Operators | SQL Operators |
|------------|-----------|---------------|
| `JSONB` | `HasKey`, `HasAnyKey`, `HasAllKeys`, `Contains`, `ContainedBy`, `PathExists`, `Custom` | `?`, `?|`, `?&`, `@>`, `<@`, `@?` |
| `NullableJSONB` | All of JSONB + `Null` | |
| `Slice[T]` | `ContainsAny`, `ContainsAll`, `ContainedBy`, `IsEmpty`, `Custom` | `&&`, `@>`, `<@` |
| `NullableSlice[T]` | All of Slice + `Null` | |

**JSONB vs JSON:** When the dialect is PostgreSQL and the column type is `jsonb`, the code generator uses the `JSONB` comparator (full operator set). For `json` columns on PostgreSQL, the `JSON` comparator is used instead — a narrower operator set (`Contains` / `HasKey` only), reached through a `::jsonb` cast because the PostgreSQL `json` type carries none of the document operators itself. The split is about which operators the *comparator* offers, not about avoiding the cast: `JSONB` needs no cast because it is only ever selected for a column that is already `jsonb`. On MySQL, all JSON columns use the `JSON` comparator regardless of column type. On SQLite neither family is selected — see the JSON comparator section above.

#### Comparator Selection by Column Type

The code generator selects the comparator based on the resolved Go type and dialect:

| Go Type | Comparator | Notes |
|---------|-----------|-------|
| `string` | `ID` or `String` | `ID` for primary keys and foreign keys; `String` for all other string columns |
| `int*`, `uint*`, `float*` | `Number[T]` | Generic over numeric type |
| `decimal.Decimal` | `String` | **Not** `Number[T]` — `decimal.Decimal` does not satisfy the `Numeric` constraint. Filtering is on the canonical string form; ordered operators stay numerically correct because the parameter is compared against a numeric column and the database coerces. The GraphQL face is `DecimalComparator` ([§26.4](#comparator-input-projection)). |
| `bool` | `Bool` | |
| `time.Time` | `Time` | |
| `time.Duration` (from `interval`) | `Number[time.Duration]` | `time.Duration` is `~int64`, so it satisfies `Numeric` and needs no family of its own. The driver encodes it as an interval, so the ordered and `Between` operators compare intervals rather than nanosecond counts. The GraphQL face is `DurationComparator` ([§26.4](#comparator-input-projection)). This is a comparator-only classification: `time.Duration` is **not** added to the increment-eligible set, so a duration column emits no `_inc` / `_dec` operators ([§26.5.4](#2654-mutation-translation)). |
| `[]byte` (from `bytea` / `blob` / `binary` / `varbinary` / `tinyblob` / `mediumblob` / `longblob`) | `Opaque[[]byte]` | All dialects. **Not** `String` — a BLOB never equals a TEXT value on SQLite, so a string comparator on a binary column matches nothing at all there, and on PostgreSQL / MySQL it matches only a caller who hand-encodes the driver's own literal form |
| `net.IP` (from `inet`) | `Opaque[net.IP]` | PostgreSQL only |
| `net.IPNet` (from `cidr`) | `Opaque[net.IPNet]` | PostgreSQL only |
| `net.HardwareAddr` (from `macaddr`) | `Opaque[net.HardwareAddr]` | PostgreSQL only |
| Enum types | `Enum[T]` | |
| `types.JSON` (from `json`) | `JSON` | PostgreSQL and MySQL. **Non-filterable on SQLite** — `comparator.JSON.Parse` has no `sqlite` arm, so the filter field is omitted on both surfaces rather than accepted and ignored |
| `types.JSON` (from `jsonb`) | `JSONB` | PostgreSQL only; falls back to `JSON` on MySQL, and is non-filterable on SQLite for the reason the `json` row gives |
| Array types (e.g., `[]string`, `UserRoleSlice`) | `Slice[T]` | PostgreSQL only; enum arrays use named slice types. **Exception:** `json[]` / `jsonb[]` resolve to `[]types.JSON`, whose element type is not `comparable`, so `Slice[T]` cannot be instantiated — those columns are **non-filterable** on the model side and on the GraphQL side alike (see [§26.4](#comparator-input-projection)) |

Nullable variants are selected automatically when the column is nullable.

**`uuid` columns select `ID` / `NullableID`, keyed on the SQL type.** Every UUID
binding filters as an identifier — the default `uuid.UUID` / `*uuid.UUID`, the
wrapper-backed integrations' `uuid.NullUUID`, and a column overridden to `string`
alike ([7.4](#74-built-in-type-integrations)) — so the comparator a `uuid` column
takes does not change with the integration. The selection is keyed on the SQL type
rather than the resolved Go type, and applies to any `uuid` column, not only PKs and
FKs: a bare `uuid` carrying a polymorphic soft-reference, or one projected through a
view, filters the same way. Keying it on the Go type's FK-conversion shape instead
would misclassify `decimal` and `time` columns, which share that shape.

**Types not named above fall back to `String`, and that remains the default.** A
Go type reaches the fallback only through `type_map` or `overrides.types` — a
consumer type sqlgen has no built-in mapping for, and therefore no knowledge of
how the driver encodes. The default is right for the common shapes: a type whose
`driver.Valuer` renders a string (`decimal.Decimal`, `ksuid.KSUID` — both
store into text columns), and a type the driver encodes natively into
a column whose text input format the operand already matches (`netip.Addr` over
`inet` accepts `{ eq: "10.0.0.1" }`). The four `Opaque[T]` rows above exist
precisely because those types are **not** in that population: sqlgen resolves
them itself, from SQL types whose storage it knows, so guessing is neither
necessary nor correct.

Two limits of the fallback are real and deliberately accepted. An override type
over a non-text column still advertises the text operators (`contains`, `like`,
…), which the database may reject at runtime — on PostgreSQL, `LIKE` against
`inet` / `macaddr` / `interval` raises SQLSTATE 42883. And an override type
whose driver encoding does not match its column's text input format compares
wrongly rather than loudly. Both are consequences of sqlgen not modeling the
type; a consumer who needs a precise filter surface for one binds it explicitly
rather than relying on the fallback. What is **not** accepted is sqlgen doing
this to a type it resolved itself — the `Opaque[T]` rows above exist so that it
never does.

### 11.3 Comparator Interface

Every comparator implements:
```go
Parse(columnName string, dialect sql.Dialect) []sql.Condition
```

Each `sql.Condition` contains a `Clause` (SQL fragment with `$` placeholder), a `Value`, and a `Column` naming the column token inside `Clause`.

**`columnName` is written verbatim, so the caller quotes it.** A comparator puts the token it receives into both `Clause` and `Column` unchanged, as `sql.Where` does, and builders render `Clause` verbatim. The generated `ToConditions` therefore passes `dialect.QuoteIdentifier(column)` ([§11.1](#111-generated-filter-struct)): a keyword, mixed-case or digit-leading column is otherwise invalid SQL. `Column` carrying the quoted token is what lets `PrefixConditions` qualify it as `u."2024_quota"` rather than `"u.2024_quota"`.

**`Column` exists so alias qualification does not have to guess.** When a read takes the O2O-join path, `sql.PrefixConditions` qualifies every filter condition with the parent alias. Where `Column` is set it qualifies that token in place; where it is empty it falls back to prepending `alias + "."` to the whole clause, which is correct only for a clause whose column is its leading token. Every comparator sets it. The fallback is what `Custom` / `sql.Raw` conditions rely on and is left unchanged.

The distinction is load-bearing rather than cosmetic: `comparator.JSON`'s MySQL arms emit `JSON_CONTAINS(col, $)`, which leads with a function name, so blind prepending yields `u.JSON_CONTAINS(col, ?)` — MySQL resolves that as a stored routine in schema `u` and fails at request time. Dropping qualification instead is not an alternative: an unqualified column is ambiguous whenever a joined table carries the same name.

The `dialect` parameter is used by:
- `In`/`Nin` operators — produce `= ANY($1)` / `!= ALL($1)` on PostgreSQL+pgx, expanded `IN ($1, $2, ...)` / `NOT IN ($1, $2, ...)` on others
- `JSON`/`JSONB` comparators — produce dialect-specific JSON operators
- Universal comparators use the dialect for placeholder style but produce standard SQL otherwise

### 11.4 Custom Conditions

All comparators support a `Custom` field: raw `sql.Condition` for arbitrary SQL injection when built-in operators are insufficient.

### 11.5 Condition Composition

The `sql` package provides both raw condition types and a fluent `ConditionBuilder` for ergonomic construction.

#### Raw Types

- `And(conditions...)` — joins conditions with AND
- `Or(conditions...)` — joins conditions with OR
- `Subquery{SQL, Args}` — nested SELECT as a condition value. Its `SQL` marks the args with bare `$` tokens, one per arg in order, or with `$1`…`$k`, where `$N` is the subquery's own `Args[N-1]` and may repeat or appear out of order; one form per subquery, not both. The builder numbers either form into the enclosing statement's positional sequence in `Conditions` order, like every other condition, so the caller never writes an enclosing-statement position or `?`. PostgreSQL renders `$N` at its absolute position, so a repeated `$N` reuses one parameter; MySQL and SQLite emit one `?` per token, with the args in token order. A `$` inside a string literal, a quoted identifier, a comment or a PostgreSQL dollar-quoted string is the SQL's own text and is not a token. Quotes match the SQL-standard way, a doubled quote escaping itself. On MySQL a backslash also escapes the character after it inside a `'…'` or `"…"` string literal, as MySQL's default `sql_mode` reads it. PostgreSQL and SQLite read a backslash there literally, and a PostgreSQL `E'…'` escape is not recognised, so write `''` on them. SQL outside both forms is the caller's responsibility: the builder neither checks nor repairs it, and passes it to the database. Most such shapes fail there, but some run without an error: on SQLite, fewer bare `$` tokens than args (the surplus args shift onto the placeholders that follow); on MySQL and SQLite, an arg no `$N` references (left out); on PostgreSQL, a `$N` past `len(Args)`, which is copied as written and so binds the enclosing statement's Nth parameter whenever that parameter exists and its type fits
- `Range{Start, End}` — BETWEEN clause
- `Exists(correlationColumn, Subquery)` — correlated `EXISTS` predicate; the parent-side qualifier is resolved by the builder, not by the caller (see [Correlated EXISTS and qualifier resolution](#correlated-exists-and-qualifier-resolution) below)
- `Raw(clause, args...)` — an opaque SQL fragment as a condition, parenthesised when rendered. Its clause marks the args with the same two token forms as a `Subquery`'s `SQL`, read by the same rules: bare `$` tokens one per arg in order, or `$1`…`$k` numbered against the clause's own args, with the same quote-aware token scan and the same pass-through of SQL outside both forms. A hand-built `Condition` with a scalar or `[]any` value is read the same way, except a `[]any` clause ending ` IN $` or ` NOT IN $`, which expands to a list

#### ConditionBuilder

A fluent builder that eliminates the need to construct `sql.Condition` structs manually. `sql.Where(column)` writes `column` verbatim, like a comparator's `columnName` ([§11.3](#113-comparator-interface)), so the caller quotes it: generated code passes `c.dialect.QuoteIdentifier(col)` for every PK, tenant and soft delete predicate. The bare names below are shorthand.

```go
// Simple conditions
cond := sql.Where("price").Gt(100.00)
cond := sql.Where("name").Like("%widget%")
cond := sql.Where("status").In("active", "pending")
cond := sql.Where("created_at").Between(startDate, endDate)
cond := sql.Where("deleted_at").IsNull()
cond := sql.Where("email").IsNotNull()

// Composition
cond := sql.And(
    sql.Where("price").Gte(50.00),
    sql.Where("stock").Gt(0),
)

cond := sql.Or(
    sql.Where("role").Eq("admin"),
    sql.Where("role").Eq("superadmin"),
)

// Nesting
cond := sql.And(
    sql.Where("active").Eq(true),
    sql.Or(
        sql.Where("role").Eq("admin"),
        sql.And(
            sql.Where("role").Eq("user"),
            sql.Where("verified").Eq(true),
        ),
    ),
)

// Subquery: In / Nin given a single sql.Subquery render a nested SELECT
cond := sql.Where("company_id").In(sql.Subquery{
    SQL:  `SELECT "id" FROM "companies" WHERE "country" = $`,
    Args: []any{"US"},
})

// Raw SQL escape hatch
cond := sql.Raw("price * quantity > $", 1000.00)
```

**Builder methods:**

| Method | SQL Produced |
|--------|-------------|
| `Eq(v)` | `col = $` |
| `Neq(v)` | `col != $` |
| `Gt(v)` | `col > $` |
| `Gte(v)` | `col >= $` |
| `Lt(v)` | `col < $` |
| `Lte(v)` | `col <= $` |
| `In(v...)` | `col IN ($, $, ...)` on every dialect; `col IN (<subquery>)` for a single `sql.Subquery` argument |
| `Nin(v...)` | `col NOT IN ($, $, ...)` on every dialect; `col NOT IN (<subquery>)` for a single `sql.Subquery` argument |
| `Like(v)` | `col LIKE $` |
| `NLike(v)` | `col NOT LIKE $` |
| `Between(a, b)` | `col BETWEEN $ AND $` |
| `IsNull()` | `col IS NULL` |
| `IsNotNull()` | `col IS NOT NULL` |

`In` / `Nin` always expand: the array-parameter form (`col = ANY($)` / `col != ALL($)` on PostgreSQL+pgx) is chosen by the comparators, from `Dialect.SupportsArrayParams()` ([Appendix A](#appendix-a-sql-builder-functions)), never by the builder. That split is what lets `comparator.Enum` take the expanded form on pgx (see [11.2](#112-comparator-types)).

All builder methods return `sql.Condition`, making them composable with `sql.And()`, `sql.Or()`, and usable anywhere a raw `sql.Condition` is accepted (including the `Custom` field on comparators).

#### Correlated EXISTS and qualifier resolution

A correlated subquery must reference a column of the **enclosing** statement's table, and that reference has to carry the qualifier the enclosing statement actually used. The qualifier is not knowable at generation time, because the same filter reaches two builders:

| Builder | `FROM` clause | Correlation must render as |
|---|---|---|
| `BuildSelect` | `FROM "tasks"` — no alias | `"tasks"."id"` |
| `BuildSelectJoin` | `FROM "tasks" t` — aliased, and every condition is alias-prefixed | `t."id"` |

A condition carrying a pre-baked qualifier is therefore correct on exactly one of the two paths and invalid SQL on the other, on every dialect. The `Exists` condition resolves this by **carrying the correlation column and never the qualifier**:

```go
sql.Exists("id", sql.Subquery{SQL: "SELECT 1 FROM ...", Args: []any{...}})
```

**Rules.**

1. **The builder supplies the qualifier.** At render time the enclosing statement resolves it once — `SelectOptions.Alias` when the statement aliases its table, `Dialect.FormatTable(table)` otherwise — and renders `<qualifier>.<QuoteIdentifier(CorrelationColumn)>` inside the subquery's correlation predicate. The same `Exists` value is therefore correct on both read paths without the generator knowing which one will run.
2. **`PrefixConditions` never rewrites it.** Alias prefixing (`prefixCondition`) prepends `alias + "."` to the leading token of a **leaf string clause**; an `Exists` is a structured condition value, like `And` / `Or` / `Subquery` / `Range`, so it is not a leaf clause and is passed through untouched — including when nested inside `And` / `Or`, which prefixing descends recursively. This is exemption **by construction**, not an opt-out flag the caller can forget to set.
3. **Placeholder numbering is unchanged.** The subquery's args participate in the enclosing statement's positional numbering in `Conditions` slice order, exactly as any other multi-arg condition — the contract `BuildSelectJoin` documents and the child-tenant filter already relies on. JOIN `On` strings still contribute nothing.
4. **Dialect differences are quoting and placeholders only.** The emitted structure is identical across PostgreSQL, MySQL, and SQLite; `$N` vs `?` and the identifier quoting style are the only deltas.

This is what [§11.1](#111-generated-filter-struct)'s relationship filters compile to, and it is the only supported way to emit a condition that references the enclosing statement's own table. Hand-built multi-identifier clauses remain the caller's responsibility to qualify, per the contract on `PrefixConditions`.
