Field naming follows `api.graphql.field_casing` — accepted values `camel_case` (default) or `snake_case`. Type names always PascalCase, Query/Mutation root names always camelCase, Enum values always SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE (a value derived from a digit-leading column name carries [§8.5](#85-naming-rules)'s `col_` guard — `2010_revenue` → `COL_2010_REVENUE`).

**Generated schema example:**

```graphql
type Product {
  id: ID!
  name: String!
  price: Decimal!
  stock: Int!
  status: ProductStatus!
  createdAt: DateTime!

  # Relationships — loaded only when selected in query
  # No per-relationship pagination args; the bulk-IN loader populates the full set
  company: Company
  reviews: [Review!]!
  tags: [Tag!]!
}

type Query {
  # Single by PK (returns null when missing — no separate exists query needed)
  product(id: ID!): Product

  # Cursor pagination — Relay Connection.
  # Ordering is determined by `cursor_keys` (see §14.2 for keyset stability).
  # No `sort` arg: applying a different ordering would invalidate cursors emitted
  # by the runtime, so custom sort is exposed only on `productList` (offset).
  products(
    filter: ProductFilter
    first: Int
    after: String
    last: Int
    before: String
  ): ProductConnection!

  # Offset pagination — ListResult envelope (totalCount lives on the envelope,
  # so no separate productCount query is generated)
  productList(
    filter: ProductFilter
    sort: [ProductSort!]
    limit: Int
    offset: Int
  ): ProductListResult!
}

type Mutation {
  createProduct(input: CreateProductInput!): Product!
  createProducts(inputs: [CreateProductInput!]!): [Product!]!
  updateProduct(id: ID!, input: UpdateProductInput!): Product!
  updateProducts(filter: ProductFilter!, input: UpdateProductInput!): [Product!]!
  upsertProduct(input: CreateProductInput!): Product!
  # Naming under §26.5.1 delete rules: only the variants the schema allows and
  # `api.operations` keeps are generated. When both are enabled, `delete<Table>` is suppressed in favor
  # of explicit `softDelete<Table>` / `hardDelete<Table>`.
  deleteProduct(id: ID!): Boolean!
}

# Relay Connection — for cursor pagination
type ProductConnection {
  edges: [ProductEdge!]!
  pageInfo: PageInfo!
  totalCount: Int!
}

type ProductEdge {
  node: Product!
  cursor: String!
}

# ListResult — for offset pagination (intentionally distinct from [Product!]!
# so the schema's *shape* signals semantics: Connection = cursor, ListResult =
# offset, [T!]! = unbounded relationship list).
# Field-for-field aligned with the runtime PaginateResult[T] (§14.1) so the
# wrapper's gqlgen.yml merge (§26.5.6) binds them directly.
type ProductListResult {
  items:      [Product!]!
  totalCount: Int!
  offset:     Int!
  limit:      Int!
  hasMore:    Boolean!
}

# Filter input types — maps 1:1 to generated Filter structs.
# The soft-delete column itself (e.g. `deletedAt: NullableTimeComparator`) is exposed
# as a regular comparator field, so callers who want to include soft-deleted
# rows simply pass any non-nil deletedAt comparator (`{}` works) — the
# runtime's auto-injected "is not deleted" condition skips whenever the
# user has set the soft-delete column comparator. No dedicated
# `includeDeleted: Boolean` flag — the existing column-level surface is
# sufficient. See §26.5.3 for the translator details.
input ProductFilter {
  name: StringComparator
  price: DecimalComparator          # decimal column — Decimal operands, see below
  status: ProductStatusComparator   # enum column — monomorphized per enum
  stock: NumericComparator
  createdAt: TimeComparator         # NOT NULL column
  deletedAt: NullableTimeComparator # nullable ⇒ distinct input type, carries isNull
  reviews: ReviewFilter             # relationship ⇒ correlated EXISTS (§11.1)
  and: [ProductFilter!]
  or: [ProductFilter!]
}

# NOT NULL columns reference this form. Nullable columns reference
# `NullableStringComparator`, which is identical plus `isNull: Boolean`.
input StringComparator {
  eq: String
  neq: String
  gt: String
  gte: String
  lt: String
  lte: String
  contains: String
  startsWith: String
  endsWith: String
  like: String
  nlike: String
  in: [String!]
  nin: [String!]
}

input NumericComparator {
  eq: Float
  neq: Float
  gt: Float
  gte: Float
  lt: Float
  lte: Float
  in: [Float!]
  nin: [Float!]
  between: NumericRange
  nbetween: NumericRange
}

# Monomorphized per enum — operands are the bound GraphQL enum, so
# `{eq: BANANA}` is a parse-time schema error, not a runtime one.
input ProductStatusComparator {
  eq: ProductStatus
  neq: ProductStatus
  in: [ProductStatus!]
  nin: [ProductStatus!]
}

input CreateProductInput {
  name: String!
  price: Decimal!
  stock: Int!
  status: ProductStatus!
  companyId: ID
}

input UpdateProductInput {
  name: String
  companyId: ID
  # Numeric columns get value + _inc + _dec operators (see §26.5.4).
  # Set at most one of `<field>`, `<field>_inc`, `<field>_dec` per request.
  stock:     Int
  stock_inc: Int
  stock_dec: Int
  price:     Decimal
  price_inc: Decimal
  price_dec: Decimal
}

input ProductSort {
  field: ProductSortField!
  direction: SortDirection!
}

enum ProductSortField {
  NAME
  PRICE
  CREATED_AT
}

enum ProductStatus {
  DRAFT
  ACTIVE
  ARCHIVED
}

enum SortDirection {
  ASC
  DESC
}
```

Which queries and mutations are generated per table is decided by the methods the schema gives the client ([4.6 Operations](#operations)), narrowed by the `api.operations` mask. A table with `api: {operations: read_only}` only gets Query fields — no Mutations. The detailed per-operation gating rules live in §26.5.1.

##### PK columns in the create input

Whether a primary-key column appears in `Create<T>Input` is decided by the table's **PK strategy** ([§8.6](#86-primary-key-strategy)), not by primary-key membership alone:

| PK strategy | In `Create<T>Input`? | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `db` (serial / auto-increment / DB default) | **No** | The database generates the value. |
| `app` (server-minted UUID) | **No** | The generated Go client mints the value. Exposing it would let an external client dictate a server-owned identity. |
| `caller` | **Yes**, as a required (`Type!`) field | Nothing generates the value. If the input omits it the INSERT writes zero-valued keys, so the client has no way to name the row it is creating. |

A composite PK is always `caller` ([§8.6](#86-primary-key-strategy)) — it is a tuple of foreign keys. A **single-column** PK that is a foreign key is `caller` for the same reason, so a 1:1 extension table's create input carries the key that names its parent row:

```graphql
# user_credentials(user_id UUID PRIMARY KEY REFERENCES users(id), provider, external_id, created_at)
input CreateUserCredentialInput {
  userID:     UUID!
  provider:   String!
  externalID: String!
  createdAt:  Time!
}
```

And a pure M2M junction's create input is exactly its key tuple:

```graphql
# task_assignees(task_id, user_id, assigned_at, PRIMARY KEY (task_id, user_id))
input CreateTaskAssigneeInput {
  taskID:     UUID!
  userID:     UUID!
  assignedAt: Time!
}

# task_labels(task_id, label_id, PRIMARY KEY (task_id, label_id)) — all-PK junction
input CreateTaskLabelInput {
  taskID:  UUID!
  labelID: UUID!
}
```

This is narrower than the Go `Create<T>Input` struct, which also carries `app`-strategy PKs as omittable fields: its audience is server-side resolver code that may mint the identity, whereas the GraphQL input's audience is the external client.

`Update<T>Input` excludes **every** PK column regardless of strategy — a PK is the row's identity, addressed through the mutation's PK arguments, never set as an attribute. An all-PK table therefore has a create input but no update input, and emits `create<Table>` / `create<Table>s` / `upsert<Table>` without `update<Table>` / `update<Table>s`.

**Empty-input rule.** `Create<T>Input` / `Update<T>Input` and their mutations are emitted only when the type would hold at least one field; gqlgen rejects an empty `input X {}` block. This suppresses the create surface for a table whose only column is a server-generated surrogate PK, and — via [§32.2](#322-roles) — for a table whose every writable column is dropped by an `access` role.

**Upsert on an all-PK table.** The conflict clause's UPDATE half excludes the conflict target, so a junction whose columns are exactly its key has nothing to set. The generated statement degrades to `ON CONFLICT (...) DO NOTHING` (PostgreSQL / SQLite) or a no-op self-assignment (MySQL, which has no `DO NOTHING`), making `upsert<T>` an idempotent "ensure this link exists".

##### Comparator input projection

Every comparator family in [§11.2](#112-comparator-types) is projected onto the GraphQL surface. Three rules govern the projection.

**Rule 1 — monomorphize the generic families whose type parameter survives the binding.** GraphQL has no generics, so `comparator.Enum[T]`, `Slice[T]` and `Opaque[T]` cannot each be a single input type: they are specialized per concrete type parameter, and the specialization reuses the binding that type already has (an enum column's comparator takes the bound GraphQL enum, not `String`; an `Opaque[net.IP]` column's takes the `IP` scalar its field already declares). **`Number[T]` is the partial exception** — every Go numeric *width* binds to the one `Float` scalar, so the type parameter collapses on the GraphQL side and the family projects **unmonomorphized** as a single `NumericComparator`. The per-`T` split for numeric widths lives in the *translator*, not the schema ([§26.5.3](#2653-filter--sort--pagination-translation)). `time.Duration` is the one `Number[T]` instantiation that does **not** collapse: it binds to the `Duration` scalar rather than `Float`, so by this rule's own keying (family, **GraphQL operand type**, nullability — see **Sharing** below) it takes its own `DurationComparator`. Monomorphizing on the operand type rather than on `T` is what makes both outcomes fall out of one rule. The alternative for enums and slices — keeping `StringComparator` and parsing at runtime — is rejected: it moves `{status: {eq: "banana"}}` from a parse-time schema rejection to a runtime error, discarding the introspection contract and the client-side codegen that depends on it.

**Rule 2 — nullability is a *separate input type*, not a conditional field.** GraphQL input types are global: a single `TimeComparator` cannot carry `isNull` for `deletedAt` and omit it for `createdAt`. So each family projects **two** input types, and a column references whichever matches its nullability:

- `<X>Comparator` — for `NOT NULL` columns. No `isNull`.
- `Nullable<X>Comparator` — for nullable columns. Same operands **plus** `isNull: Boolean` (`true` ⇒ `IS NULL`, `false` ⇒ `IS NOT NULL`), projecting the model-side `Null *bool`.

This mirrors the `String` / `NullableString` split on the Go side exactly, and matches the translator pair that already exists (`translateTimeComparator` / `translateNullableTimeComparator` — [§26.5.3](#2653-filter--sort--pagination-translation)). Operand types are identical between the two; nullability adds `isNull` and nothing else.

**Rule 3 — a comparator input is emitted only when some column references it.** This holds for **both** forms, not just the nullable twin: a schema with no nullable time column emits no `NullableTimeComparator`, and a schema with no boolean column emits no `BooleanComparator`. The rule is a correctness requirement, not a size optimisation. A family's operand type may name a scalar that is itself declared only on use ([§26.4.1](#2641-scalar-marshaling)) — `TimeComparator` operands are typed `Time`, `DecimalComparator` operands are typed `Decimal` — so an input emitted with nothing referencing it can reference a scalar the schema never declares, and gqlgen rejects the document. Deriving the declarations and the references from the same per-column projection ([§26.5.3](#2653-filter--sort--pagination-translation)) keeps the two in step by construction. A companion range input (`NumericRange`, `TimeRange`) is declared exactly once alongside whichever form of its family is emitted, since `between` / `nbetween` name it from either.

The `Custom` field every comparator carries ([§11.4](#114-custom-conditions)) is **never** projected — it is a raw-SQL escape hatch, and exposing it over HTTP would be an injection surface. (It is a field on each family, not a `comparator.Custom` type.)

| Go comparator | GraphQL input | Operand type | Operators |
|---|---|---|---|
| `String` / `NullableString` | `StringComparator` | `String` | `eq neq gt gte lt lte contains startsWith endsWith like nlike in nin` |
| `ID` / `NullableID` | `IDComparator` | `ID` | `eq neq gt gte lt lte in nin` |
| `Number[T]` / `NullableNumber[T]` | `NumericComparator` | `Float` | `eq neq gt gte lt lte in nin between nbetween` |
| `Bool` / `NullableBool` | `BooleanComparator` | `Boolean` | `eq neq` |
| `Time` / `NullableTime` | `TimeComparator` | `Time` | `eq neq gt gte lt lte in nin between nbetween` |
| `String` / `NullableString` on a **decimal** column | `DecimalComparator` | `Decimal` | `eq neq gt gte lt lte in nin` |
| `Enum[T]` / `NullableEnum[T]` | `<EnumName>Comparator` (`<EnumName>EnumComparator` on collision — see below) | the bound GraphQL enum | `eq neq in nin` |
| `JSON` / `NullableJSON` | `JSONComparator` | `JSON`, `String` | `contains hasKey` |
| `JSONB` / `NullableJSONB` | `JSONBComparator` | `JSON`, `String`, `[String!]` | `hasKey hasAnyKey hasAllKeys contains containedBy pathExists` |
| `Slice[T]` / `NullableSlice[T]` | `<Elem>SliceComparator` | `[<Elem>!]`, `Boolean` (`isEmpty`) | `containsAny containsAll containedBy isEmpty` |
| `Number[T]` / `NullableNumber[T]` on a **`time.Duration`** column | `DurationComparator` | `Duration` | `eq neq gt gte lt lte in nin between nbetween` |
| `Opaque[[]byte]` / `NullableOpaque[[]byte]` | `BytesComparator` | `Bytes` | `eq neq gt gte lt lte in nin` |
| `Opaque[net.IP]` / `NullableOpaque[net.IP]` | `IPComparator` | `IP` | `eq neq gt gte lt lte in nin` |
| `Opaque[net.IPNet]` / `NullableOpaque[net.IPNet]` | `CIDRComparator` | `CIDR` | `eq neq gt gte lt lte in nin` |
| `Opaque[net.HardwareAddr]` / `NullableOpaque[net.HardwareAddr]` | `MacAddrComparator` | `MacAddr` | `eq neq gt gte lt lte in nin` |

Each row names the `NOT NULL` form. The nullable form of the same row is `Nullable<X>Comparator` with the identical operand set plus `isNull: Boolean`, per Rule 2.

**`<EnumName>Comparator` disambiguates against the fixed families.** A SQL enum PascalCasing to `Duration`, `Time`, `Numeric`, `Decimal`, `IP` or `CIDR` derives an input name a fixed family already owns. When that happens the enum's input takes the spelling **`<EnumName>EnumComparator`**, along with its `Nullable` twin (`Nullable<EnumName>EnumComparator`) and its translator (`translate<EnumName>EnumComparator`). Without it the column silently inherits the fixed family's operand set — a `Duration`-named enum column advertising `gt` / `lt` / `between` / a `DurationRange` that no enum translator can serve, which is the accept-and-ignore class Rule 1 exists to remove.

`<Elem>SliceComparator` needs no such rule: the name always ends in `Slice` before `Comparator`, so it cannot equal any fixed family name whatever the element type is. Enum monomorphization is the only row that can reach the fixed set.

The disambiguation is keyed on the **fixed** owned names only — the families in the table above, their `Nullable` twins, the range inputs, and the four fixed type names in [GraphQL type name ownership](#graphql-type-name-ownership) below. It is deliberately **not** keyed on the rest of the schema: an emitted input name is part of the published API contract, and a name that shifted because an unrelated table was added would break persisted client queries. A collision that survives disambiguation — an enum named `duration` (suffixed to `DurationEnumComparator`) beside one named `duration_enum` (which derives that name directly) — is a generation error rather than a second suffix, for the same reason.

**Dialect gating.** `JSONBComparator`, `<Elem>SliceComparator`, `IPComparator`, `CIDRComparator` and `MacAddrComparator` are emitted **only** under `input.dialect: postgres`, matching the PostgreSQL-only comparator rule in [§11.2](#112-comparator-types). On MySQL a `jsonb` column falls back to `JSONComparator`, exactly as the model side does; on SQLite, where `comparator.JSON` has no dialect arm, a `json` / `jsonb` column is non-filterable on both sides instead ([§11.2](#112-comparator-types)). Array columns and the `inet` / `cidr` / `macaddr` types do not exist on those dialects. `BytesComparator` is emitted on **all** dialects — `bytea` on PostgreSQL and the `blob` / `binary` / `varbinary` family on MySQL and SQLite all resolve to `[]byte`. `DurationComparator` is likewise ungated: `interval` is PostgreSQL-only, but a `time.Duration` column is reachable on any dialect through `type_map` / `overrides.types`.

**Sharing.** One input type per (family, **GraphQL operand type**, **nullability**) triple across the whole project — a single `TaskStatusComparator` no matter how many tables and views filter on that enum, a single `NullableStringSliceComparator` per element type, and a single `NumericComparator` for every Go numeric width, since all of them bind to `Float` (Rule 1). Keying on the operand type rather than the Go type parameter is what makes the numeric collapse fall out of the rule instead of contradicting it — and, by the same key, what splits `Number[time.Duration]` back out into `DurationComparator`, since `time.Duration` binds to `Duration` rather than to `Float`. This is the same sharing rule the comparator *translators* follow ([§26.5.3](#2653-filter--sort--pagination-translation)), which are likewise keyed on the nullable variant.

**Decimal columns.** `decimal.Decimal` does not satisfy `comparator.Numeric`, so the model side filters decimals through `comparator.String` on the canonical string form. `DecimalComparator` is the GraphQL face of that: operands are typed with the `Decimal` scalar (not `String`), and the ordered operators are numerically correct because the parameter is compared against a numeric column — the database coerces, not the string collation. A decimal column therefore supports `{ price: { gt: "100.50" } }`.

**Opaque columns.** `BytesComparator`, `IPComparator`, `CIDRComparator` and `MacAddrComparator` are the GraphQL face of `comparator.Opaque[T]` ([§11.2](#112-comparator-types)). Their operands are typed with the **same scalar the column's own field declares** — a `payload: Bytes!` field filters through `payload: BytesComparator` whose operands are `Bytes`, so the value a client reads back is exactly the value it can filter on. That identity is the point: without this projection these columns advertise `StringComparator`, and a client that round-trips a base64 `Bytes` value into `{ payload: { eq: … } }` gets zero rows with no error, because the model side compares a binary column against a text parameter. The text operators are absent for the reason [§11.2](#112-comparator-types) gives — `LIKE` does not exist on `inet` / `cidr` / `macaddr`, and on `bytea` it matches raw bytes.

**Duration columns.** `DurationComparator` is the GraphQL face of `comparator.Number[time.Duration]`. Operands are typed with the `Duration` scalar (not `Float`), and its `between` / `nbetween` name a `DurationRange` companion input declared once alongside the family, exactly as `NumericRange` and `TimeRange` are. Filtering is interval-native — the driver encodes `time.Duration` as an interval, so `{ dur: { gt: "1h" } }` compares intervals rather than nanosecond counts. Sending the Go duration string to the database as text instead would be wrong as well as untyped: PostgreSQL reads `-2h45m0s` as `-1h15m`, applying the sign to the leading field only.

**Non-filterable columns.** Two shapes are filterable on **neither** side — no field in the GraphQL input, no entry in the translator, and no field on the model `<T>Filter` either. A column whose Go type cannot satisfy the comparator package's `T comparable` constraint — `json[]` / `jsonb[]`, which resolve to `[]types.JSON`. And a `types.JSON` column under `input.dialect: sqlite`, whose comparator family has no SQL arm for that dialect ([§11.2](#112-comparator-types)). Both fall out of one predicate over the resolved comparator, which is what makes the model side and the GraphQL side agree by construction rather than by parallel rules; [§26.5.3](#2653-filter--sort--pagination-translation)'s completeness lint enforces that the two agree. Note this constraint binds `Slice[T]` only; `Opaque[T]` is parameterized on `any` precisely so that the non-comparable `[]byte` / `net.IP` / `net.IPNet` remain filterable ([§11.2](#112-comparator-types)).

##### GraphQL type name ownership

A GraphQL document has **one flat type namespace**: scalars, enums, object types and input types all share it, and gqlparser rejects a second declaration of any name (`Cannot redeclare type Duration.`). sqlgen derives names into that namespace from three independent sources — the fixed set it always owns, the consumer's SQL identifiers, and the consumer's `api.graphql.scalars` — so the namespace is validated as a whole rather than per source.

**The owned set.** Every name the generated schema can declare:

| Source | Names |
|---|---|
| GraphQL spec built-ins | `String`, `Int`, `Float`, `Boolean`, `ID` |
| Fixed | `Query`, `Mutation`, `PageInfo`, `SortDirection` |
| Scalars in use | each declared scalar — built-in registry and `api.graphql.scalars` alike ([26.4.1](#2641-scalar-marshaling)) |
| Enums in use | each enum's Go type name ([4.11](#411-enum-overrides)) |
| Comparator families | each emitted `<X>Comparator` / `Nullable<X>Comparator` and its range input |
| Per table / view | `<T>`, `<T>Connection`, `<T>Edge`, `<T>ListResult`, `<T>Filter`, `<T>SortField`, `<T>Sort`, `Create<T>Input`, `Update<T>Input` |
| Nested mutations, as emitted ([26.5.1](#2651-exposed-resolver-surface)) | `Create<T>WithRelatedInput`, `Update<T>WithRelatedInput`, `Upsert<T>WithRelatedInput`, the enum `<T>ConflictTarget`, and per edge `<T><Edge>CreateNested`, `<T><Edge>UpdateNested`, `<T><Edge>CreateInput` |

**Two claims on one name is a generation error.** `sqlgen generate` fails, naming both claimants, the contested name, and the remedy. It is an error and not a silent rename because sqlgen owns only one of the two spellings in the general case: it can suffix a comparator input it derives (above), but it cannot rename the enum or table the consumer's schema declares, so there is no rename that makes every colliding document valid. Deferring instead to gqlgen turns a config-level mistake into a `Cannot redeclare type` at a later stage that names neither the enum nor the table responsible.

The remedies are the naming overrides that already exist: `enums.<name>.struct_name` ([4.11](#411-enum-overrides)), `tables.<name>.struct_name` ([4.8](#48-tableconfig-per-table)), `views.<name>.struct_name` ([4.9](#49-viewconfig-per-view)), or renaming the consumer scalar in `api.graphql.scalars`. Excluding the entity from the API surface also resolves it, since an unreferenced name is never declared (Rule 3).

This validation runs only when the GraphQL surface is generated — the namespace it protects is GraphQL's. The Go side has its own collision rules ([8.5](#85-naming-rules), [13.7.3](#1373-validation-rules)) and they are unaffected.

##### Views on the GraphQL surface

A view is projected exactly as a table is, gated to reads. The emitted surface per API-enabled view is closed:

| Emitted | When |
|---|---|
| `type <V>` object type | always |
| `<V>Connection` / `<V>Edge` / `<V>ListResult` envelopes | always |
| `input <V>Filter` (columns + `and` / `or`) | always |
| `input <V>Sort` + `enum <V>SortField` | always |
| `Query.<view>(pk…): <V>` | only when the view has a resolved primary key — an `@pk` annotation, or for a materialized view a qualifying unique index ([§16.4](#164-generated-artifacts-views-vs-tables), [§16.5.2](#1652-discovery)) |
| `Query.<views>(filter, first, after, last, before): <V>Connection!` | only when `cursor_keys` resolves for the view ([§4.13](#413-config-validation-rules)) |
| `Query.<view>List(filter, sort, limit, offset): <V>ListResult!` | always |
| Field-selection walker + filter / sort translators + envelope bindings | always |
| **Any** Mutation field, `Create<V>Input`, `Update<V>Input` | **never** |

A view has no relationships ([§16.4](#164-generated-artifacts-views-vs-tables)), so its object type is columns-only, its walker has no relationship cases, and a view read is exactly **one** query under the [§25.1](#251-query-count-guarantee) contract. Materialized views emit this identical surface — `Refresh` / `RefreshConcurrently` are Go-client-only and appear nowhere in the schema ([§29.2.5](#2925-view-tenancy)).

**Gating.** `views.<name>.api.enabled: false` excludes the view entirely. `views.<name>.api.operations` narrows the three read keys (`get`, `paginate`, `connection`) subtractively; naming any mutation operation there is a **config error**, not a silent no-op ([§4.13](#413-config-validation-rules)) — the block cannot express a mutation on a read-only entity, and saying so beats ignoring a knob the user deliberately turned.

**Tenancy.** A tenanted view's queries are tenant-scoped by the generated client underneath the resolver ([§29.2.5](#2925-view-tenancy)). The API layer adds no tenancy logic of its own; it inherits the scope because it calls the scoped client method.

#### 26.4.1 Scalar Marshaling

gqlgen requires every non-primitive scalar to be marshalable in one of four ways:

1. **Spec built-ins.** `String`, `Int`, `Float`, `Boolean`, `ID` — handled by gqlgen with no consumer-side code.
2. **gqlgen-bundled built-ins.** `Time`, `Map`, `Upload`, `Any`, `Int64` — gqlgen ships `MarshalX` / `UnmarshalX` for these. sqlgen writes **no marshaler body** for them, but it does merge a `models:` entry, pinning the scalar to the bundled marshaler that carries the declared `go_type` (`Int64` + `int64` → `graphql.Int64`, `Time` + `time.Time` → `graphql.Time`). The entry is not redundant with gqlgen's own defaults: `injectBuiltins` binds `Int64` to the **two-entry** list `[graphql.Int, graphql.Int64]`, and a generated position takes `Model[0]`, so an `int64` column routed onto `Int64` would take an `int` input field in front of an `int64` model, and an input translator that does not compile. Pinning the marshaler collapses the list to the declared type in every position — and removes the `Model[0]` ordering dependency the "Numeric width binding" note below would otherwise have to re-check on every gqlgen bump.

   Both halves of `marshaling: builtin` are config-validated, because neither failure announces itself: the scalar **name** must be one gqlgen bundles (gqlgen leaves an unrecognised scalar unbound and silently binds it to `string`), and the `go_type` must be one that bundled marshaler carries (gqlgen otherwise binds its own type). Either way the result is the same shape as any other unbound scalar — a `panic("not implemented")` field resolver on read, a non-compiling translator on write. An entry declaring `marshaling: builtin` with **no** `go_type` binds nothing to check — it reaches no column, declares no `scalar`, and emits no `models:` entry — so it stays legal. It is also the one shape that is genuinely silent: the unresolved-declaration warning below skips an empty `go_type`, so a typo'd bare `builtin` entry is inert rather than diagnosed.
3. **Method-based marshaling.** Type has `MarshalGQL(io.Writer)` and `UnmarshalGQL(any) error` methods. gqlgen picks them up via `gqlgen.yml` model mapping. **This is where sqlgen-shipped runtime types live.**
4. **External marshalers.** Free functions `MarshalX(v T) graphql.Marshaler` and `UnmarshalX(v any) (T, error)` declared in a Go package the gqlgen.yml `models:` entry references. Used for third-party types (`uuid.UUID`, `decimal.Decimal`) that don't ship with the marshaling methods.

**Sqlgen-shipped scalar types.** The sqlgen runtime ships custom types that already model nullability and JSON-shape semantics: `types.JSON`, `types.DateTime`, `types.NullDateTime`. These types implement `MarshalGQL(io.Writer)` and `UnmarshalGQL(any) error` natively, using only stdlib (`io.Writer`, `any`) — **no gqlgen import is added to the runtime module, the stdlib-only invariant holds.** `types.JSON.UnmarshalGQL` accepts any JSON shape (object, array, scalar, null) and re-encodes to bytes; shape constraints are a resolver-layer concern, not enforced at the type boundary (see §7.6 for the rationale).

GraphQL-side behavior:
- When a column's resolved Go type is one of these, sqlgen emits a `scalar X` declaration into the generated `.graphqls` on first use (deduped — once per scalar, not once per column).
- The wrapper merges a `models:` entry into the consumer's `gqlgen.yml` binding the GraphQL scalar to the runtime type.
- The non-null variant (`DateTime`) and the Null wrapper (`NullDateTime`) are emitted as **two separate GraphQL scalars** — see "Null-wrapper scalar pairing" below.
- No `MarshalX` / `UnmarshalX` is emitted into `graph/scalars_gen.go` for these — the methods live on the runtime types themselves.

**Null-wrapper scalar pairing.** Several Go types relevant to sqlgen — `uuid.NullUUID`, `decimal.NullDecimal`, `types.NullDateTime`, the `database/sql.NullX` family — are **struct wrappers** that encode null through a `Valid bool` field rather than through a Go pointer. gqlgen's standard nullability mechanism is pointer-based (a nullable schema field of scalar `T` produces a `*T` resolver signature), and gqlgen has no first-class story for null-wrapper structs (`grep NullUUID` against the gqlgen repo returns zero results).

To preserve the model layer's wrapper-based shape (which is required for clean pgx scanning, FK extraction in the relationship loaders per §15.2.1, and the wrapper unwrap path), sqlgen exposes **a paired GraphQL scalar per wrapper**:

- The non-null variant binds to the bare Go type (`uuid.UUID`, `decimal.Decimal`, `types.DateTime`).
- The Null variant binds to the wrapper struct (`uuid.NullUUID`, `decimal.NullDecimal`, `types.NullDateTime`) and serializes the wrapper's `Valid` field as GraphQL nullability on the wire.

**Spec-built-in partners.** The `database/sql.NullX` family pairs differently from the three above: its non-null partner is a **GraphQL spec built-in** (`String`, `Boolean`, `Int`, `Float`) or the gqlgen-bundled `Time`, not a second registry entry. Only the Null member is registered, because the non-null member is what sqlgen already resolves a `NOT NULL` column of that type to. The wire-format invariant below is unaffected — `NullInt32` and `Int` both carry a JSON number, `NullString` and `String` both carry a JSON string — and the `Valid` field stays a Go-side detail. These entries exist because `overrides.use_pointers: false` ([§4.7](#47-overrideconfig)) makes every nullable column of a `nullSQL` type resolve to one of these wrappers; without them such a column resolves to `String` in front of a non-string Go field, which is both a wrong schema and a non-compiling input translator.

Unmarshaling a `NullInt16` / `NullInt32` range-checks the incoming value: gqlgen binds the `Int` scalar to a Go `int`, which is wider than the column, and silently truncating would write a different number than the client sent.

**Schema-side rule.** A column's GraphQL field type is determined by the column's resolved Go type, not by the SQL nullability flag in isolation:

- Resolved Go type matches the non-null entry → field type is `<Scalar>!` (GraphQL non-null).
- Resolved Go type matches a Null wrapper entry → field type is `<NullScalar>` (GraphQL nullable). The `!` is omitted because the wrapper itself can carry an absent value, and gqlgen's pointer wrap (`*<wrapper>`) at the resolver boundary lets the seed translate `nil → wrapper{Valid: false}` on input.

**Wire-format invariant.** Both members of a pair MUST share an identical wire-format contract — the consumer-facing JSON shape is a primitive (string for UUID / Decimal / DateTime, arbitrary value for JSON), or `null` for the Null variant. The `Valid bool` is a Go-side implementation detail and never appears on the wire. A consumer issuing a mutation against `userID: NullUUID` writes `{ userID: "550e8400-..." }` or `{ userID: null }` — never `{ userID: { uuid: "...", valid: true } }`. The Unmarshal function on the Null scalar collapses `nil → wrapper{Valid: false}` and `string → wrapper{<UnderlyingField>: parsed, Valid: true}`.

**Resolver / seed boundary.** Because gqlgen wraps nullable scalars in pointers, the seed/translator layer for the Null variant follows a fixed pattern:

```go
// Input translation: gqlgen gives us *uuid.NullUUID; the wrapper IS our model field type.
var v uuid.NullUUID
if in.UserID != nil {
    v = *in.UserID
}
// nil pointer → uuid.NullUUID{Valid: false}; non-nil → wrapper as-is

// Output: model field is uuid.NullUUID (struct value). The marshaler handles
// Valid → null on the wire, so the resolver returns &row.UserID unconditionally.
```

The Null variant's marshaler is the single place that maps `!Valid → graphql.Null`; the resolver layer never branches on `Valid`.

**Built-in scalar registry:**

| Scalar | Bound Go type | Source | Marshaler |
|--------|---------------|--------|-----------|
| `String` / `Int` / `Float` / `Boolean` / `ID` | `string` / `int` / `float64` / `bool` / `string` | GraphQL spec | built-in — but see "Numeric width binding" below: gqlgen binds `Int` and `Float` to a fixed, narrow set of Go types, and a column of any other width needs an anchor |
| `Time` | `time.Time` | gqlgen-bundled | bundled — `models:` pinned to `graphql.Time` (category 2) |
| `JSON` | `types.JSON` (default) or `json.RawMessage` (override) | sqlgen runtime / stdlib | **method-based, native on the type** when bound to `types.JSON`; **sqlgen-generated external marshalers** (passthrough) when bound to `json.RawMessage`. Both bindings produce the same `JSON` scalar in the schema. |
| `DateTime` | `types.DateTime` | sqlgen runtime | **method-based, native on the type** |
| `NullDateTime` | `types.NullDateTime` | sqlgen runtime | **method-based, native on the type** |
| `UUID` | `uuid.UUID` | stdlib or third-party | **sqlgen-generated external marshalers** — `String()` to marshal, and the selected integration's string constructor to unmarshal ([7.4](#74-built-in-type-integrations), "Parsing a UUID from a string"); no defensive `Nil → Null` shim. Registered under every UUID integration; all three spell the Go type `uuid.UUID`, but **not** the parse call — gofrs has no `Parse`, so the marshalers cannot hardcode one spelling. |
| `NullUUID` | `uuid.NullUUID` | third-party | **sqlgen-generated external marshalers** — emits `Null` when `!Valid`. Registered only for the **wrapper-backed** integrations — see "UUID integrations and the `NullUUID` entry" below. |
| `Decimal` | `decimal.Decimal` | third-party | **sqlgen-generated external marshalers** (uses `String()` / `decimal.NewFromString`) |
| `NullDecimal` | `decimal.NullDecimal` | third-party | **sqlgen-generated external marshalers** — emits `Null` when `!Valid` |
| `Bytes` | `[]byte` | stdlib | **sqlgen-generated external marshalers** — base64 std encoding |
| `Duration` | `time.Duration` | stdlib | **sqlgen-generated external marshalers** — Go duration string |
| `IP` | `net.IP` | stdlib | **sqlgen-generated external marshalers** — `net.ParseIP` |
| `CIDR` | `net.IPNet` | stdlib | **sqlgen-generated external marshalers** — `net.ParseCIDR` |
| `MacAddr` | `net.HardwareAddr` | stdlib | **sqlgen-generated external marshalers** — `net.ParseMAC` |
| `NullString` | `sql.NullString` | stdlib | **sqlgen-generated external marshalers** — emits `Null` when `!Valid`; partner is the spec built-in `String` |
| `NullBool` | `sql.NullBool` | stdlib | **sqlgen-generated external marshalers** — partner is the spec built-in `Boolean` |
| `NullInt16` | `sql.NullInt16` | stdlib | **sqlgen-generated external marshalers** — partner is the spec built-in `Int`; range-checked on unmarshal, because gqlgen binds `Int` to a Go `int` |
| `NullInt32` | `sql.NullInt32` | stdlib | **sqlgen-generated external marshalers** — partner is the spec built-in `Int`; range-checked on unmarshal |
| `NullInt64` | `sql.NullInt64` | stdlib | **sqlgen-generated external marshalers** — partner is the spec built-in `Int` |
| `NullFloat64` | `sql.NullFloat64` | stdlib | **sqlgen-generated external marshalers** — partner is the spec built-in `Float` |
| `NullTime` | `sql.NullTime` | stdlib | **sqlgen-generated external marshalers** — RFC 3339; partner is the gqlgen-bundled `Time` |
| Custom scalar (consumer-declared) | consumer type | consumer | consumer-supplied — `api.graphql.scalars` declares mode (`builtin` / `method` / `external`); sqlgen emits no body |

**Numeric width binding.** The `Int` and `Float` rows above are the only registry entries whose bound Go type is not a single type. A column resolves to the width its SQL type declares — PostgreSQL `smallint` → `int16`, `real` → `float32`, MySQL `tinyint` → `int8`, `int unsigned` → `uint32` — while the GraphQL field stays `Int` / `Float`. gqlgen answers that in two different ways depending on the position, and both have to be handled:

- **Generated positions** (create/update input fields, resolver arguments) take the FIRST Go type in the scalar's `models:` list — `int` for `Int`, `float64` for `Float` — regardless of the column. sqlgen bridges the difference with a plain conversion in the input translator.
- **Bound positions** (a field of the row struct, which sqlgen binds via `models:`) require an EXACT Go type match against some entry in that list. gqlgen ships marshalers for `int` / `int32` / `int64` and `float64` only, and a field of any other width matches none of them — it is not an error, it silently degrades to a `panic("not implemented")` field resolver.

sqlgen therefore appends **marshaler anchors** to the `Int` / `Float` `models:` lists for every width an exposed column actually resolves to, restating gqlgen's own entries first so the generated positions are untouched. Every integer width anchors on a marshaler **gqlgen already ships** (`graphql.Int8`, `graphql.Int16`, `graphql.Uint`, `graphql.Uint8`, `graphql.Uint16`, `graphql.Uint32`, `graphql.Uint64` — present in the runtime package, merely absent from its default list), so sqlgen emits no code and inherits gqlgen's own overflow errors. `float32` is the one width gqlgen has no marshaler for anywhere, so sqlgen emits that single pair into `graph/scalars_gen.go`.

The anchors are emitted only when a narrowed width is in use, and the GraphQL schema is unchanged either way — the wire type stays `Int` / `Float`, no `scalar` is declared, and no field changes shape.

**Array columns.** A PostgreSQL array binds through its ELEMENT, and gqlgen types a generated list field as `[]<first model>` — `[]int` for `[Int!]!`. Against a model carrying `[]int32` there is no bridge at all: Go has no conversion between slices of differing element types, and an input translator has no expression to emit. For these columns sqlgen dictates the generated field's Go type outright via `models.<Input>.fields.<field>.type`, so gqlgen emits the model's own `[]int32` and the translator assigns it directly. The scalar case is deliberately left on the conversion above — it is sound, and dictating it would change every numeric input field in the schema to buy nothing.

**Consumer-declared scalars: sqlgen wires, the consumer marshals.** `graph/scalars_gen.go` covers the **built-in registry only** — the table above. sqlgen emits no `MarshalX` / `UnmarshalX` for an `api.graphql.scalars` entry, because it cannot know the intended wire format for a type it does not ship and cannot type-check the consumer's package to verify a guess. What sqlgen contributes is the `scalar <Name>` declaration (on first use by a column, deduped like every other scalar) and the gqlgen `models:` binding; the marshaling comes from whichever mode the entry declares — gqlgen's own bundled marshaler (`builtin`), the type's `MarshalGQL` / `UnmarshalGQL` methods (`method`), or the consumer's free functions in `marshaler_package` (`external`). The `external` binding uses the same discovery-anchor shape as the registry's own category-4 entries; only the package differs.

**Additions, not overrides.** A `go_type` the built-in registry already binds — **or a scalar *name* it already uses** — is rejected at config validation rather than honored. Both axes matter, and the name axis is the more damaging: sqlgen identifies a scalar by name downstream of the Go-type lookup, and scalar registration is first-write-wins by name, so an entry named `Decimal` does not add a scalar but takes over the registry's slot, leaving real `decimal.Decimal` columns bound to the consumer's Go type with no emitted marshaler. The GraphQL spec built-ins (`String`, `Int`, `Float`, `Boolean`, `ID`) are reserved for the same reason a `scalar String` declaration would break the schema. gqlgen's other bundled scalars (`Int64`, `Map`, `Upload`, `Any`) are **not** reserved — declaring one with `marshaling: builtin` is the supported way to route a column onto them, for a `go_type` its bundled marshaler carries (category 2 above). The registry entry carries more than the binding — the Null-wrapper pairing below, and the `DecimalComparator` operand narrowing keyed on the resolved scalar name — and a `ScalarBinding` has no way to express either. Rebinding `decimal.Decimal` would therefore split the `Decimal` / `NullDecimal` pair, breaking the wire-format invariant, and silently revert numeric columns to text comparators. Consumers who need a different treatment of a registry type change the Go binding itself (`overrides.types`), which moves both members of the pair together.

**One Go type, one scalar.** The column→scalar lookup is keyed by Go type, so a Go type resolves to exactly one GraphQL scalar. Two entries declaring the same `go_type` is a config error rather than a silent race — only one could ever be consulted, and the map offers no way to say "this column gets scalar A and that one gets scalar B" for a single Go type.

**A Go type with no binding is an error.** Every API-visible column must resolve to a schema enum, a built-in registry entry, an `api.graphql.scalars` declaration, or a GraphQL spec built-in. A Go type matching none of them is rejected at `generate` time, naming the column, the Go type, and the two ways to bind it. It is **not** silently emitted as `String`: that yields a schema advertising `String` in front of a non-string Go field, which gqlgen answers with a `panic("not implemented")` field resolver on read and a `string`-typed input field the translator does not compile against — a diagnostic arriving as a Go type error at the far end of a multi-stage pipeline, naming neither the column nor the cause. This is the same rule the "Detection" paragraph below already states for `api.graphql.scalars` entries, applied to the column side.

A column dropped from every API surface by its [§32.2](#322-roles) access role (`hidden` / `internal`) is exempt: it names no GraphQL type anywhere in the emitted schema, so requiring a binding for it would make `access: hidden` — the documented way to keep a column *out* of the API — the one setting that forces the column to be described *to* the API.

**Unresolved declarations warn.** A declared scalar that no API-exposed column resolves to produces a generation warning naming the entry and its `go_type`. It is a warning, not an error, because an unused declaration is sometimes correct: a column excluded from the API by its [§32.2](#322-roles) access role or by `api.enabled: false` registers no scalar, and a declaration may legitimately land before the column that will use it. The check needs the resolved table contexts, so it fires at `generate` time rather than `sqlgen validate`. A mistyped `go_type` is not what this warning catches: the rule above catches that case harder, because the column is then left with no binding and generation fails outright rather than warning and continuing.

**Consumer scalars and nullability.** A consumer-declared scalar has no Null-variant pairing and needs none: a nullable column bound to one emits a nullable field, and gqlgen wraps the Go type in a pointer on both the bound row struct and the generated input. The pairing machinery exists specifically for struct wrappers that encode null in a `Valid bool` field, which gqlgen's pointer mechanism cannot express.

A Null-variant entry is registered automatically when a column resolves to a Go type that matches the `nullable.type` field of an override declared in `overrides.types.<sql_type>.nullable` (§7.4) — the consumer doesn't list each Null scalar separately. Built-in integrations (`uuidgoogle`, `uuidgofrs`, `decimal`, `dateTimeOverride`) populate the wrapper Go type so the registry pickup is automatic.

**UUID integrations and the `NullUUID` entry.** The `NullUUID` scalar is registered only when the package's UUID integration is a **wrapper-backed** one — `github.com/google/uuid` or `github.com/gofrs/uuid/v5` ([7.4](#74-built-in-type-integrations)). The standard library ships no `NullUUID`, so a stdlib-bound package — the default — resolves nullable `uuid` columns to `*uuid.UUID`, which is gqlgen's ordinary pointer nullability and needs no pairing at all: the column emits a nullable field of scalar `UUID`, the `NullUUID` scalar is never declared, and `graph/scalars_gen.go` carries no `MarshalNullUUID` / `UnmarshalNullUUID` pair. This falls out of the general rule above rather than being a special case — the registration is driven by a resolved `nullable.type`, and the stdlib integration declares none. The filter surface is identical either way (`NullableIDComparator`), because comparator selection reads through the wrapper ([7.3](#73-nullable-handling)).

Both wrapper-backed integrations declare the same two Go type strings — `uuid.UUID` and `uuid.NullUUID` — and the registry is keyed by Go type string. One pair of registry entries therefore serves either library without change, and **cannot distinguish them**: nothing in `uuid.NullUUID` says which package it came from. That is sound only because [7.4](#74-built-in-type-integrations) holds one UUID library per generated package, enforced by the [4.13](#413-config-validation-rules) validation row. Without that rule the registry would bind a single scalar to two different Go types in one schema, which the "One Go type, one scalar" rule above exists to prevent.

**IPv4 normalization on the `IP` scalar.** `UnmarshalIP` collapses an IPv4 address to its 4-byte form (`ip.To4()` when non-nil, the parsed value otherwise) before returning it. `net.ParseIP` returns the **16-byte** IPv4-in-IPv6 representation for a dotted-quad address, and a driver encodes that into a PostgreSQL `inet` as `::ffff:10.0.0.1/128` rather than `10.0.0.1/32`. Both render as `"10.0.0.1"` through `net.IP.String()`, so the GraphQL round-trip hides the difference entirely — but the stored value is a different `inet`, and it matches neither a text-literal comparison nor the subnet operators (`<<`, `<<=`, `>>`, `>>=`), and it is what any non-sqlgen reader of that column sees. The guard is required, not cosmetic: `To4()` returns nil for a genuine IPv6 address, which must pass through untouched. Genuine IPv6 values (`2001:db8::1`, `::1`) are unaffected; an explicitly IPv4-mapped input (`::ffff:10.0.0.1`) normalizes to `10.0.0.1`, which is the only representation PostgreSQL `inet` has for it anyway. Placing it in `UnmarshalIP` covers the filter path as well as the write path, with no second normalization anywhere: gqlgen routes **every** `IP` operand through the scalar's own unmarshaler, list elements included, so an `IPComparator` operand is already normalized by the time `translateIPComparator` sees it. Values read back out of the database need no normalization either — the driver decodes `inet` into the 4-byte form already.

**No defensive zero-value shim.** Unlike gqlgen's bundled `MarshalUUID` (which silently emits `Null` when the value equals `uuid.Nil`), sqlgen's `MarshalUUID` writes the underlying string unconditionally. A non-null field holding the Go zero value is a model-layer bug — the schema's `!` would be violated by a soft shim, and silent null emission masks the underlying issue. Consumers that need null semantics use the Null variant (`NullUUID`) at the schema level.

**Generated file: `graph/scalars_gen.go`** — holds the external `MarshalX` / `UnmarshalX` functions for every **built-in registry** category-4 scalar in use, including both members of any registered Null pair (e.g., emits both `MarshalUUID` / `UnmarshalUUID` and `MarshalNullUUID` / `UnmarshalNullUUID` when a column of either Go type is in scope). Not emitted at all when every scalar in the schema falls into categories 1–3 or is consumer-declared — a consumer-declared `external` scalar is marshaled from its own `marshaler_package`, so it contributes nothing here. **Bindings use the discovery-anchor pattern** — the `model:` path points at the package where the marshalers live (the resolver dir for these; `marshaler_package` for a consumer-declared scalar), with the symbol name acting purely as the discovery anchor; gqlgen infers the Go type from the marshaler signature, so no Go type alias declaration is needed. This mirrors gqlgen's own `_examples/scalars/model/model.go::MarshalTimestamp` shape.

```yaml
# Merged into the consumer's gqlgen.yml at wrapper time
models:
  UUID:
    model: <consumer>/<resolver_dir>.UUID            # discovery anchor — no Go type declaration
  NullUUID:
    model: <consumer>/<resolver_dir>.NullUUID        # paired Null scalar — emitted only when a NullUUID column is in scope
  Decimal:
    model: <consumer>/<resolver_dir>.Decimal
  NullDecimal:
    model: <consumer>/<resolver_dir>.NullDecimal
```

**Detection.** sqlgen carries a built-in registry of known types (`uuid.UUID`, `uuid.NullUUID`, `shopspring/decimal.Decimal`, `decimal.NullDecimal`, `json.RawMessage`, etc.) and the marshaling mode each requires. For unknown types appearing in `api.graphql.scalars`, the consumer must declare `marshaling: method | external | builtin`; codegen errors otherwise rather than silently producing a non-compiling resolver. (No reflection — detection is purely config-driven.)

**Why generate, not vendor:** the consumer already has `uuid.UUID` / `decimal.Decimal` in their `go.mod` via the existing sqlgen integration; adding a sqlgen-vendored marshaler library would force a second import of the same dep and risk version drift. Generating into the consumer's project keeps the existing single-source-of-truth.

### 26.5 GraphQL Resolver Generation

Generated resolvers are **concrete implementations** of the gqlgen-generated resolver interfaces. They translate inputs → unified-client call → outputs, with no business logic. The generated resolvers translate GraphQL field selections into the core client's `FieldOptions`, so relationship loading uses the client's batched `GetMany` strategy (1 + count(O2M selected) + 2 \* count(M2M selected) queries per request, regardless of result-set size — see [Section 25.1](#251-query-count-guarantee)).

#### 26.5.1 Exposed Resolver Surface

Not every method on the unified client becomes a root resolver. The exposed surface is curated to match the conventions established by Hasura, PostGraphile, and Prisma's GraphQL plugins, which keeps the schema small and predictable. Per-row computed mutations (`Increment`, `Decrement`) are folded into update inputs as **input operators**, not separate root fields — see §26.5.4.

**Views.** The table below is the **per-table** surface. A view's surface is the read-only subset — object type, envelopes, filter / sort inputs, and the `<view>` / `<views>` / `<view>List` queries, never a mutation — enumerated in full under [§26.4 Views on the GraphQL surface](#views-on-the-graphql-surface). The `Excluded` table below applies to views unchanged.

**Per-table surface.** Every row's gate is the `api.operations` mask key that names the row's backing client method, plus the schema fact that decides whether the client has the method at all ([4.6 Operations](#operations)). One key, one method: no key gates a surface backed by a method it does not name. With no mask, every key is on.

| Surface | Generated when... | Backed by client method |
|---------|-------------------|-------------------------|
| `<table>(id): <Type>` query | `api.operations` includes `get` | `Get` |
| `<table>s(filter, first, after, last, before): <Type>Connection!` query (cursor) | `api.operations` includes `connection` | `Connection` — ordering driven by `cursor_keys` (§14.2); no schema-level `sort` arg, see §26.5.3 |
| `<table>List(filter, sort, limit, offset): <Type>ListResult!` query (offset) | `api.operations` includes `paginate` | `Paginate` (sort threads through `translate<T>Sort` into `PaginateInput.Sort`, see §26.5.3) |
| `create<Table>(input)` mutation | `api.operations` includes `create` | `Create` |
| `create<Table>s(inputs)` mutation | `api.operations` includes `create_many` | `CreateMany` |
| `update<Table>(id, input)` mutation | `api.operations` includes `update` | `Update` (with `_inc` / `_dec` input operators dispatching to `Increment` / `Decrement` server-side) |
| `update<Table>s(filter, input)` mutation | `api.operations` includes `update_where` | `UpdateWhere` |
| `upsert<Table>(input)` mutation | `api.operations` includes `upsert` AND the table emits `<Table>ConflictPK` ([9.5](#upsert-conflict-keys)) | `Upsert` |
| `create<Table>WithRelated(input)` mutation | `nested_mutations` enables the `create` family for the table, the table has an eligible relationship, and `api.operations` includes `create_with_related` and `create` (below) | `CreateWithRelated` |
| `update<Table>WithRelated(id, input)` mutation | same, with the `update` family and `update_with_related` and `update` | `UpdateWithRelated` |
| `upsert<Table>WithRelated(input, conflictTarget)` mutation | same, with the `upsert` family and `upsert_with_related` and `upsert`, and a conflict target is left to pass (below) | `UpsertWithRelated` |
| `delete<Table>(id): Boolean!` mutation | `api.operations` includes `hard_delete` and not `soft_delete` (or the table has no soft-delete column) | `HardDelete` |
| `delete<Table>(id): <Type>` (nullable) mutation | `api.operations` includes `soft_delete` and not `hard_delete`, and the table has a soft-delete column | `SoftDelete` |
| `hardDelete<Table>(id): Boolean!` + `softDelete<Table>(id): <Type>` mutations | `api.operations` includes both, and the table has a soft-delete column | `HardDelete` / `SoftDelete` (no bare `delete<Table>` is generated) |
| `restore<Table>(id): <Type>` mutation | `api.operations` includes `restore`, and the table has a soft-delete column | `Restore` |

**Excluded from the GraphQL surface (intentionally):**

| Excluded method | Why | How to express in GraphQL instead |
|-----------------|-----|-----------------------------------|
| `Exists` | redundant with single-by-PK | `<table>(id)` returns null when missing |
| `Count` | folded into `<Type>Connection.totalCount` and `<Type>ListResult.totalCount` | `<table>List(filter, limit: 0).totalCount` for "count only, no rows" |
| `GetMany(ids)` | derivable | `<table>s(filter: { id: { in: [...] } })` |
| `UpdateMany(items)` | a batch of per-row updates, each with its own key and input, has no idiomatic GraphQL shape | `update<Table>` per row, or `update<Table>s(filter, input)` where one input applies to every row |
| `Find(filter)` | derivable | `<table>s(filter, first: 1)` then take edge |
| `Increment` / `Decrement` | per-row computed mutations idiomatically belong inside update inputs | `update<Table>(id, input: { stock_inc: 5 })` — see §26.5.4 |
| `UpsertMany` | no batch-upsert mutation is generated; the batch form exists for server-side composition, and the M2M `connect` verb that needs it reaches it through [9.9](#99-nested-mutations) rather than through a root field | `upsert<Table>` per row, or `create<Table>s` where the rows are known to be new |
| Tx primitives, savepoints | transaction lifecycle is server-internal | not exposed; the consumer composes mutations in a single request and wraps them in a transaction with gqlgen middleware |
| `Restore` (when soft delete is disabled) | meaningless | not generated |
| Per-relationship pagination args | the runtime loader issues one bulk `IN` per relationship and has no per-row `LIMIT` | relationships emit as `[Type!]!` — see [§26.12](#2612-known-limitations) |

This matches the cross-library pattern: every per-row computed mutation becomes an input operator, exists / find / get-many fold into the list query, and transaction primitives never cross the GraphQL boundary.

**Naming rules for delete/restore** (over the delete variants the table has — `soft_delete` and `restore` need a soft-delete column — and the mask keeps):

| Surviving delete variants | Generated mutations |
|-----------------------|---------------------|
| hard delete only | `delete<Table>(id): Boolean!` |
| soft delete only | `delete<Table>(id): <Table>` (returns the soft-deleted row, nullable), `restore<Table>(id): <Table>` (nullable; only when `restore` survives the mask) |
| both | `hardDelete<Table>(id): Boolean!`, `softDelete<Table>(id): <Table>` (nullable), `restore<Table>(id): <Table>` (nullable; only when `restore` survives the mask) — no bare `delete<Table>` is generated, forcing clients to choose explicitly |

Returning the entity from soft delete and restore matches Hasura's convention and lets the client use a `FieldOptions` selection on the result.

##### Narrowing the API surface: `api.operations`

The Go client generates every method the schema allows ([4.6 Operations](#operations)), and nothing in config narrows it. The API is where exposure is decided: a consumer who hand-writes a resolver to add a guard the generated one cannot express (a tenant check that spans tables, an authorization step keyed on request state) still needs the generated *client* method underneath it, while wanting the generated *mutation* gone so there is only one door.

`api.operations` is that knob — a **mask** over the operations the API may expose, and the only per-operation control sqlgen has:

```yaml
api:
  enabled: true
  operations: read_only          # default mask for every table
  graphql: { enabled: true }

tables:
  task_labels:
    api:
      operations:                # replaces the global mask for this table
        create: false            # no createTaskLabel / createTaskLabels
        upsert: false            # no upsertTaskLabel
                                 # client.TaskLabels().Create(...) is untouched
```

**Semantics:**

- **Presets.** The bare-string form (`operations: read_only`) and an object form with an optional `preset` plus individual keys both work. Presets are an explicit enumeration over the API keys, not a partial overlay — a key a preset does not name resolves to off:

  | Preset | Keys on |
  |--------|---------|
  | `all` | every key (the default when no mask is set) |
  | `read_only` | `get`, `paginate`, `connection` |
  | `append_only` | `read_only` + `create`, `create_many`, `create_with_related` |
  | `no_delete` | every key except `soft_delete`, `hard_delete`, `restore` |
  | `no_hard_delete` | every key except `hard_delete` |

  Each `…_with_related` key follows the base it composes, which is what makes `append_only` yield `create_with_related` alone. The two delete presets keep all three, since a nested `disconnect` is an FK null-out on O2M, not a delete.
- **Keys.** `get`, `paginate`, `connection`, `create`, `create_many`, `update`, `update_where`, `upsert`, `soft_delete`, `hard_delete`, `restore`, `create_with_related`, `update_with_related`, `upsert_with_related` — each the snake-case name of the client method its surface calls (table above).
- **Resolution order.** `tables.<name>.api.operations` replaces `api.operations` **wholesale** — it is not merged. Absent at both levels means no mask.
- **Subtractive only.** The effective API surface is the client's schema-allowed set **intersected** with the mask. Every generated resolver delegates to the Go client, so the API can never expose an operation the client does not generate. An explicit per-table entry set `true` for an operation the schema does not allow — `soft_delete` / `restore` without a soft-delete column, `upsert` or `upsert_with_related` without any conflict target, a `…_with_related` key whose family `nested_mutations` does not enable for the table or for which the table has no eligible edge — is ignored and **warns**, naming the table, the key and the missing fact ([4.13](#413-config-validation-rules)); a global mask that over-reaches is silent, since one mask written for a whole schema will legitimately exceed some tables. The same scope applies to `upsert` on a table that has a unique conflict target but emits no `<Table>ConflictPK` ([9.5](#95-edge-case-behaviors)): the client has `Upsert`, but the flat `upsert<Table>` has no constant to hard-code and is omitted (below), and an explicit per-table `upsert: true` **warns**, naming the table, while a global mask stays silent. A table with no conflict target at all gets the first warning only, so one key is never reported twice.
- **Reads are maskable too.** Masking `get`, `paginate` or `connection` hides the query while the client method stays available to hand-written resolvers. This asymmetry is the point: the API surface is not required to mirror the client.
- **Only API operations may be named.** `get_many`, `update_many`, `exists`, `count`, `increment`, `stream`, and `upsert_many` name client methods no API surface calls ([Excluded from the GraphQL surface](#2651-exposed-resolver-surface) above), so naming one in an `api.operations` block is a hard error rather than a silently-ignored key. `get_many` and `update_many` are rejected on the same rule, not as a special case: `<table>List` is backed by `Paginate` and `update<Table>s` by `UpdateWhere`, so the keys that gate them are `paginate` and `update_where`. Whenever a mask is set, the masked set's `GetMany` and `UpdateMany` are off, so nothing downstream can read either as an API answer.
- **Input types follow their mutations.** `Create<T>Input` / `Update<T>Input` are emitted only when at least one mutation that consumes them survives the mask, so masking away every create-class operation removes the input type with it rather than leaving an orphan gqlgen model. One shape still leaves `Create<T>Input` unreferenced, and it is accepted as harmless, since gqlgen allows an unused input: a table that emits no `<T>ConflictPK` ([9.5](#95-edge-case-behaviors)) and whose mask leaves `upsert_with_related` as its only create-class mutation keeps the input for that nested upsert, and the nested upsert is then omitted when the [9.9.4](#994-eligibility-rules) projection leaves it no edge (**E7**).
- **Composes with `api.enabled`.** `tables.<name>.api.enabled: false` remains the whole-table off switch; the mask is for narrowing a table that stays exposed.
- **Surface-agnostic.** The mask sits on `api`, not `api.graphql`, so REST and gRPC inherit it when they land.

The `access` column roles ([§32.2](#322-roles)) narrow which *columns* cross the API boundary; `api.operations` narrows which *operations* do. Together they let a consumer expose a deliberately small API over a full-strength Go client.

##### Nested mutations on the GraphQL surface

The three `…WithRelated` mutations ([9.9](#99-nested-mutations)) are additive: `create<Table>`, `update<Table>` and `upsert<Table>` are **byte-identical** to what they were before nested mutations were enabled.

**They cannot fold into the existing three.** `create<Table>` and `upsert<Table>` are projected from the same `Create<Table>Input`, so a nested member added to that input would be advertised on both mutations and honoured reliably by neither — the schema would accept a field the executor drops, which is the accepted-and-ignored class the one-field-map invariant ([26.5.3](#2653-filter--sort--pagination-translation)) exists to prevent. Each nested mutation therefore takes its own wrapper input, projected from the Go wrapper type of the same name, which *contains* the flat input rather than restating it.

**`upsert<Table>WithRelated` takes a `conflictTarget` argument; `upsert<Table>` does not.** The flat mutation hard-codes the PK conflict target, so on a table whose PK is generated and absent from the caller's input it always takes the insert branch — harmless there, because nothing downstream depends on which branch ran. On the nested mutation it is not harmless: the update-side verb block is reachable from both branches, so an upsert that silently always inserted would make `disconnect` match nothing. The nested mutation therefore takes the generated `<Table>ConflictTarget` enum as an argument defaulting to `PK`, and the flat mutation is left exactly as it is. The enum declares `PK` for the primary-key target and, for each unique target, the SCREAMING_SNAKE form of its columns (`EMAIL`, `SKU_WAREHOUSE_ID`), so the argument reads `conflictTarget: <Table>ConflictTarget! = PK`. A unique target is declared only when every one of its columns is API-writable (`public` or `write_only`, [32.3](#323-per-surface-behavior)), because a caller can pick a row with `ON CONFLICT` only by a value it supplies; `PK` is declared whenever the table has a primary-key target. On a table with no primary-key target there is no `PK` to default to, and the argument is required; if the access projection leaves such a table with no target at all, the nested upsert mutation is omitted, as a mask would omit it. A table that emits no `<Table>ConflictPK` gives the flat mutation nothing to hard-code, so it has no `upsert<Table>`; its `upsert<Table>WithRelated` stays whenever a unique target is left to pass. On MySQL the argument does not choose which constraint fires: `ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE` takes the update branch on any unique violation ([9.5](#upsert-conflict-keys) MySQL note), and the target shapes only the update half's column list. A call that writes every column of the named target and collides on a different unique column therefore updates that row on MySQL, where PostgreSQL and SQLite return `CONFLICT`; a call that leaves a target column unwritten — the default `PK` on a database-generated key — carries no conflict clause and returns `CONFLICT` on every dialect ([9.5](#upsert-conflict-keys)). The resulting asymmetry — two upsert mutations with different conflict semantics — is deliberate and recorded in [26.12](#2612-known-limitations); nothing has asked for a conflict target on the flat form, and adding one is a separate scope decision.

**The input types are projected from the Go types.** Each wrapper holds the flat input under the table's own name (`user: CreateUserInput!`) and one member per nested edge, named the way the relationship field on the object type is (`events: UserEventsCreateNested`). On `Update<Table>WithRelatedInput` the flat member is **nullable**. Every field of the flat update input is optional, so an update that touches only nested rows can omit the member, and the parent write then issues no `UPDATE` at all ([9.5](#95-edge-case-behaviors)). A verb takes a list of non-null elements (`create: [UserEventsCreateInput!]`, `connect: [UUID!]`). On a **has-one** edge it takes one value instead (`create: AssetPrimaryDocumentCreateInput`, `connect: UUID`), matching the pointer member on the Go block. A nested child input is the target's projected create input minus the traversed FK and the discriminator. A GraphQL input type needs at least one field, so if nothing else is left the child input cannot be declared, and that edge's GraphQL blocks carry no `create`. The Go surface keeps the verb.

**A `…WithRelated` mutation requires its flat mutation on the API.** `api.operations` masks `create_with_related`, `update_with_related` and `upsert_with_related` the way it masks every other operation. On the masked set, each one implies the base it composes. So masking `create` off the API also removes `create<Table>WithRelated`. Without that, a mask written to leave one hand-guarded door into a table would leave a second, generated door through the nested mutation. For the same reason, a family whose flat input is suppressed (the table has no API-writable column) is not emitted. The requirement is on the masked operations, not on the emitted flat mutation, and there is one case where the two differ: on a table that emits no `<Table>ConflictPK`, `upsert<Table>WithRelated` still needs `upsert` on the mask but survives without `upsert<Table>`, taking a required `conflictTarget` (above). Naming a nested mutation beside its masked-off base, as in `create_with_related: true` beside `create: false` in one mask, is a config error ([4.13](#413-config-validation-rules)) rather than a silent drop.

**`update<Table>WithRelated` applies its `_inc` / `_dec` operators in its own transaction.** The flat member is `Update<Table>Input`, so it carries the operator pair [26.5.4](#2654-mutation-translation) adds, and `UpdateWithRelated` takes no increments. When any operator is set, the resolver runs three steps inside one transaction: `UpdateWithRelated` as a savepoint, then the `Increment` calls, then the read-back. The nested mutation therefore stays the single atomic write [9.9](#99-nested-mutations) promises. It does not commit its nested rows and then fail on an increment. The pairing rules of 26.5.4 apply unchanged: setting and incrementing one column, or incrementing and decrementing it, is `INVALID_INPUT`. This differs deliberately from `update<Table>`, whose sequence 26.5.4 does not wrap.

**Nested error attribution reaches the client.** A failure inside a nested block carries `extensions.path: ["<Edge>"]` naming the relationship that failed, read off `*NestedMutationError.Edge` ([22.2](#222-constraint-errors)) rather than parsed out of the message. See [26.5.5](#2655-error-mapping) for the code mapping.

**A hidden entity gets no nested member.** An edge whose target is `api.enabled: false`, or whose nested input would expose an `api`-hidden column, is absent from the nested input type on the GraphQL surface — the write-side mirror of the read side-channel rule ([9.9](#99-nested-mutations), rule **E7**). The same holds one level down, for a target that stays exposed but masks what a verb writes through. `create` needs the target's API `create`. An O2M / has-one `connect` / `disconnect` / `clear` needs the target's mask to keep `update_where`, the key that gates the target's own filter-scoped update. A verb the target's mask removes is absent from both blocks, and an edge left with no verb gets no member. The Go surface is unaffected: `api` gates the API, never the client.

**Mutation-result nullability rules:** `create<Table>` / `update<Table>` / `upsert<Table>` / `create<Table>s` / `update<Table>s` return non-nullable (`Product!` / `[Product!]!`) — failures surface as GraphQL errors, never null results. Delete-class mutations (`softDelete<Table>`, `restore<Table>`) return nullable `Product` so the client can distinguish "not found" (null) from "internal error" (GraphQL error). Hard delete returns `Boolean!` (true on delete, false on missing).

#### 26.5.2 Field Selection Translation — The Central Mechanism

This is the load-bearing piece. Every guarantee depends on the walker being recursive and complete.

Per-entity generated function that walks gqlgen's selection set tree and produces a fully-populated `FieldOptions`:

```go
// graph/sqlgenresolver/field_options_gen.go — generated per entity
func productFieldOptionsFromContext(ctx context.Context) *<pkg>.ProductFieldOptions {
    return productFieldOptionsFromCollected(graphql.CollectFieldsCtx(ctx, nil))
}

func productFieldOptionsFromCollected(fields []graphql.CollectedField) *<pkg>.ProductFieldOptions {
    fo := &<pkg>.ProductFieldOptions{}
    for _, f := range fields {
        switch f.Name {
        case "id":        fo.ID = true
        case "name":      fo.Name = true
        case "price":     fo.Price = true
        case "createdAt": fo.CreatedAt = true
        case "company":
            fo.Company = companyFieldOptionsFromCollected(graphql.CollectFields(f.Selections, nil))
        case "reviews":
            // O2M / M2M produce a Connection-shaped field at the root level — but
            // *relationship* fields are flat [Type!]! per §26.4 (no per-rel pagination),
            // so the walker descends straight into the field's sub-selections.
            fo.Reviews = reviewFieldOptionsFromCollected(graphql.CollectFields(f.Selections, nil))
        case "tags":
            fo.Tags = tagFieldOptionsFromCollected(graphql.CollectFields(f.Selections, nil))
        }
    }
    return fo
}
```

**Connection unwrapping.** For root queries returning `<Type>Connection`, the GraphQL selection looks like `products { edges { node { company { name } } } }`. The walker descends `edges` → `node` → real field selections via a shared `unwrapConnectionAndWalk` helper — one impl in a generated `graph/sqlgenresolver/connection_walker_gen.go`.

**Fragment & directive handling.** `graphql.CollectFieldsCtx` and `graphql.CollectFields` already flatten named and inline fragments, apply `@skip` / `@include` directives, and resolve aliases transparently (the walker sees the underlying field name). No custom fragment expansion needed.

**Aliased duplicate selections — one name, several entries.** "Transparently" resolves the alias to its underlying *name*, not to a single entry. gqlgen groups collected fields by `(Name, Alias)`, so `{ a: edges { node { email } } b: edges { node { name } } }` reaches the walker as **two** `CollectedField`s both named `edges`, and `{ x: orders { total } y: orders { createdAt } }` as two both named `orders`. The walker's column arms are idempotent (`fo.<F> = true`) and survive that; every other arm assigns, so without a rule the last alias would win and the earlier ones would render off columns the `SELECT` never fetched — a well-formed response carrying the Go zero value, with no error raised.

**The rule is union, and it is applied before the switch.** Every walker loop — the two envelope descents in `unwrapConnectionFields` and each per-table `<table>FieldOptionsFromCollected` — runs over a coalesced view of its input in which each field name appears exactly once, carrying the union of the sub-selections every alias of it collected. That restores the invariant the `case` arms are written against (a name is handled once), so no arm needs to know aliasing happened.

Union is the whole of the correct answer here rather than a lossy merge, and both halves of that are structural. A relationship field takes **no** GraphQL arguments — the relationship shape is a flat `[Type!]!` with no per-relationship pagination ([§26.4](#264-graphql-schema-generation)), and filter / sort arguments on relationship fields are deferred ([§26.12](#2612-known-limitations)) — so two aliases of one relationship can differ *only* in what they select, never in what they would load. And gqlgen renders every alias from the one value the resolver returned, so a projection covering both aliases makes both correct off a single load. The union therefore costs no extra query and the [§25.1](#251-query-count-guarantee) count is unchanged: two aliases of one O2M relationship remain `1 + 1`. Row identity ([above](#2652-field-selection-translation--the-central-mechanism), "Row identity") is evaluated once against the unioned result, so an alias that names no column cannot add identity columns to a sibling alias that does.

The coalesce unions at the `[]graphql.CollectedField` level — collecting each alias's own selections and appending the results — rather than by concatenating the underlying `ast.SelectionSet`s. That is a correctness requirement, not a style choice: gqlgen keys its per-request `CollectFields` cache on the *address and length* of the selection set it is passed, and a slice synthesized by the walker is not retained by that cache, so a later allocation of the same length could land on the recycled address and take a stale hit. Every cache key must stay on memory gqlgen itself holds.

**Walker-completeness lint (codegen-time).** Every **API-readable** column, and every relationship into an API-exposed entity (table or view), MUST have a corresponding case in the generated walker. Every access-restricted column ([§32.3](#323-per-surface-behavior)), and every relationship into a hidden entity ([§26.4](#264-graphql-schema-generation)), MUST NOT. Codegen fails if either direction is violated over the exposed set. This catches the walker's only failure mode (a missing case ⇒ silently nil in the response) at generate time. Combined with a per-table generated unit test that builds a deeply-nested GraphQL query touching every relationship and asserts the produced `FieldOptions` tree, the recursive walker is the regression guard for the §25.1 query-count contract.

**Selected ⇒ available, unselected ⇒ nil.** If a relationship is selected at runtime but the walker did not produce a corresponding `FieldOptions` entry (impossible if the lint above passes), the field resolver returns nil — it does **not** lazy-load. This fails fast.

**What the walker narrows, and what it cannot.** The `FieldOptions` the walker produces describes the *request*, not the projection the read ultimately needs: cursor encoding, relationship mapping, and O2O NULL detection each read a column no GraphQL field names. Those columns are unioned back into the `SELECT` by the client method that needs them (Section 9.6, "Structurally required columns"), never by the walker — so a narrowed request cannot strand the data it did ask for.

**Row identity — a selection set that names no column.** Not every selectable field maps to a column. `__typename`, an edge's `cursor`, and every `PageInfo` field are resolved from the row's *existence* rather than from any value on it, so a request can legally select only those: `{ users(first: 1) { edges { cursor } } }`, `{ user(id:) { __typename } }`, `{ orders { __typename } }`. Translating those to an all-false `FieldOptions` would hand the client the one value [9.6](#96-per-call-options) reserves for "the caller wants no rows at all", and the read would short-circuit on a row the request did ask for. The walker therefore projects the entity's **row-identity columns** — its primary key, or for a view with no `@pk` ([16.4](#164-generated-artifacts-views-vs-tables)) its resolved `cursor_keys`, or failing both its first column — whenever a selection set it walked named no column of its own. The row identity is the whole addition: columns the read *derives* rather than returns stay with the client method that reads them, so the two rules compose without either restating the other.

The one selection that genuinely wants no rows is a **count-only envelope** — `{ totalCount }` on a `<T>Connection`, or `{ totalCount hasMore offset limit }` on a `<T>ListResult`.
