**`cache.version` manual kill switch.** Operators can bump `cache.version` in YAML (default `0`) to force-invalidate every cached table and view on next `sqlgen generate` — regenerates every fingerprint. Use cases: emergency response to a data-correctness bug, forcing a cache flush after a non-struct-affecting semantic change (custom serializer changes, etc.).

**PK types are values, not pointers.** Every PK passed to the cache key helpers must be a value type (scalar like `uuid.UUID`, `int64`, `string`; or a composite-PK struct value). Pointer types stringify to the underlying memory address via `%v` and produce a different cache key on every call. The generated per-table `keyFor{Table}(pk T)` helpers are typed with concrete value `T`, so generated code can't hit the mistake; user-direct callers (`cache.SetAs`, custom `InvalidationSource`, admin tools) must dereference at the boundary.

### 27.6 Cache Invariant

**The cache only ever contains full entities.** This is a hard invariant that prevents serving incomplete data from cache.

| Scenario | FieldOptions | Hydration | Cache Behavior |
|----------|:-----------:|:---------:|---------------|
| Full fetch | nil | N/A | Query DB → cache result → return |
| Partial fetch | non-nil (column flags only) | Enabled | Return partial to caller; hydrate full entity in background → cache full |
| Partial fetch | non-nil (column flags only) | Disabled | Return partial to caller; **do not cache** |
| Any fetch with relationship flag | non-nil (relationship flag set) | N/A | **Cache bypass.** Direct DB JOIN for o2o / separate `GetMany` for o2m / m2m. No cache read, no cache write. |
| Cache hit | N/A | N/A | Return full entity from cache (always complete) |

Because the cache always contains full entities and mutations always invalidate, there is no risk of serving stale partial data. TTL ensures eventual expiry even if an invalidation event is missed.

**One key = one entity = one table.** Relationships (children) are never cached as part of the parent entity. Each entity is cached independently under its own key. This eliminates cross-entity invalidation dependencies — updating a review never requires invalidating its parent product's cache entry.

**Relationship-loading calls bypass the cache entirely.** Relationships are expressed as boolean fields on the per-table `{Table}FieldOptions` struct, mixed in alongside column flags. There is no separate `WithXxx()` method layer — the same struct controls "which columns to SELECT" and "which relationships to load":

- `Get(pk)` with `FieldOptions = nil`, or `FieldOptions` where only column flags are set → cache-through, parent row only.
- `Get(pk)` with **any** relationship-typed flag set on `FieldOptions` (e.g. `ProductFieldOptions.Metadata = true`) → cache-bypass. Direct DB JOIN for o2o, separate `GetMany` for o2m / m2m. No cache read, no cache write.
- `GetMany(...)` → no cache in either shape (multi-row filters have too many permutations).

**Rationale:** Caching the JOIN result in the parent entry would violate the one-key-one-table invariant and create cross-entity invalidation chains (a child mutation chasing up to invalidate every parent that joined to it). Caching parent-only while callers expect the joined shape would silently drop relationship data on cache hits. Bypass is the only approach that preserves the invariant without hiding complexity — the JOIN stays fast (single query; no performance regression relative to the non-cache baseline). Users who need cached relationship data compose it from cached parent + child `Get` calls client-side.

### 27.7 Cache Behavior by Operation

| Operation | Cache Behavior |
|-----------|---------------|
| `Get(pk)` — full, no relationships | **Read-through:** Check cache → return on hit. On miss → query DB → set cache → return. Concurrent misses on the same key collapse via `singleflight` + an in-flight cache re-check inside the flight callback (so stragglers that observed the outer miss before a sibling flight populated the cache return the populated value instead of running a duplicate DB query). |
| `Get(pk)` — partial (column flags only), hydration on | **Read-through + hydrate:** Check cache → return on hit. On miss → query DB partial → return to caller → async hydrate full → cache full. One hydration per `(table, pk)` at a time. |
| `Get(pk)` — partial (column flags only), hydration off | **Pass-through:** Query DB partial → return to caller. No cache read, no cache write. |
| `Get(pk)` — **any relationship flag set on `FieldOptions`** | **Cache bypass.** Direct DB JOIN for o2o / separate `GetMany` for o2m+m2m. No cache read, no cache write. See 27.6 for rationale. |
| `GetMany(input)` | **No cache.** Multi-row queries with filters are not cached (too many permutations). |
| `Create` / `CreateMany` | **Set:** After successful insert, populate cache with the new entity(s) (full entity returned by DB). |
| `Update` / `Upsert` / `Increment` / `SoftDelete` / `HardDelete` / `Restore` | **Invalidate:** `Invalidate(key)` single-entity invalidation via `backend.InvalidateMany`. |
| `UpsertMany` | **Invalidate many:** `InvalidateMany(keys(AffectedPKs))`, as the `*Many` row below. It is a direct write path with its own `hook.OpUpsertMany` ([21.2](#212-hook-types)), so it needs its own arm — the invalidation switch has no permissive default that would cover it. |
| `CreateWithRelated` / `UpdateWithRelated` / `UpsertWithRelated` | **Nothing of their own.** They have no `MutationOp` and dispatch no invalidation; every inner call invalidates under its own op, on its own table. See [9.9.9](#999-observability). |
| `UpdateMany` / `SoftDeleteMany` / `HardDeleteMany` / `RestoreMany` | **Invalidate many:** `InvalidateMany(keys(AffectedPKs))`. |
| `UpdateWhere` / `SoftDeleteWhere` / `HardDeleteWhere` / `RestoreWhere` | **Invalidate many:** `InvalidateMany(keys(AffectedPKs))` — identical to the `*Many` row above. Every `*Where` method captures the matched rows' PKs before it returns (`RETURNING` on PostgreSQL/SQLite, a pre-`SELECT` on MySQL), the same capture the event fan-out reads, so the predicate's row set is known by the time invalidation runs. A predicate matching zero rows invalidates nothing. Prior-fingerprint orphans are left to TTL and to a deliberate `InvalidateTable` sweep rather than swept incidentally by a whole-table pattern wipe on every call. |
| Mutation on a **no-PK table** | Does not apply. No-PK tables are skipped from generation entirely ([§9.4b](#94b-no-pk-tables-are-skipped)); no client method exists to mutate them. Use `primary_key.columns` to opt in, then the standard cache rules above apply. |
| `Raw` / `RawExec` | No cache interaction. |

After every mutation that affects a cached table, the hook also pattern-invalidates any views listing that table in `invalidate_on` (27.11).

**Nested mutations are exactly the composition of their inner calls, with two asymmetries worth stating.** A nested write's terminal read selects relationships, and any relationship flag bypasses the cache entirely (27.6), so a nested write can never leave a stale composite entity behind. And **nested creates do not warm the cache**, although flat `Create` / `CreateMany` do: the inner calls pass a nothing-selected `FieldOptions` so they can skip the return fetch ([9.6](#96-per-call-options)), which means there is no entity to write through — warming would cost back the very read the escape exists to avoid. Both are deliberate; see [9.9.9](#999-observability).

**`CallOptions.SkipCache` interaction:** When the caller passes `SkipCache: true` via per-call options (Section 9.6), the cache hook bypasses both read-through (no cache check on `Get`) and write-through (no cache set on miss, no invalidation on mutation) for that call. Hydration is also suppressed — no background goroutine is launched. The DB operation executes normally. `SkipCache` applies to the entire operation including relationship loads, since `CallOptions` propagate through the relationship loading pipeline. `SkipHooks` implies `SkipCache`.

**M2M junction tables inherit the cache, and only one read path reaches it.** A detected or
config-declared junction is an ordinary table to every rule above: it inherits global
`cache.enabled`, gets a composite cache key (27.5), a schema fingerprint, and the full set of
invalidation arms. What it does *not* get is a cached read from the M2M edge it exists to serve.
The relationship loader's junction query is both a relationship load (27.6) and a multi-row `IN`
(the `GetMany` row above), so it is issued directly on the connection — outside the query-hook
chain, and therefore outside the cache. The relationship-filter `EXISTS` subquery (11.1, “Relationship filters”) is a
`WHERE`-clause fragment rather than a read, so it does not reach the cache either. The junction's
**own `Get(pk)`** — the by-pair membership read, exposed in Go and, when the API is enabled, as
`<junction>(<localFK>:, <referenceFK>:)` — is the one path that does.

Two consequences worth acting on:

- **A junction reached only through its M2M edge pays invalidation for a read that never hits.**
  Every mutation on it dispatches invalidation — one key per affected pair, including for a
  `*Where` delete, the shape an "unlink everything" takes. Opt out with
  `tables.<junction>.cache.enabled: false`; the tri-state pointer is per-table, so nothing else
  changes, and the opt-out is honored at the invalidation arm itself — an uncached table
  dispatches no backend call at all.
- **A junction whose by-pair `Get` is hot should stay cached.** Membership and ACL link tables
  (`user_roles`, `user_permissions`) are read this way far more often than they are written, and
  that read is read-through like any other `Get(pk)`. Note that `Exists(pk)` does **not** substitute
  for it: read-through is gated on the `Get` op for *every* table, so `Exists` always queries the
  database. Callers who want the cached membership check call `Get(pk)` and test for `nil`.

The default is inheritance either way — sqlgen does not infer which of the two shapes a given
junction is.

### 27.8 Hydration

When `hydration.enabled` is true and a `Get` request uses `FieldOptions` to select only a subset of columns:

1. The result is returned to the caller immediately (partial data from DB)
2. A background goroutine fetches the full entity from DB (all columns, no FieldOptions)
3. The full entity is serialized and stored in cache
4. Future `Get` calls for the same PK hit the cache and return the full entity

The hydration goroutine respects `hydration.timeout` and is fire-and-forget — failures are logged but don't affect the caller.

```
Caller: Get(pk, FieldOptions{ID: true, Name: true})
    │
    ├── Cache miss → DB query (SELECT id, name FROM ...)
    │   └── Return {ID, Name} to caller immediately
    │
    └── Background hydration (async)
        └── DB query (SELECT * FROM ... WHERE id = $1)
            └── Cache.Set(key, fullEntity, ttl)
```

When `hydration.enabled` is false, partial fetches bypass the cache entirely — no read, no write. This is safe because the cache invariant (section 27.6) guarantees that only full entities exist in cache. A subsequent full fetch (no FieldOptions) will populate the cache normally.

### 27.9 Invalidation Strategies

Cache invalidation uses two complementary mechanisms: TTL as a safety net and source-driven invalidation for immediate consistency. Invalidation signals can come from sqlgen's event system (section 28), external event systems (Kafka CDC, PostgreSQL LISTEN/NOTIFY, webhooks), or direct programmatic calls.

#### TTL-Based (always active)

Every cache entry has a TTL from config. Entries expire automatically.

- **Role:** Safety net. Guarantees entries eventually expire even if an event is lost, a subscriber is down, or a mutation occurs outside sqlgen.
- **Limitation:** Stale reads are possible within the TTL window.

#### Source-Driven Invalidation

The cache supports three layers of invalidation, from most automated to most flexible:

```
Layer 1 (convenience):  FromEventSubscriber(event.Subscriber) → InvalidationSource
                        Bridges sqlgen's event system automatically

Layer 2 (generic):      InvalidationSource → InvalidationHandler → cache
                        User implements for Kafka CDC, webhooks, pg LISTEN/NOTIFY, etc.

Layer 3 (direct):       c.Invalidate(ctx, table, pk)
                        User calls directly from their own code
```

**Layer 1 — sqlgen event system (zero wiring):**

When using sqlgen's event system (section 28), the `cache.FromEventSubscriber` adapter translates mutation events into invalidation signals automatically:

```go
c, _ := <pkg>.NewCache(backend,
    <pkg>.WithInvalidationSource(cache.FromEventSubscriber(eventSub)),
)
```

An event carries the bare SQL name in `Table` and the schema in `Schema` ([28.3](#283-event-structure)), so the adapter rebuilds the `hook.TableName` value from the two: `schema.table` when `Schema` is set, the bare name when it is empty ([5.5](#55-schema-qualification--table-naming) "Schema in Generated Code").

**Layer 2 — custom event sources (generic interface):**

Users with their own event infrastructure (Kafka CDC, custom pub/sub, PostgreSQL LISTEN/NOTIFY, etc.) implement `InvalidationSource` to feed invalidation signals:

```go
type kafkaCDCSource struct { /* ... */ }
func (k *kafkaCDCSource) Subscribe(handler cache.InvalidationHandler) (cache.InvalidationSubscription, error) { /* ... */ }
func (k *kafkaCDCSource) Close() error { /* ... */ }

c, _ := <pkg>.NewCache(backend,
    <pkg>.WithInvalidationSource(myKafkaCDCSource),
)
```

A Layer 2 source names a table by its `hook.TableName` value: `schema.table` for PostgreSQL (`"public.products"`), the bare name for MySQL and SQLite. A bare name sent for a PostgreSQL table matches no cached table and invalidates nothing; the facade's "unknown or non-cached table" error is returned to the source.

**Layer 3 — direct programmatic calls:**

The generated `Cache` struct exposes invalidation methods directly. Users call these from any context — webhook handlers, custom middleware, admin tools. **Prefer generated `<pkg>.TableXxx` constants over raw strings** (typos fail at compile time; raw strings fall through the unknown-table switch with a descriptive runtime error):

```go
import "github.com/teandresmith/sqlgen/hook"

c.Invalidate(ctx, <pkg>.TableProducts, productID)
c.InvalidateMany(ctx, <pkg>.TableProducts, []any{id1, id2, id3})
c.InvalidateTable(ctx, <pkg>.TableProducts) // clears every fingerprint generation

// Layer 2 dynamic-table handlers cast at the boundary, in the constant's
// form ("public.products" on PostgreSQL, "products" on MySQL / SQLite):
c.Invalidate(ctx, hook.TableName(rawTableStr), pk)
```

**These layers compose.** A single `*Cache` instance can have an `InvalidationSource` for automated cross-instance invalidation AND receive direct `Invalidate` calls for ad-hoc scenarios.

- **Role:** Immediate consistency. Reduces the stale window from TTL duration to event propagation latency (typically milliseconds).
- **Limitation:** Events can be lost (network partition, subscriber crash). TTL covers this gap.

#### InvalidationSource Interface

The `InvalidationSource` interface lives in the `cache/` runtime package (stdlib + `golang.org/x/sync` only). It abstracts over any event system that can produce table/PK invalidation signals:

```go
package cache

import "github.com/teandresmith/sqlgen/hook"

// InvalidationSource feeds cache invalidation signals from any event system.
// The cache subscribes at construction and unsubscribes at Close().
type InvalidationSource interface {
    Subscribe(handler InvalidationHandler) (InvalidationSubscription, error)
    Close() error
}

// InvalidationSignal carries one invalidation instruction. A struct rather
// than positional parameters so future fields (operation, fingerprint, ...)
// extend the extension point without breaking every InvalidationSource
// implementation again.
type InvalidationSignal struct {
    Table  hook.TableName // the generated TableXxx constant's value: "public.products" on PostgreSQL, "products" on MySQL / SQLite
    Schema string         // SQL schema; informational (Table already carries it), may be empty
    Tenant string         // stringified row tenant for tenanted tables ("%v" form, 29.5); empty when unknown
    PKs    []any          // primary keys to invalidate; empty = full-table invalidation
}

// InvalidationHandler receives invalidation signals. Custom
// InvalidationSource implementations that speak in raw strings (Kafka CDC
// topic names, webhook payloads) cast at the boundary, in the constant's
// form (schema-qualified on PostgreSQL):
//   handler(ctx, cache.InvalidationSignal{Table: hook.TableName(schema + "." + rawTable), PKs: pks})
type InvalidationHandler func(ctx context.Context, signal InvalidationSignal) error

type InvalidationSubscription interface {
    Unsubscribe() error
}
```

**Semantics:**
- `PKs` contains specific primary keys to invalidate (one per affected entity). Element type matches 27.3's `Cache.Invalidate*` contract: scalar PK for single-PK tables, the generated `XXXPK` struct value for composite-PK tables.
- Empty `PKs` signals full-table invalidation (dispatched through `Backend.InvalidatePattern` via the fingerprint-agnostic pattern; 27.5).
- `Tenant` carries the `%v`-stringified tenant of the affected rows for tenanted tables — byte-identical to the tenant segment of the 29.5 key grammar, so the receiving facade rebuilds exact keys without knowing the concrete tenant type. For a tenanted table whose tenant column is **not** part of the primary key, an empty `Tenant` degrades the signal to a full-table clear (tenant-in-PK tables stay precise — each PK carries its tenant).
- The handler is synchronous — the source waits for it to return before proceeding. The precise per-PK path propagates backend errors so ACK-capable transports redeliver; the tenant-less full-table fallback performs its safe over-eviction, emits the cache error signal, and returns nil (ACK) — a redelivered tenant-less signal could never gain a tenant, so redelivery makes no progress.

#### Cache Public Invalidation Methods

The generated `Cache` struct exposes these methods for direct programmatic invalidation:

```go
func (c *Cache) Invalidate(ctx context.Context, table hook.TableName, pk any) error
func (c *Cache) InvalidateMany(ctx context.Context, table hook.TableName, pks []any) error
func (c *Cache) InvalidateTable(ctx context.Context, table hook.TableName) error
```

These methods are the same ones called internally by the mutation hook and the `InvalidationSource` handler. All invalidation paths converge on shared internal helpers — key construction, metrics emission, circuit-breaker accounting, and the final `Backend.InvalidateMany` / `Backend.InvalidatePattern` call.

#### FromEventSubscriber Adapter

The `cache` package provides a built-in adapter that bridges `event.Subscriber` to `InvalidationSource`:

```go
// FromEventSubscriber creates an InvalidationSource that translates sqlgen
// mutation events into cache invalidation signals. Subscribes to all tables
// and all mutation actions with an empty SubscribeOptions{}.
//
// The zero-option form — FromEventSubscriber(sub) — is the user-facing
// constructor. Options are used by the generated *Cache facade to wire
// observability (metrics) at construction time.
func FromEventSubscriber(sub event.Subscriber, opts ...EventAdapterOption) InvalidationSource

// EventAdapterOption configures the InvalidationSource returned by
// FromEventSubscriber.
type EventAdapterOption func(*eventAdapter)

// WithEventMetrics wires a MetricsRecorder so handler-returned errors are
// recorded via MetricsRecorder.Error(schema, table, "invalidate", err)
// before propagating to the underlying event.Handler. The generated facade
// always supplies this; user-direct callers may omit it.
func WithEventMetrics(m MetricsRecorder) EventAdapterOption
```

**Semantics:**

- **Synchronous per event.** Each incoming `event.Event` produces exactly one `InvalidationHandler` call carrying `InvalidationSignal{Table, Schema, Tenant, PKs: []any{ev.PK}}` — the tenant forwarded verbatim from `ev.Metadata["tenant"]` (29.6), so tenanted tables invalidate precisely cross-instance. Publisher-side batching (`event.Publisher.PublishBatch`) is preserved transparently — transports fan out one handler call per event, the adapter forwards 1:1.
- **Idempotent by backend contract.** `Backend.Invalidate` / `InvalidateMany` for an absent key is a success. At-least-once transports (NATS redelivery, Kafka replay) are safe without `event.ID` dedup.
- **Error routing.** When the handler returns an error, the adapter (1) records it via `MetricsRecorder.Error(schema, table, "invalidate", err)` when `WithEventMetrics` is wired, and (2) returns the error from the inner `event.Handler` so ACK-capable transports redeliver. Fire-and-forget transports drop it after their own error step. Nothing is silently swallowed. The adapter emits this metric itself with the `ev.Schema` label; `InvalidationSignal.Schema` also carries the value informationally, but the generated facade resolves its own per-table schema constant and Layer 2 implementers may leave the field empty.

#### Transaction-Safe Invalidation

When a mutation hook detects it is running inside a transaction (via `database.FromContext(ctx)`), it registers the cache operation on `tx.OnCommit` rather than firing immediately. Rollback discards the registration. This reuses the same pattern used for events (section 18.6).

Post-commit ordering is deterministic: `database.Tx.OnCommit` preserves FIFO order within a depth (`database/transaction_test.go:TestOnCommitCallbackOrdering`). Because cache is the outermost hook in the generated client, its `OnCommit` registration is appended after the event hook's, so events fire first and cache invalidation fires second on commit. Rollback discards both.

`FromEventSubscriber` and custom `InvalidationSource` inputs are **already post-commit** (events only fire after commit), so invalidation from those layers is fired immediately — no nested `OnCommit` needed.

`CallbackMode` defaults to `CallbackAsync`; the async path executes callbacks on `context.Background()` — cache invalidation MUST NOT read request-scoped metadata from the callback's ctx. Closure-captured key + table is all the backend call needs. Both sync and async paths retry a failed callback once before giving up; cache invalidation is idempotent by contract (27.3) so the retry is safe.

#### Circuit Breaker

A per-`*Cache` circuit breaker (`cache.Breaker`) guards every backend call. Sustained failures open the circuit; cache reads short-circuit to "miss" and cache writes / invalidations are skipped until a `HalfOpen` probe succeeds and the breaker closes.

State transitions (defaults: `failure_threshold: 5`, `probe_interval: 30s`, `half_open_max_probes: 1`):

```
Closed   --N consecutive failures-->   Open
Open     --probe_interval elapsed-->   HalfOpen
HalfOpen --success-->                  Closed   (counter reset)
HalfOpen --failure-->                  Open     (immediately — one probe is enough)
```

Success in `Closed` resets the consecutive-failure counter. Transitions emit `MetricsRecorder.CircuitBreakerStateChange(from, to)`.

When the breaker is open, the DB operation still executes normally — the cache is non-authoritative. TTL remains the safety net.

#### Cache Error Policy

The cache MUST NOT break user-facing calls. A failing `Get` surfaces as a cache miss; a failing `Set` / `Invalidate*` is dropped from the caller's error path. Every cache backend error routes through a three-pronged policy:

1. **Structured telemetry.** `MetricsRecorder.Error(schema, table, op, err)`.
2. **Textual log fallback.** `OnErrorFunc` callback; default `DefaultOnCacheError` logs to stderr (swappable via `WithOnError`).
3. **Breaker feedback.** Every error calls `breaker.RecordFailure()`.

All three fire in order so a misconfigured logger cannot mask a cache outage. Marshal / unmarshal errors route through the same policy; unmarshal errors additionally treat the call as a cache miss (fall through to DB) — the entry is not auto-deleted, since TTL + the fingerprint segment (27.5) already handle stale-payload scenarios.

#### Why TTL + Source-Driven Are Both Required

| Scenario | TTL Only | Source Only | TTL + Source |
|----------|:--------:|:-----------:|:------------:|
| Normal mutation | Stale for up to TTL | Immediate invalidation | Immediate invalidation |
| Event lost (network issue) | Stale for up to TTL | **Stale indefinitely** | Stale for up to TTL |
| Mutation outside sqlgen (raw SQL) | Stale for up to TTL | **Stale indefinitely** | Stale for up to TTL |
| Single instance (no pub/sub) | Works fine | Unnecessary overhead | Works fine (events are local) |

Events without TTL is dangerous — a lost event means a cache entry that never expires. TTL without events means unnecessary staleness. Together they provide the best of both.

### 27.10 Serialization

| Serializer | Module | Size | Speed | Human-Readable | Use Case |
|------------|--------|------|-------|:--------------:|----------|
| `json` | `encoding/json` (stdlib, core) | Larger | Slower | Yes | Development, debugging, cache inspection |
| `msgpack` | `github.com/teandresmith/sqlgen/cache/msgpack` (separate module) | ~30% smaller | ~2x faster | No | Production with high cache volume |
| `custom` | User-supplied `cache.Serializer` | Varies | Varies | Varies | Custom encoders (Protobuf, Avro, etc.) |

The serializer is configurable globally only — a single decode path per process keeps the cache debuggable (one format to inspect in `redis-cli` / admin tools) and eliminates cross-key decoder-mismatch risk. Users who need per-type encoding implement `cache.Serializer` as a dispatching wrapper and pass it via `WithSerializer(...)`. The `Serializer` interface is stdlib-compatible:

```go
type Serializer interface {
    Marshal(v any) ([]byte, error)
    Unmarshal(data []byte, v any) error
}
```

**Auto-injection.** When `cache.serializer: "msgpack"` is set, the generator emits the `cache/msgpack` import in `cache_gen.go` and defaults the serializer to `msgpack.New()` — same pattern as driver selection (pgx vs stdlib). The consumer runs `go mod tidy` once; the dependency lands only in projects that opted in. `WithSerializer(...)` still wins when passed — users can inject a preconfigured encoder pool, custom tags, or a test double.

**Validation timing.**

- At YAML parse time: `cache.serializer` must be one of `json`, `msgpack`, `custom`, or unset. Unset defaults to `json`.
- At `NewCache` construction time: `cache.serializer == "custom"` with no `WithSerializer(...)` fails with an error naming the config line. `json` and `msgpack` never error at construction — both are generator-resolved.

The serializer choice feeds the schema fingerprint (27.5), so switching from `json` to `msgpack` (or vice versa) produces a new key namespace — cached bytes are never read under the wrong decoder.

### 27.11 View Cache Invalidation

Views (section 16) can be cached like tables. Since views are read-only, they have no mutations of their own to trigger invalidation. Instead, view caches are invalidated when their **source tables** are mutated.

**View caching is opt-in.** Unlike tables, views do NOT inherit the global `cache.enabled` setting. A view is cached only when `view.cache.enabled: true` is set explicitly AND `view.invalidate_on` is non-empty. Both are hard validation errors otherwise (parse-time + post-parse; see 4.9). Rationale: tables self-invalidate via the mutation hook — inheriting `enabled: true` is safe. Views have no mutations; inheriting the global flag would silently create TTL-only view caches (stale data bounded only by TTL).

Config specifies which tables invalidate which views:

```yaml
views:
  product_summary:
    struct_name: ProductSummary
    sql: "./views/product_summary.sql"
    cache:
      enabled: true
      ttl: "15m"
    invalidate_on:
      - products          # mutations on products invalidate this view's cache
      - reviews           # mutations on reviews also invalidate it
```

When a mutation hook fires on `products` or `reviews`, the generated cache hook consults a codegen-time `patternsForSourceTable(table hook.TableName) []string` map and calls `Backend.InvalidatePattern(ctx, pattern)` for each matching view. The map is keyed by each source table's `hook.TableName` value ([5.5](#55-schema-qualification--table-naming) "Schema in Generated Code"), so an `invalidate_on` entry may be bare or schema-qualified — `products` and `public.products` name the same source, as in config keys. No capability check — `InvalidatePattern` is a mandatory method on `Backend` (27.3).

Validation at post-parse time: every `invalidate_on` table name must resolve to a table in the parsed schema AND be included in generation (not excluded via `exclude_columns` / generation filters). Referencing an excluded table is a hard error — no mutation hook would fire for it, so the view cache would silently never invalidate from that source.

**Materialized views ([16.5](#165-materialized-views-postgresql)):** every rule in this section applies to a cached matview unchanged, including the non-empty `invalidate_on` requirement. In addition, the matview's generated `Refresh` / `RefreshConcurrently` methods invalidate the matview's own cache entries on success (no-op when the matview is not cached; deferred to commit inside a transaction). The two invalidation vectors are complementary: a matview's stored rows change **only** at refresh time, so refresh-driven self-invalidation is what actually tracks its content changes; source-table-driven `invalidate_on` clears are harmless for a matview (the cleared entries still matched the stored snapshot — the cost is extra cache misses, never incorrectness) and the requirement is kept so the view-cache config surface stays uniform rather than special-casing matviews.

### 27.12 Cache Warming

Cache warming (pre-populating the cache on startup) is **not supported**. The cache warms naturally through read-through population — the first `Get` for an entity misses, queries the DB, and populates the cache for subsequent reads.

This is a deliberate choice: cache warming is primarily relevant for in-memory caches that lose all state on process restart. For distributed caches (Redis, Memcached), data survives redeployments and warming is unnecessary. Since the cache interface is pluggable and sqlgen does not ship a built-in backend, the common case is a distributed cache where cold starts are not a concern.

There is no `cache.warm` config. A warming query — "the top 1000 products by access frequency" — is a statement about one workload's traffic, not about the schema, so it has no schema-derivable form for the generator to emit; consumers who need it issue the reads themselves at startup through the generated client, which populates the cache by the same read-through path.

### 27.13 Cache Metrics

The cache hook exposes metrics via a pluggable `MetricsRecorder` interface. The interface lives in the core `cache/` runtime package (stdlib + `golang.org/x/sync` only). An optional convenience module (`metrics/otel/`) provides a ready-made OpenTelemetry implementation.

#### MetricsRecorder Interface

```go
import "github.com/teandresmith/sqlgen/hook"

// MetricsRecorder receives cache operation signals. Consumers implement this
// to bridge to their metrics system (Prometheus, OTel, Datadog, StatsD, etc.).
//
// schema is the resolved schema string — "public" (or user-configured) for
// PostgreSQL, "" for MySQL / SQLite. Matches the schema segment baked into
// the cache key (27.5). Always passed explicitly so same-name tables in
// different schemas don't collapse into a single metric series.
//
// table is the generated TableXxx constant's value, which carries the schema
// whenever the table has one ("public.products" on PostgreSQL, "products" on
// MySQL / SQLite — 5.5). A recorder that labels schema and table separately
// strips the schema + "." prefix from table, as metrics/otel does.
type MetricsRecorder interface {
    // Counter-style events (call-per-occurrence).
    Hit(schema string, table hook.TableName)
    Miss(schema string, table hook.TableName)
    Set(schema string, table hook.TableName)
    Invalidate(schema string, table hook.TableName)
    Error(schema string, table hook.TableName, op string, err error)
    HydrationStart(schema string, table hook.TableName)
    HydrationComplete(schema string, table hook.TableName, err error)
    CircuitBreakerStateChange(from, to CircuitState)

    // Histogram-style events (duration observed from the start of the backend
    // call to its return — does not include serialization time).
    GetLatency(schema string, table hook.TableName, d time.Duration)
    SetLatency(schema string, table hook.TableName, d time.Duration)
    InvalidateLatency(schema string, table hook.TableName, d time.Duration)
}
```

**Metric descriptions:**

| Method | When Called | Useful For |
|--------|-----------|------------|
| `Hit` | Cache read returns a cached entity | Hit rate monitoring |
| `Miss` | Cache read returns nil (no entry or expired) | Miss rate, cold start detection |
| `Set` | Entity written to cache (after DB read or create) | Write volume |
| `Invalidate` | Cache entry invalidated (mutation, pattern delete, direct call) | Invalidation rate |
| `Error` | Cache backend returns an error (read, write, or invalidate) | Backend health — `op ∈ {"get","set","invalidate","invalidate_many","invalidate_pattern"}` |
| `HydrationStart` | Background hydration goroutine launched | Hydration volume |
| `HydrationComplete` | Background hydration finished (success or failure) | Hydration failure rate |
| `CircuitBreakerStateChange` | Circuit breaker transitions between Closed/Open/HalfOpen | Outage detection (not schema-labeled — breaker is `*Cache`-scoped) |
| `GetLatency` / `SetLatency` / `InvalidateLatency` | Observed backend-call duration | Tail-latency monitoring (histogram / distribution) |

When no `MetricsRecorder` is provided, the cache hook operates with zero metrics overhead — a single nil-check per call path, no counters, no allocations.

`MetricsRecorder` complements the pull-based `StatsReporter` (27.3) — `MetricsRecorder` for event-driven alerting, `StatsReporter` for point-in-time introspection.

#### Registration

```go
c, err := <pkg>.NewCache(backend,
    <pkg>.WithMetricsRecorder(myMetrics), // optional
)
```

#### Consumer-Provided Implementation (Prometheus example)

```go
type promMetrics struct {
    hits   *prometheus.CounterVec
    misses *prometheus.CounterVec
    errors *prometheus.CounterVec
}

// tableLabel strips the schema from the constant's value ("public.products"
// → "products"): the schema has its own label.
func tableLabel(schema string, table hook.TableName) string {
    return strings.TrimPrefix(string(table), schema+".")
}

func (m *promMetrics) Hit(schema string, table hook.TableName)  {
    m.hits.WithLabelValues(schema, tableLabel(schema, table)).Inc()
}
func (m *promMetrics) Miss(schema string, table hook.TableName) {
    m.misses.WithLabelValues(schema, tableLabel(schema, table)).Inc()
}
func (m *promMetrics) Error(schema string, table hook.TableName, op string, err error) {
    m.errors.WithLabelValues(schema, tableLabel(schema, table), op).Inc()
}
// ... implement remaining methods
```

#### Optional OpenTelemetry Package

A ready-made OTel implementation is provided as a separate Go module so the core runtime stays dependency-free:

```
github.com/teandresmith/sqlgen/metrics/otel/   ← imports go.opentelemetry.io/otel (own go.mod)
```

This follows the same isolation pattern as the driver packages (`database/pgx/`, `database/stdlib/`). The consumer imports it only if they use OTel:

```go
import sqlgenotel "github.com/teandresmith/sqlgen/metrics/otel"

c, _ := <pkg>.NewCache(backend,
    <pkg>.WithMetricsRecorder(sqlgenotel.New(nil)), // nil → otel.GetMeterProvider()
)
```

The OTel package emits the following instruments:

| Metric Name | Type | Labels | Unit | Description |
|-------------|------|--------|:----:|-------------|
| `sqlgen.cache.hits` | Counter | `schema`, `table` | — | Cache hits |
| `sqlgen.cache.misses` | Counter | `schema`, `table` | — | Cache misses |
| `sqlgen.cache.sets` | Counter | `schema`, `table` | — | Cache writes |
| `sqlgen.cache.invalidations` | Counter | `schema`, `table` | — | Cache invalidations |
| `sqlgen.cache.errors` | Counter | `schema`, `table`, `op` | — | Cache backend errors |
| `sqlgen.cache.hydrations` | Counter | `schema`, `table`, `status` (`success`/`error`) | — | Background hydrations |
| `sqlgen.cache.circuit_breaker` | Gauge | `state` (`closed`/`open`/`half_open`) | — | Current circuit breaker state |
| `sqlgen.cache.get.duration` | Histogram | `schema`, `table` | seconds | Backend `Get` latency |
| `sqlgen.cache.set.duration` | Histogram | `schema`, `table` | seconds | Backend `Set` latency |
| `sqlgen.cache.invalidate.duration` | Histogram | `schema`, `table` | seconds | Backend `Invalidate*` latency |

**Schema label value.** `"public"` (or the user-configured value) for PostgreSQL; `""` (empty) for MySQL / SQLite. OTel and Prometheus both treat empty-label values as first-class dimensions, so mixed-dialect deployments stay queryable without recording-rule gymnastics. `sqlgen.cache.circuit_breaker` is not schema-labeled because the breaker is `*Cache`-scoped, not per-table.

**Table label value.** The bare SQL name (`"products"`) on every dialect. The recorder receives the `hook.TableName` value, which is schema-qualified on PostgreSQL (`"public.products"`, [5.5](#55-schema-qualification--table-naming) "Schema in Generated Code"), and strips the `schema.` prefix, so a series reads `{schema="public", table="products"}` and the two labels never repeat each other. Same-named tables in two schemas (`public.users`, `audit.users`) stay distinct series through the `schema` label.

All metrics use the `sqlgen.cache` namespace. Consumers who need custom metric names or labels should implement the `MetricsRecorder` interface directly instead of using the OTel package.

---

## 28. Event System

The event system provides a general-purpose publish/subscribe mechanism for mutation lifecycle events. It supports cache invalidation, audit trails, change data capture, real-time notifications, and cross-service communication.

### 28.1 Overview

When a mutation occurs through the generated client, an event is published describing what changed. Subscribers react to these events asynchronously. The event system is:

- **Optional** — disabled by default, zero overhead when unused
- **Transport-agnostic** — pluggable backends (Redis Pub/Sub, NATS, PostgreSQL LISTEN/NOTIFY, Kafka, etc.)
- **Injected via hooks** — the mutation hook publishes events after successful operations
- **Transaction-safe** — events are deferred during transactions and only published on successful commit; discarded on rollback (section 18.5)
- **Decoupled from caching** — events serve multiple purposes, not just cache invalidation

### 28.2 Package Structure

All event types and interfaces live in the `event/` package at the runtime module root, following the same pattern as `database/`:

```
github.com/teandresmith/sqlgen/
├── event/                                 ← Event system types and interfaces
│   └── event.go                           ← Event, Action, Config, Publisher, Subscriber
```

**Module rules:**
- `event/` depends only on the Go standard library (stdlib-only, like `database/`, `sql/`, `comparator/`)
- `event/` is part of the runtime module — imported by generated code
- `event/` MUST NOT import from parser, CLI, or other runtime packages
- Transport implementations (Redis, NATS, Kafka, etc.) are provided by the consumer or third-party packages, not by `event/`

### 28.3 Event Structure

```go
package event

type Event struct {
    ID        string            `json:"id"`                 // unique event ID (UUID v4 or v7 per generation.uuid_version)
    Table     string            `json:"table"`              // bare SQL table name (e.g., "products"); the schema travels in Schema
    Schema    string            `json:"schema"`             // schema name (e.g., "public")
    Action    Action            `json:"action"`             // what happened
    PK        any               `json:"pk"`                 // primary key of the affected entity (simple or composite)
    Input     any               `json:"input"`              // mutation input (*CreateInput, *UpdateInput, filter, etc.)
    Timestamp time.Time         `json:"timestamp"`          // when the mutation occurred
    Metadata  map[string]string `json:"metadata,omitempty"` // context metadata via event.Config.MetadataFunc (28.8); reserved key "tenant" is system-owned (29.6)
}

type Action string

const (
    Create Action = "create"
    Update Action = "update"
    Delete Action = "delete" // soft or hard
    Upsert Action = "upsert"
)
```

**`Table` is the bare SQL name, not the `hook.TableName` value.** On PostgreSQL the constant's value carries the schema (`"public.products"`, [5.5](#55-schema-qualification--table-naming) "Schema in Generated Code"); the event keeps the two in separate fields, so transports that route by them — natsbus subjects are `{prefix}.{schema}.{table}` — do not repeat the schema. A consumer that needs the constant's value rebuilds it from `Schema` and `Table`, as `cache.FromEventSubscriber` does ([27.9](#279-invalidation-strategies)).

**Wire format.** The `Event` struct carries stable `json` tags so the serialized form is
independent of Go field names and survives generator upgrades. Transports that serialize
(natsbus, Redis, Kafka adapters) marshal to these snake_case keys; `Metadata` is omitted when
empty. The `PK` and `Input` fields are `any` — they decode as `map[string]any` on the receiving
side unless the transport's codec is given the concrete Go types (subscribers type-assert per
[section 28.6](#286-event-input)).

**Metadata provenance and reserved keys.** `Metadata` is populated at mutation-hook entry from
two sources, merged per event: (1) the consumer-supplied `event.Config.MetadataFunc(ctx)`
([section 28.8](#288-configuration)) — request-scoped values such as `actor`, `request_id`, or a
W3C `traceparent`; and (2) the system tenant stamp on tenanted tables ([section 29.6](#296-event-metadata)).
The key `"tenant"` is **system-owned**: it is applied last and `MetadataFunc` cannot override it.
All other keys, including `"traceparent"`, belong to the consumer. Because these values live in
the request context — which is not available in the deferred `Tx.OnCommit` callback (it runs on
`context.Background()`; sections 18.5, 27.9) — they are read **synchronously at hook entry**,
before any `OnCommit` registration, never from the publish-time ctx.

### 28.4 Publisher Interface

The publisher interface is intentionally minimal — transports vary widely in their capabilities:

```go
type Publisher interface {
    // Publish sends an event. Implementations may buffer, batch, or send immediately.
    Publish(ctx context.Context, event Event) error

    // PublishBatch sends multiple events. Default implementation calls Publish in a loop.
    PublishBatch(ctx context.Context, events []Event) error

    // Close flushes pending events and releases resources.
    Close() error
}
```

Events are published via a generated mutation hook. The hook fires **after** a successful mutation — failed mutations do not produce events.

**Within a transaction**, events are deferred via `Tx.OnCommit` (section 18.5) and only published on successful commit. If the transaction rolls back, all deferred events are discarded. Outside a transaction, events fire immediately after each mutation.

**Registration:** The user provides a `Publisher` via `WithEventPublisher`. The generated `New()` constructor internally builds per-entity event hooks and prepends them to the mutation hook chain (outermost position — captures final result after all user hooks). The user never calls `WithMutationHook` for events.

```go
client := <pkg>.New(db,
    <pkg>.WithEventPublisher(myRedisPublisher),   // event hooks wired internally
    <pkg>.WithMutationHook(myAuthHook),           // user's own hooks
)
```

**Which mutations produce events:**

| Operation | Event Action | Events |
|-----------|-------------|--------|
| `Create` | `Create` | 1 event per created entity |
| `CreateMany` | `Create` | 1 event per entity in the batch |
| `Update` | `Update` | 1 event per updated entity |
| `UpdateMany` | `Update` | 1 event per entity in the batch |
| `UpdateWhere` | `Update` | 1 event per affected row |
| `Upsert` | `Upsert` | 1 event per upserted entity |
| `SoftDelete` | `Delete` | 1 event per deleted entity |
| `SoftDeleteMany` | `Delete` | 1 event per entity in the batch |
| `SoftDeleteWhere` | `Delete` | 1 event per affected row |
| `HardDelete` | `Delete` | 1 event per deleted entity |
| `HardDeleteMany` | `Delete` | 1 event per entity in the batch |
| `HardDeleteWhere` | `Delete` | 1 event per affected row |
| `Restore` | `Update` | 1 event per restored entity |
| `RestoreMany` | `Update` | 1 event per entity in the batch |
| `RestoreWhere` | `Update` | 1 event per affected row |
| `Increment` | `Update` | 1 event per incremented entity |

**Batch operations** produce multiple events. The generated terminal sets `MutationContext.AffectedPKs` (a `[]any`) with all affected PKs after the mutation completes. The event hook iterates `AffectedPKs` to build one event per entity, then calls `Publisher.PublishBatch`. Transports that support native batching (Redis pipelines, Kafka batch produce) can optimize internally; simple implementations iterate and call `Publish` per event.

Each fanned-out event carries the **per-entity** input (not the full batch slice). For `CreateMany` the per-entity input is the i-th `*Create<Struct>Input`; for `UpdateMany` it is the i-th `Update<Struct>Item`; for `HardDeleteMany` / `SoftDeleteMany` / `RestoreMany` the per-entity input is `nil` because the PK already travels via `Event.PK` and a redundant `[]int64` payload would cost wire bandwidth without adding information. `*Where` ops carry the operation's payload (the `*Filter` for delete/restore-class `*Where`, the `*UpdateInput` for `UpdateWhere`) shared across every fanned-out event — there is no per-row input shape since the same predicate produced all N rows. This shape keeps wire cost O(N) on serialization (vs. O(N²) when every event closes over the full caller slice) and lets subscribers run one type-switch across single-op and batch shapes uniformly.

**PK resolution:** The terminal always populates `MutationContext.AffectedPKs`, even for fire-and-forget operations (empty `FieldOptions`). For Create with `db`-generated PKs, the terminal resolves the ID via `RETURNING` or `LastInsertId` when events are enabled — the caller still receives `nil`, but the PK is captured for event publishing.

**`CallOptions.SkipEvents` interaction:** When the caller passes `SkipEvents: true` via per-call options (Section 9.6), the event hook suppresses publishing for that mutation. No events are collected, deferred, or published — regardless of whether the mutation occurs inside or outside a transaction. This is useful for bulk data imports, internal system operations, or migrations where event noise is undesirable.

### 28.5 Subscriber Interface

Subscribers register handlers for specific tables, actions, or both:

```go
type Subscriber interface {
    // Subscribe registers a handler. Returns a Subscription that can be cancelled.
    Subscribe(opts SubscribeOptions, handler Handler) (Subscription, error)
    Close() error
}

type SubscribeOptions struct {
    Tables  []string // filter by table (empty = all tables)
    Actions []Action // filter by action (empty = all actions)
    Group   string   // consumer group for load balancing (empty = broadcast to all)
}

type Handler func(ctx context.Context, event Event) error

type Subscription interface {
    Unsubscribe() error
}
```

**Consumer group:** When `Group` is set, events are distributed across subscribers in the group (each event processed by exactly one subscriber). When empty, events are broadcast to all subscribers. This maps to Redis Pub/Sub (broadcast) vs Redis Streams consumer groups (distributed), or NATS queue groups.

**Handler error semantics:** A `Handler` that returns a non-nil error signals "redeliver me." The signal is honored by transports that support redelivery (durable/at-least-once backends — e.g. NATS JetStream, Redis Streams, Kafka): the message is negatively acknowledged and retried per the transport's policy, routing to a dead-letter destination after the configured maximum delivery attempts. Transports that cannot redeliver (at-most-once backends — the in-memory bus, core NATS) instead route the error to their configured error handler (where one is offered) rather than retrying; the event is not redelivered. Handlers should therefore be idempotent under at-least-once transports, and error returns are always observable — never silently discarded.

### 28.6 Event Input

Every event carries the **per-entity** mutation input. For single-op mutations (`Create` / `Update` / `Upsert` / `Increment`), `Event.Input` is the same pointer the caller passed to the mutation (`Increment` passes its input by value) — **except** on tables that declare a `write_only` / `internal` column (§32), where the event hook publishes a redacted clone of the same concrete type with those columns blanked; for `Increment` on a redacted target column, the delta (`Amount`) is blanked while the column selector is preserved (subscribers' type-switch is unaffected; only the sensitive values are cleared). Tables with no redacted column are byte-unchanged. See [32.3](#323-per-surface-behavior). For batch mutations (`CreateMany` / `UpdateMany`), `Event.Input` is the i-th element of the caller's input slice — typed as the same per-entity shape the single-op variant uses, so subscribers can run one type-switch across both shapes. `UpsertMany` follows the same per-entity rule with one difference: the slice it indexes is the **deduped** one its terminal publishes, not the caller's, because that is the slice index-aligned with `AffectedPKs` ([28.9](#289-generated-event-hook-architecture)). For ops without a per-entity input shape (`HardDelete` / `SoftDelete` / `Restore` and their `*Many` variants), `Event.Input` is `nil` — the PK already travels via `Event.PK`. For `*Where` ops, `Event.Input` is the operation's shared payload — `*Filter` for delete/restore-class `*Where`, `*UpdateInput` for `UpdateWhere` — applied across every fanned-out event; the `*Filter` is itself a redacted clone when the table's filter can carry a redacted column ([32.3](#323-per-surface-behavior)).

```go
type Event struct {
    // ...
    Input any // per-entity mutation input — see "shape table" below
    // ...
}
```

| Op | `Event.Input` shape |
|---|---|
| `Create` | `*Create<Struct>Input` |
| `CreateMany` | `*Create<Struct>Input` (i-th element of `[]*Create<Struct>Input`) |
| `Update` | `*Update<Struct>Input` |
| `UpdateMany` | `Update<Struct>Item` (i-th element of `[]Update<Struct>Item`) |
| `Upsert` | `*Create<Struct>Input` |
| `UpsertMany` | `*Create<Struct>Input` (i-th element of the **deduped** `[]*Create<Struct>Input`, not the caller's slice — see [28.9](#289-generated-event-hook-architecture)) |
| `Increment` | `IncrementInput[<Struct>IncrementColumn]` (by value) |
| `HardDelete` / `SoftDelete` / `Restore` (single + `*Many`) | `nil` (PK on `Event.PK`) |
| `UpdateWhere` | `*Update<Struct>Input` (shared across N events) |
| `HardDeleteWhere` / `SoftDeleteWhere` / `RestoreWhere` | `*<Struct>Filter` (shared across N events; redacted clone on a redacted table) |

The `Input` field is typed `any` in the `Event` struct. Subscribers type-assert to the concrete input type for their table — the per-entity shape means one case arm covers both the single-op and batch variants:

```go
eventSub.Subscribe(event.SubscribeOptions{
    Tables: []string{"products"},
}, func(ctx context.Context, e event.Event) error {
    switch input := e.Input.(type) {
    case *CreateProductInput:
        // Matches Create AND CreateMany (one type-switch arm covers both).
        log.Printf("product created: %s", input.Name)
    case *UpdateProductInput:
        // Matches Update AND UpdateWhere — only set fields are present (omittable).
        if v, ok := input.Price.Get(); ok {
            log.Printf("product price changed to %v", v)
        }
    case UpdateProductItem:
        // Matches UpdateMany — pairs the per-row PK with the per-row UpdateInput.
        if v, ok := input.Input.Price.Get(); ok {
            log.Printf("product price changed to %v", v)
        }
    case nil:
        // HardDelete / SoftDelete / Restore (single + *Many) — PK is on e.PK.
        log.Printf("product %v deleted", e.PK)
    }
    return nil
})
```

**No payload serialization is needed.** The event carries the typed input directly. The `Publisher` implementation serializes it when sending to transport (JSON, msgpack, etc.) as part of normal event serialization.

**Pre-mutation and post-mutation entity state are not provided.** Consumers who need the full entity can use `FieldOptions` to control what the mutation returns, or fetch the entity in their own hooks. Consumers who need before/after diffs for audit trails should capture old state in their own mutation hook.

**No-PK tables emit no events.** Tables that have no primary key (and no `tables.<name>.primary_key.columns` override — see [§8.6](#86-primary-key-strategy)) are skipped from generation entirely (see [§9.4b](#94b-no-pk-tables-are-skipped)). No client exists to mutate the table, so no event is ever published for it. Use `primary_key.columns` to opt the table back in, after which the standard event behavior in this section applies.

### 28.7 Transport Implementations

Custom transport implementations are implemented by the consumer or third-party packages against the `Publisher` and `Subscriber` interfaces. Two reference implementations are provided: an in-memory bus (for testing and local development) and a NATS transport.

**Common transport implementations:**

| Transport | Delivery | Ordering | Persistence | Use Case |
|-----------|----------|----------|:-----------:|----------|
| In-memory (provided) | At-most-once | Per-topic | No | Testing, local development, single-process apps |
| NATS core (provided) | At-most-once | Per-subject | No | High throughput, low latency — `natsbus.New(conn)` |
| NATS JetStream (provided) | At-least-once | Per-stream | Yes | Durable streaming, redelivery/DLQ/replay — opt-in via `natsbus.New(conn, natsbus.WithJetStream(...))` ([28.7.1](#2871-provided-implementations)) |
| Redis Pub/Sub | At-most-once | Per-channel | No | Simple invalidation, real-time notifications |
| Redis Streams | At-least-once | Per-stream | Yes | Reliable event processing with consumer groups |
| PostgreSQL LISTEN/NOTIFY | At-most-once | Per-channel | No | No extra infrastructure needed |
| Kafka | At-least-once | Per-partition | Yes | High-volume change data capture |

#### 28.7.1 Provided Implementations

Two reference implementations are shipped with the project. The module rule is: **stdlib-only implementations live in the runtime module as sub-packages; implementations with external dependencies are separate Go modules** with their own `go.mod`.

```
event/
├── event.go                 ← interfaces (Publisher, Subscriber, etc.)
├── memorybus/
│   └── memorybus.go         ← in-memory implementation (stdlib-only, part of runtime module)
└── natsbus/
    ├── go.mod               ← separate module: github.com/teandresmith/sqlgen/event/natsbus
    ├── go.sum
    └── natsbus.go           ← NATS implementation (depends on github.com/nats-io/nats.go)
```

**In-memory bus (`event/memorybus/`):**

- Stdlib-only — part of the runtime module, no extra `go.mod`
- Synchronous dispatch within a single process
- Supports `Subscribe` with table/action filtering and consumer groups
- Thread-safe via `sync.RWMutex`
- Primary use case: unit/integration tests and single-process applications
- Not suitable for multi-process or distributed deployments

```go
bus := memorybus.New()
client := New(db, WithEventPublisher(bus))

// Subscribe in tests
sub, _ := bus.Subscribe(event.SubscribeOptions{
    Tables: []string{"products"},
}, func(ctx context.Context, e event.Event) error {
    // assert on event
    return nil
})
defer sub.Unsubscribe()
```

**NATS transport (`event/natsbus/`):**

- Separate Go module (`github.com/teandresmith/sqlgen/event/natsbus`) — depends on `github.com/nats-io/nats.go`
- Implements both `Publisher` and `Subscriber`
- Subject pattern: `{prefix}.{schema}.{table}` (configurable prefix, default `sqlgen.events`)
- Consumer groups map to NATS queue groups

The bus has two modes. **Core mode is the default and is unchanged**: `natsbus.New(conn)`
publishes fire-and-forget over core NATS (at-most-once, no persistence). All richer behavior is
**opt-in** through option funcs; adding an option never changes the zero-config path.

```go
nc, _ := nats.Connect(nats.DefaultURL)
bus := natsbus.New(nc)                       // core mode — at-most-once, identical to a plain publish
client := New(db, WithEventPublisher(bus))
```

**JetStream mode (opt-in, durable).** `WithJetStream(StreamConfig)` publishes to a persisted
JetStream stream and makes subscribers durable consumers with explicit acknowledgement:

```go
bus := natsbus.New(nc, natsbus.WithJetStream(natsbus.StreamConfig{
    Name:        "SQLGEN_EVENTS",
    MaxAge:      30 * 24 * time.Hour,
    DedupWindow: 2 * time.Minute,            // broker-side dedup keyed on the Nats-Msg-Id header
}))
```

- **At-least-once delivery.** Durable consumers are created via the concrete
  `bus.SubscribeWith(opts, handler, ...SubscribeOption)`. A `Handler` returning `nil` acks the
  message; a non-nil error naks it for redelivery with backoff (the
  [section 28.5](#285-subscriber-interface) Handler-error contract). After the consumer's maximum
  delivery attempts the message routes to a dead-letter subject. The plain `Subscribe` remains a
  core real-time tap (at-most-once) even in JetStream mode.
- **Idempotency.** Each message sets the JetStream `Nats-Msg-Id` header to `Event.ID`, so the
  broker's dedup window collapses duplicate publishes without any consumer-side bookkeeping.
- **Replay / backfill.** A newly added durable consumer can rebuild its projection from stream
  history via `DeliverAll`, a start time, or a start sequence.
- **Consumer knobs are natsbus-local.** Durable name, max-deliver, dead-letter subject, and
  delivery start policy are supplied as natsbus subscribe options — they are **not** added to
  `event.SubscribeOptions` (which stays the stdlib-only, transport-agnostic filter type). Because
  a variadic parameter would change the method signature and break `event.Subscriber` satisfaction,
  the knobs ride a **separate concrete method** `*natsbus.Bus.SubscribeWith(opts, handler,
  ...SubscribeOption)`; the interface method `Subscribe(opts, handler)` is frozen, so code that
  holds the value as an `event.Subscriber` gets core-filter semantics unchanged.

**Trace-context propagation (opt-in).** `Event.Metadata["traceparent"]` — populated by the
consumer's `event.Config.MetadataFunc` ([section 28.8](#288-configuration)) — is lifted to a NATS
header on publish. On the subscribe side, `WithContextPropagation` reads that header and hands
the `Handler` a ctx that **continues the producing request's span** instead of a context-less
`context.Background()`. The option takes a small natsbus-local propagator adapter (Inject/Extract
over `nats.Header`), so the natsbus module does not take a hard OpenTelemetry dependency; `event/`
never imports a propagator (it is stdlib-only, section 28.2).

**Wire headers.** natsbus carries `Nats-Msg-Id` (dedup), `traceparent` (tracing), and
`Sqlgen-Envelope-Version` (schema-version) as NATS **headers**, out of band from the JSON
envelope. Unknown headers are ignored by older consumers, so header additions are backward
compatible. Any change to the subject scheme or body encoding bumps `Sqlgen-Envelope-Version`.

**Additional opt-in options:**

- `natsbus.Connect(url, ...ConnectOption)` — a blessed constructor that dials with
  production-sane defaults (infinite reconnect, a reconnect buffer so publishes during a blip are
  not lost, drain-on-close, disconnect/reconnect callbacks), returning a bus ready to pair with
  `WithJetStream`. `New(conn)` remains for callers who own their `*nats.Conn`.
- `natsbus.WithSubscribeErrorHandler(func(ctx, event.Event, error))` — invoked when a `Handler`
  returns an error on an at-most-once (core) subscription, so failures are observable instead of
  discarded. `WithRetry(n, backoff)` adds bounded in-process retry before the error handler on
  core mode.
- `natsbus.WithActionSubjects()` — publishes to `{prefix}.{schema}.{table}.{action}` so a
  consumer can let the broker filter by action (e.g. subscribe to `...tasks.create`). This
  changes the subject scheme, so it is opt-in and bumps the envelope version.
- `natsbus.WithCodec(codec)` — replaces the default JSON encoding for the event body (e.g.
  protobuf, msgpack) where a non-JSON wire format is required.

### 28.8 Configuration

**YAML config (`sqlgen.yml`):**

```yaml
events:
  enabled: true
```

**EventConfig (YAML):**

| Field | Type | Default | Description |
|-------|------|---------|-------------|
| `enabled` | `bool` | `false` | Enable event publishing. |

**Per-table event overrides:**

```yaml
tables:
  audit_logs:
    events:
      enabled: false                # don't publish events for audit log writes (avoid recursion)
```

**Runtime config (`event.Config`):**

Provided at client construction via `WithEventPublisher`:

```go
client := New(db,
    WithEventPublisher(publisher, func(c *event.Config) {
        c.OnError = func(ctx context.Context, events []event.Event, err error) {
            metrics.EventPublishFailures.Inc()
            logger.Error("event publish failed", "err", err, "count", len(events))
        }
        c.MetadataFunc = func(ctx context.Context) map[string]string {
            return map[string]string{
                "actor":      auth.ActorFrom(ctx),
                "request_id": middleware.RequestIDFrom(ctx),
            }
        }
    }),
)
```

| Field | Type | Default | Description |
|-------|------|---------|-------------|
| `OnError` | `func(ctx, []Event, error)` | `log.Printf` to stderr | Called when `PublishBatch` fails. Mutation always succeeds — publish failure is never propagated to the caller. |
| `MetadataFunc` | `func(ctx) map[string]string` | `nil` (no metadata added) | Called once per mutation-hook entry to derive context metadata (e.g. `actor`, `request_id`, `traceparent`) merged into every resulting `Event.Metadata`. See below. |

**`MetadataFunc` timing and merge.** `MetadataFunc` is invoked **once at mutation-hook entry**,
where the request context is still live — the same point the tenant stamp is read
([section 29.6](#296-event-metadata)) — and **never** from the deferred `Tx.OnCommit` callback,
which runs on `context.Background()` (sections 18.5, 27.9). Its returned map is **shallow-cloned
into each fanned-out event** so per-row system stamps do not bleed across a batch. The system key
`"tenant"` is applied **after** the user map and cannot be overridden; every other key, including
`"traceparent"`, is the consumer's. When `MetadataFunc` is `nil` the event `Metadata` is
unchanged from prior behavior (only the tenant stamp appears, and only on tenanted tables), so
generated output for non-users is byte-identical.

**Event ID generation:** Event IDs are UUID strings, controlled by the `generation.uuid_version` config (`v4` or `v7`) and resolved at generation time — no runtime config needed. The generated event hook uses **the package's selected UUID integration** ([7.4](#74-built-in-type-integrations)), emitting that integration's string-form generation call from the table in [7.4](#74-built-in-type-integrations) "Generating UUID values" — `uuid.NewV4().String()` for the standard library, `uuid.NewString()` for `github.com/google/uuid`, `uuid.Must(uuid.NewV4()).String()` for `github.com/gofrs/uuid/v5`, and each library's v7 spelling under `uuid_version: v7`. The event-hooks file imports that one library and no other, so a package stays within the one-UUID-library-per-generated-package rule ([7.4](#74-built-in-type-integrations)) whatever its columns resolve to. A package with no `uuid` column selects no integration and falls back to the standard library, so enabling events adds no module dependency.

### 28.9 Generated Event Hook Architecture

The event hook is **generated code** in the user's package (`event_hooks_gen.go`), not a generic runtime function. This allows type-safe access to entity clients, PK types, and serialization.

**Generated files (when `events.enabled: true`):**

```
user's package/
├── models_gen.go
├── client_gen.go
├── event_hooks_gen.go   ← per-entity event hooks, buildEventHooks(), config types
```

**Hook registration:** `WithEventPublisher` is the only API the user calls. The generated `New()` constructor builds per-entity event hooks scoped via `hook.ForTable` and prepends them to the mutation hook chain (outermost position):

```go
func New(querier database.Querier, opts ...ClientOption) *Client {
    // ... resolve options ...
    if options.eventPublisher != nil {
        eventHooks := buildEventHooks(options.eventPublisher, options.eventConfig)
        options.mutationHooks = append(eventHooks, options.mutationHooks...)
    }
    // ... construct entity clients with combined hooks ...
}
```

**Per-entity hook pattern:**

```go
func newProductEventHook(publisher event.Publisher, config event.Config) hook.MutationHook {
    return func(next hook.MutationHandler) hook.MutationHandler {
        return func(ctx context.Context, mc *hook.MutationContext) (any, error) {
            // Execute the mutation (and all inner hooks)
            result, err := next(ctx, mc)
            if err != nil {
                return result, err
            }

            // Check SkipEvents via CallOptions
            // ...

            // Build events from mc.AffectedPKs (always populated by terminal)
            events := make([]event.Event, len(mc.AffectedPKs))
            for i, pk := range mc.AffectedPKs {
                events[i] = event.Event{
                    ID:        uuid.New().String(), // or uuid.Must(uuid.NewV7()).String() per uuid_version
                    Table:     "products", // bare SQL name; the schema travels in Schema (28.3)
                    Schema:    mc.Schema,
                    Action:    mapOpToAction(mc.Op),
                    PK:        pk,
                    Input:     mc.Input,
                    Timestamp: time.Now(),
                }
            }

            // Transaction-aware publishing
            publish := func(ctx context.Context) error {
                if err := publisher.PublishBatch(ctx, events); err != nil {
                    config.OnError(ctx, events, err)
                }
                return nil
            }

            if tx := database.FromContext(ctx); tx != nil {
                tx.OnCommit(publish)
            } else {
                publish(ctx)
            }

            return result, nil
        }
    }
}
```

**Resulting hook chain:**

```
[panic recovery]
  → productEventHook (generated, outermost — only fires for products table)
  → orderEventHook   (generated — only fires for orders table)
    → userAuthHook    (user's hook)
      → terminal (DB mutation — sets mc.AffectedPKs)
```

**Nested mutations publish through their inner calls, not on their own behalf.** The three `…WithRelated` methods have no `hook.MutationOp` ([21.2](#212-hook-types)), so no event hook fires for the wrapper: each inner `Create` / `CreateMany` / `UpdateWhere` / `UpsertMany` / `HardDeleteMany` publishes its own events under its own op and table, in the execution order of [9.9.6](#996-execution-order) — parent first, then per edge in byte order of the relationship's Go field name. Because those events are registered as `OnCommit` callbacks, they flush FIFO after the **root** transaction commits, not when the nested method returns; and when a nested mutation runs at savepoint depth and that savepoint rolls back, its callbacks are discarded rather than promoted ([18.6](#186-deferred-side-effects)), so a rolled-back nested write publishes nothing at all.

`OpUpsertMany` maps to the existing `event.Upsert` action rather than a new one, so a subscriber filtering on `event.Upsert` receives batched upserts without changing its filter. Its redaction arm ([32.3](#323-per-surface-behavior)) must be **per row**: `UpsertMany` sets `mc.Input` to a slice, so an arm that passed the input through unchanged would give every fanned-out event the entire batch, un-redacted. The slice it publishes is the **deduped** one, not the caller's — the dedupe ([9.5 Batch upsert](#batch-upsert--dedupe-return-shape-and-key-resolution)) removes rows the write never carried, and the published slice is what stays index-aligned with `AffectedPKs`, which is what a per-row fanout indexes.

### 28.10 Use Cases

#### Cache Invalidation

Events power cache invalidation (section 27.9). The cache subscribes to mutation events via `cache.FromEventSubscriber(eventSub)` passed to `NewCache`. Each event produces one synchronous `InvalidationHandler` call that routes through the same internal helpers as direct `Cache.Invalidate*` calls.

### 28.11 Cache Invalidation via Events

The cache system (section 27) can receive invalidation signals from any event source through the `InvalidationSource` interface (section 27.9). The sqlgen event system is **one possible source**, not the only one:

```
sqlgen Event System (single publisher)
    │
    ├── Cache (via FromEventSubscriber adapter)  → cache.Delete(key)
    ├── Audit subscriber                         → write audit log
    ├── Notification subscriber                  → send alert
    └── CDC subscriber                           → stream to Kafka

External Event System (Kafka CDC, webhooks, pg LISTEN/NOTIFY, etc.)
    │
    └── Cache (via custom InvalidationSource)    → cache.Delete(key)

Direct Programmatic Call
    │
    └── cacheHooks.Invalidate(ctx, table, pk)    → cache.Delete(key)
```

The cache does not define its own `Publisher` or event types. When using sqlgen's event system, the `cache.FromEventSubscriber` adapter translates `event.Event` into `InvalidationSignal` values (section 27.9) — including the row's tenant stamp from `Event.Metadata["tenant"]` (29.6). When using external systems, users implement `InvalidationSource` to feed signals from any source. For ad-hoc scenarios, `Invalidate`/`InvalidateMany`/`InvalidateTable` are called directly.

**Tenanted tables invalidate precisely cross-instance.** The receiving `Cache` routes a tenanted-table signal through the same per-PK row-derived path local invalidation uses: it rebuilds each exact `…:tenant:{X}:…:pk:{id}` key from the signal's tenant string (byte-identical to the local key via the 29.5 `%v` round-trip) and its **own** codegen-constant fingerprint — under a rolling deploy each instance only ever evicts keys it itself wrote, so mixed fingerprints across instances are safe. Tenant-in-PK tables are precise even without a stamp (each signal PK carries its tenant). A tenant-less signal for other tenanted tables degrades to the observable full-table clear rather than erroring — a hard error would only make ACK-capable transports redeliver a signal that can never succeed.

This means:
- **Source-agnostic** — cache invalidation is not coupled to sqlgen's event system
- **Multiple invalidation sources compose** — an `InvalidationSource` for cross-instance consistency + direct `Invalidate` calls for ad-hoc needs
- **Cache is optional** — if caching is disabled, the event system still works for audit/CDC/notifications
- **Events are optional** — if events are disabled, caching falls back to TTL-only mode with local mutation hook invalidation (section 27.9)
- **Custom topic mapping** — external event systems can map arbitrary topics/channels to table entities via their `InvalidationSource` implementation

---

## 29. Tenancy

SQLGen's tenancy primitive handles **mandatory tenant scoping** at the SQL layer — every generated read and mutation on a tenanted table is structurally incapable of crossing tenant boundaries. It does NOT try to be a policy/authorization engine; fine-grained "can user X read resource Y" logic belongs in a policy tool (Cerbos, OPA, custom middleware) layered on top. Tenancy composes with soft delete (section 17), caching (section 27), and events (section 28) — no feature requires re-coordination when tenancy is enabled.

### 29.1 Overview

Shared-schema multi-tenancy means every tenanted table carries a tenant-scoping column (`tenant_id`, `workspace_id`, `org_id`, etc.), and every query must filter by the current tenant. The failure mode is well-known: a developer forgets the filter once, and the query silently returns cross-tenant data.

SQLGen treats this as the same class of problem as soft delete (section 17): a column-driven behavior that, once declared, auto-applies to every generated operation unless explicitly opted out of. The primitive is small:

- **One config block** declaring the tenant column globally (29.2).
- **Per-table override** for tables that opt out or use a different column (29.2).
- **One runtime injection point** — `TenantResolver` pulls the active tenant from `context.Context` (29.3).
- **Auto-injected at codegen** — every generated `Get*` / `*Where` / `Update*` / `*Delete*` / `Create*` gets the tenant filter on the WHERE side and the tenant value on the INSERT side without additional per-method config.
- **One escape hatch** — `CallOptions.SkipTenancy` for reporting, admin, and cross-tenant maintenance (section 9.6).

**Scope: flat / single-level tenancy.** One tenant column per table, one resolved tenant per request, one filter per query. Hierarchical tenancy — nested org → workspace → project, group membership, multi-level resolvers — is out of scope; see [29.11](#2911-constraints).

Design parallels to internalize:

| Parallel | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| **Soft delete** (section 17) | Same column-driven auto-injection pattern: tenancy adds its predicate to every query for the same reason, and at the same point, that soft delete adds `deleted_at IS NULL`. |
| **Type overrides** (section 7.5) | Tenant-column type config reuses the `TypeOverride` shape. Most of the time no config is needed — the parser already resolves the column's Go type. |
| **CallOptions.SkipCache / SkipHooks** (section 9.6) | Escape-hatch pattern is the same. `SkipTenancy` joins the family; it is orthogonal to `SkipHooks` because tenancy runs in the SQL builders, not as a hook. |

### 29.2 Configuration

#### 29.2.1 Global `tenancy:` block

```yaml
tenancy:
  enabled: true
  column: workspace_id           # default column name checked against every table and view
  required: true                 # missing tenant in ctx → error (fail-closed)
  type:                          # optional — derived from schema unless overridden
    type: uuid.UUID
    import: github.com/google/uuid
```

| Field | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `enabled` | `bool` | `false` | Global switch. When `false`, no tenancy codegen runs regardless of column presence. |
| `column` | `string` | `""` (required when `enabled: true`) | Column name checked against every table **and view** during detection (29.2.3). Common values: `tenant_id`, `workspace_id`, `org_id`. |
| `required` | `bool` | `true` | When `true`, a missing/zero tenant from `TenantResolver` is a hard error returned from every tenanted op (reads and writes). When `false`, missing tenant skips the filter — effectively becomes a cross-tenant query. `false` is almost always wrong; only flip it if the app has a verified reason. |
| `type` | `TypeOverride` (same shape as section 4.7) | auto-detected | Go type + import for the tenant column. See 29.2.4 for resolution rules. |

**Why `required: true` is the default.** Missing-tenant silently skipping the filter would recreate the exact footgun tenancy is meant to prevent. Opting in to the risk is explicit.

#### 29.2.2 Per-table override

```yaml
tables:
  audit_logs:
    tenancy:
      enabled: false             # opt-out — table is global, not tenant-scoped

  legacy_widgets:
    tenancy:
      column: org_id             # table uses a different column name

  documents:
    tenancy:
      required: false            # this table allows cross-tenant reads (rare, explicit)
```

`TableTenancyConfig` (tri-state pointers — `nil` means inherit global):

| Field | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `enabled` | `*bool` | Per-table opt-in/out. Overrides global. A table with `enabled: false` has no tenant filter regardless of whether the column exists. |
| `column` | `*string` | Per-table column name override. Useful for legacy schemas that predate a standardized column name. |
| `required` | `*bool` | Per-table override of the fail-closed rule. |
| `type` | `*TypeOverride` | Per-table type override. Rarely needed. |

**Precedence:** per-table override → global → detection. A `nil` pointer inherits the next level down.

**Views use the same block under `views.<name>.tenancy`** with identical field shapes and precedence — see [29.2.5](#2925-view-tenancy) for the two places view semantics deliberately differ (nullability handling, and the absence of any write path).

#### 29.2.3 Detection

When `tenancy.enabled: true`, the generator runs a detection pass during schema resolution. It covers **every generated entity — tables and views alike**:

1. For each table **or view**, look for a column matching `effective_column` (per-entity override or global `tenancy.column`).
2. If the column exists → the entity is **tenanted**.
3. If the column does not exist → the entity is **shared** (no filter injected).
4. If the entity has `tenancy.enabled: false` (`tables.<name>` / `views.<name>`) → force **shared**, even if the column exists (explicit opt-out wins).
5. If the entity has `tenancy.enabled: true` but the column does not exist → **hard codegen error** naming the entity and the expected column name.

Detection-based inclusion mirrors soft delete (section 17). A schema with 50 tables doesn't need 50 config entries; only the opt-outs and oddities do.

**Views are not exempt.** A view that carries the tenant column is tenanted under the same five rules — the read path is scoped exactly as a table's is. Applying detection to tables only would leave every tenant-shaped view reading across tenants while the tables beside it were scoped, which is the failure mode tenancy exists to prevent. Views are read-only, so rules 1–5 are the whole story for them; there is no mutation half. See [29.2.5](#2925-view-tenancy).

#### 29.2.4 Type Resolution

The tenant column's Go type is resolved in this order (first wins):

1. **Per-table `tenancy.type` override** (YAML).
2. **Global `tenancy.type`** (YAML).
